Week 3 · Lecture


Learning from labels:
classifiers, neural networks
& embeddings


  
    Dr. Philipp K. Masur
    Computational Analysis of Digital Communication · Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

title: CADC
section: A machine that learns by doing
text:
A machine that learns by doing

  


Seven clicks, and the training is real: a small network is fitted to the twenty reviews in the browser when the page loads, seeded so the run is the same every time. The ‹ › beside the step counter, or the arrow keys once you have clicked into it, go back and forth; at either end the keys move on through the deck.
The opening screen is a neuron, alive: signals arrive along the dendrites, the cell body glows as they are summed, and a pulse fires down the axon. Click 1: the 1943 unit laid over it: inputs on the dendrites, a weight on each, a sum in the cell body, a threshold f on the axon. Same shape, and that is the whole content of the metaphor. Say so now, so nobody leaves thinking the machine thinks.
Click 2: the cell unfolds into a network (fifteen words in, four hidden units, one output) with twenty short reviews and their human labels. The weights are random. Click 3: its verdicts. Ten of twenty wrong, each marked red, Not good at all among them.
Click 4: train. The edges change, the loss falls, and the red bands go one by one. Watch Boring.: right at the start, then wrong from epoch 40, because what fixed other reviews broke it. At epoch 53 two are still wrong, Boring. and Not boring at all. Click 5: twelve more epochs, and it learns those two; all twenty are right at epoch 65. Click 6: one hidden unit turns red for Not good at all and blue for Not boring at all. The two reviews differ only in good and boring, and this unit is where the network tells them apart. Click 7: the question of the lecture. It has seen these twenty 65 times and gets every one. Would it get the next twenty?
Do not explain the training here; Part IV takes this network apart. The point now is only that nobody wrote a word list.

title: CADC
text:
The Navy revealed the embryo of an electronic computer today that it expects will be able to walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself and be conscious of its existence. […] Later perceptrons will be able to recognize people and call out their names and instantly translate speech in one language to speech and writing in another language, it was predicted.
The New York Times, 8 July 1958, on Frank Rosenblatt’s perceptron


Sixty-eight years later, the last sentence is true and the first is not. This lecture is about what the machine in between actually does.


New Navy device learns by doing: Psychologist shows embryo of computer designed to read and grow wiser. (1958, July 8). The New York Times, p. 25.


Rosenblatt’s perceptron was the network you just watched, minus the hidden layer. The press conference was at the Office of Naval Research; the machine that “learned by doing” was an IBM 704 simulating twenty neurons. The claims are worth reading slowly: the room will recognise them from 2023. The method’s history is a history of this sentence being made, withdrawn in 1969 when Minsky and Papert showed what a perceptron cannot learn, and made again in 1986, 2012 and 2022.

title: CADC
text:
Last week ended here

A dictionary is a vector of weights over the columns of the document–term matrix (+1, −1, 0), declared by you before the machine sees a text
Against a hand-coded gold standard, no dictionary reached α = .35; the classifiers in the same paper reached .39 to .50, the humans .75 and up
The list was not wrong about the words. It was wrong about the texts, and not good is the reason
This week the weights are learned from labelled texts, and the result is scored against human coding exactly as the word list was


Same matrix, same validation. What changes is who writes the weights.

title: CADC
text:
This lecture

  
    I
    Learning from labels
    Inductive instead of deductive; the pipeline; what a model is for
  
  
    II
    Train, test, overfit
    Why a model that fits perfectly is the one to distrust
  
  
    III
    A classifier, end to end
    One tidymodels workflow from split to F1, then swap the algorithm
  
  
    IV
    Neural networks
    The unit, the hidden layer, and how the weights are found
  
  
    V
    Word embeddings
    Words as vectors; a representation the model did not have to learn
  
  
    VI
    Weeks 1 to 3 in one table
    Where every method so far lands against the same gold standard
  


Thirty seconds. Part III is the long one, and there is no break. Part VI is one table and the week’s plan.

title: CADC
text:
Deductive and inductive

A dictionary is deductive: the rule comes first (happy means positive), and the texts are read through it
It is also deterministic: the same words produce the same score, however they are arranged
A human coder does something else: reads the whole sentence, weighs the words against each other, decides in context
Inductive approaches start from the coder’s decisions and let the machine work out which features of a text predict them
The promise: the scalability of the dictionary with the validity of the coder (never quite kept, as Part VI shows)


Deductive: the researcher supplies the rules. Inductive: the researcher supplies examples, and the rules are inferred.

Topic models are not taught this year; the column stays because students meet them in papers and should be able to place them. The reading for the projects covers them.

title: CADC
text:
The pipeline with a classifier

  


Same row as weeks 1 and 2, pixel for pixel. What is new is under the row: the method needs an input it did not need before (texts you coded yourself), and that input is split before anyone looks at it. The split reaches across to step 04 on purpose: the test set is the hand-coded subset the validation loop compares against. The algorithm oval sits where last week’s word list sat.
Two things to point at. The hand-coded sample is coded once and used twice, for training and for testing, which is why it is split. And labelling the rest is conditional: a model that fails step 04 does not get to label anything.

title: CADC
text:
A worked case



de León, Vermeer and Trilling (2023): how do elections change what Mexican news outlets publish and what readers share on Facebook?
83,054 articles, far too many to code by hand. 2,000 were coded into six topics, and a support vector machine was trained on 80% of them and tested on the rest
With precision and recall above .75 on every topic, it labelled the full sample













Two thousand coded, eighty-one thousand classified. The ratio is the method’s whole appeal, and the test on held-out articles is what makes it defensible.


de León, E., Vermeer, S., & Trilling, D. (2023). Electoral news sharing: A study of changes in news coverage and Facebook sharing behaviour during the 2018 Mexican elections. Information, Communication & Society, 26(6), 1193–1209. https://doi.org/10.1080/1369118X.2021.1994629 Figure drawn from their Table 1.


Walk along the pipeline: the hand-coded sample, the split, the classifier, the test, and only then the labels for everyone else. They compared 18 classifiers on the held-out articles, three kinds of preprocessing with six algorithms, and an SVM on the full text came first. The two coders agreed at α = .79.
Then the figure, which is the reason for doing all this. During the campaign, outlets shift a little, from 32% to 37% of their articles. Readers shift a lot, from 34% to 55% of their shares, and every other topic but sports loses share. That is the news gap closing, and it is only visible because 81,000 articles had a label. The comparison is a routine period a year later (March to July 2019), not the time before the election.

title: CADC
text:
Statistical modelling: learn f


set.seed(311)
data <- tibble(x = rnorm(50, 3.5, 1.2),
               y = 4 + 2 * x + rnorm(50, 0, 2))

fit <- lm(y ~ x, data = data)
coef(fit)

Output



(Intercept)           x 
   4.042616    1.909887 



Fifty observations, one predictor, one outcome: the model is a line, y = a + b·x
Fitting finds the a and b that make the line pass closest to the points
The regression reading: at x = 0 the line is at 4.0, and one unit more x gives 1.9 units more y

title: CADC
section: Prediction: use f on an x you never saw
text:
Prediction: use f on an x you never saw


new <- tibble(x = c(-1, 5))

predict(fit, newdata = new)

Output



        1         2 
 2.132729 13.592050 



No observation has x = −1 or x = 5, but a y is returned for each anyway
Machine learning is this second use, taken seriously: fit on what you have, predict what you do not
The line stays the same; you ask it a different question

title: CADC
text:
Two vocabularies for one thing



Machine learning says
Statistics says




feature
independent variable, predictor


label
dependent variable, outcome


labelled data set
a data set with both


to train a model
to estimate, to fit


classifier
a model for a nominal outcome


to annotate
to code, by hand


training and test set
the sample, and the data you never have




The last row is the real difference: statistics rarely holds data back to check its own predictions. Machine learning always does.


van Atteveldt, W., Trilling, D., & Arcíla Calderón, C. (2022). Computational analysis of communication. Wiley. Chapter 8.

title: CADC
section: Two goals, and what each gives up
text:
Two goals, and what each gives up



Explaining


Explaining is what statistics is about
Does X relate to Y, in the population?
Few predictors, so each coefficient can be read and defended
The parameters are the result



Predicting


Predicting is what text classification and machine learning are about
How well can Y be guessed from what we have?
Thousands of predictors, most of them collinear; nobody reports them
The predictions are the result; the parameters are a means



In this course the classifier’s output becomes a variable in a study. Its job is to predict; the explaining happens afterwards, with the variable it produced.

title: CADC
text:
Fifteen points


set.seed(42)
sim <- tibble(x = runif(15, 1, 7),
              y = x^3 + rnorm(15, 0, 10))

ggplot(sim, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point()

Simulated, so the truth is known: y is x cubed plus noise
The next three slides fit three models to these fifteen points and ask which one to trust
The Playground’s How much freedom is too much is this simulation with a slider












PLAYGROUNDHow much freedom is too much

title: CADC
text:
A line: too little freedom


ggplot(sim, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm",
              formula = y ~ x)

Two parameters. The line misses the curve systematically: too high on the left, too low on the right
Underfitting: the model is too simple for the pattern in the data
The errors are large on the training data already, and would be on new data too

title: CADC
text:
A ninth-degree polynomial: too much


ggplot(sim, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm",
              formula = y ~ poly(x, 9))

Ten parameters for fifteen points. The curve visits every observation, noise included
Overfitting: the model has learned the sample, not the process
Its training error is nearly zero. Ask what it would predict for x = 6.5

title: CADC
text:
A cubic: about right


ggplot(sim, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm",
              formula = y ~ poly(x, 3))

Four parameters, and the shape of the process that made the data
Misses individual points, follows the curve: the errors that remain are the noise
In a real problem nobody tells you the degree. Something has to stand in for knowing the truth













y ~ x^3 in an R formula is not a cubic: ^ means interaction crossing there, so it collapses to y ~ x. poly(x, 3) is. Worth one sentence, since half the room will type the first version in the lab.

title: CADC
section: What stands in for the truth: data the model never saw
text:
What stands in for the truth: data the model never saw

Let the three models predict 200 fresh points from the same process
























You will never have the fresh two hundred. So you make them: hold part of your labelled data back before you fit anything.


One click. Before it, only the fifteen training points: the freer the model, the smaller the error, so the ninth-degree polynomial looks like the best of the three. The click adds the fresh points and extends each curve across their whole range. The cubic now has the smallest error, and the ninth-degree polynomial is by far the worst. The error is the root mean squared error, the typical distance between a point and its prediction.
The 454 is mostly the edges. Of the 200 fresh points, 31 lie beyond the outermost training points, which is where the ninth-degree curve drops off the chart. Inside the training range the three errors are 24, 11 and 18, so the cubic still wins, by less. The Playground’s How much freedom is too much shows the full error curve, degree by degree.

title: CADC
text:
Hold part back

  


Four clicks, on the deck’s own data: 5,250 abstracts, one tile per fifty, coloured by discipline. The opening screen is the file as it came, sorted by class: cut it at 80% and the test set would be all statistics. Click 1: shuffled once, with a seed, so the same split comes back tomorrow. Click 2: the cut: four in five train, the fifth is sealed, with the lock; nothing below this slide looks at it until the confusion matrix. Click 3: stratified: the class shares under both halves are the same; that is what strata = label did on the earlier slide. Click 4 is the trap: eight settings tried, the best kept because it scored best on the test set. The arrow from the sealed box back into the model is the leak, and the .81 is no longer an estimate of anything. Tuesday’s lab comes back to this; do not give its trap away here.
Say two rules out loud before moving on. Eighty to twenty is a convention, not a law. And every preprocessing decision, the vocabulary included, is learned from the training set and only applied to the test set: the recipe in Part III does exactly that. The test set is the two hundred fresh points from the last slide; it only works if it stays fresh.

title: CADC
text:
Other designs

  


Seven clicks; ‹ › or the arrow keys go back and forth. The opening screen is the hold-out split from the last two slides, and its limit: every model has settings, and choosing them needs a score that is not the test score. Click 1: cut a validation part out of the training data. Every decision lands on it, and the test set still sees one model once; the cost is 1,050 coded abstracts that train nothing.
Clicks 2 to 5 are k-fold cross-validation, slowly. Click 2: the 4,200 training abstracts in five folds of 840. Click 3: round 1 in full. Folds 2 to 5 fit the model, fold 1 scores it, and since the model never saw fold 1 the score is honest: .733 for Part III’s logistic regression. Click 4: rounds 2 to 5, each fold sitting out once, so every abstract is scored once by a model that did not see it. Click 5: the mean of the five, .737, is the estimate for this setting, and the spread (± .005) says how far to trust it. These are real scores, on the same five folds the tuning grid uses.
Click 6: do the five rounds once per setting and keep the best mean. The four rows are from the network’s grid in Part V. Click 7: the order in which the numbers are used. The folds choose the setting, the chosen setting is fitted once more on all 4,200 training abstracts, and the test set is scored once and reported. Nothing else about the test set is ever computed.

title: CADC
text:
Testing is validation

The test set carries the human labels. Scoring the model on it is exactly last week’s comparison of an instrument with a gold standard
Same confusion matrix, same accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and κ, per class, with the base rate beside them
The only new thing: the labels the model is scored on were not used to build it. Last week that was automatic, because nobody trains a dictionary
Report the test-set score, the size of the test set, and the class frequencies; without them nobody can judge the score


Everything in Part III of last week applies unchanged; only the instrument is new.

title: CADC
text:
Three abstracts: which discipline?
arXiv preprintReversible temperature exchange upon thermal contactAbstract. According to a well-known principle of thermodynamics, the transfer of heat between two bodies is reversible when their temperatures are infinitesimally close. As we demonstrate, a little-known alternative exists: two bodies with temperatures different by an arbitrary amount can completely exchange their temperatures in a reversible way if split into infinitesimal parts that are brought into thermal contact sequentially.physicsarXiv preprintSinging Style Transfer Using Cycle-Consistent Boundary Equilibrium Generative Adversarial NetworksAbstract. Can we make a famous rap singer like Eminem sing whatever our favorite song? Singing style transfer attempts to make this possible, by replacing the vocal of a song from the source singer to the target singer. This paper presents a method that learns from unpaired data for singing style transfer using generative adversarial networks.computer sciencearXiv preprintAdversarial Attacks and Defences CompetitionAbstract. To accelerate research on adversarial examples and robustness of machine learning classifiers, Google Brain organized a NIPS 2017 competition that encouraged researchers to develop new methods to generate adversarial examples as well as to develop new ways to defend against them. In this chapter, we describe the structure and organization of the competition and the solutions developed by several of the top-placing teams.statistics

Read one out loud, then ask the room to name the three disciplines before the click. The first is easy: thermodynamics has a vocabulary of its own. The third is the interesting one. It reads like computer science, and its authors filed it under statistics. Keep that in mind for the confusion matrix: the model’s errors will sit exactly there. A click shows all three labels at once. The labels are what the authors chose when they submitted the paper, and they are the only coding this data set has.

title: CADC
text:
The workflow

  splitinitial_split()hold part back
  reciperecipe()from text to features
  modelmultinom_reg()which algorithm, which settings
  workflowworkflow()recipe and model, as one object
  fitfit()on the training data
  predictpredict()on the test data
  evaluateconf_mat()against the test labels


The next slides take these seven steps one at a time; the row of chips above each slide shows where we are
Together they are steps 02 to 04 of the pipeline, written as code


The recipe, the model and the workflow are objects you can print, share and reuse. Swapping the algorithm changes one of them.


Kuhn, M., & Silge, J. (2022). Tidy modeling with R. O’Reilly. https://www.tmwr.org

title: CADC
text:
Split first
splitrecipemodelworkflowfitpredictevaluate


library(tidymodels)

set.seed(42)                                   # the split is reproducible
split <- initial_split(science, prop = .8,     # 80 / 20
                       strata = label)         # each class keeps its share

train_data <- training(split)
test_data  <- testing(split)

tibble(set = c("training", "test"),
       n = c(nrow(train_data), nrow(test_data)))

title: CADC
text:
The recipe
splitrecipemodelworkflowfitpredictevaluate


rec <- recipe(label ~ text, data = train_data) |>   # predict label from text
  step_tokenize(text) |>                            # 1 · words
  step_stopwords(text) |>                           # 2 · drop the grammar
  step_tokenfilter(text, min_times = 20,            # 3 · the 1,000 most frequent
                   max_tokens = 1000) |>            #     words seen 20+ times
  step_tf(text)                                     # 4 · the document–term matrix

baked <- rec |> prep() |> bake(new_data = NULL)
baked |> select(label, tf_text_data, tf_text_quantum) |> print(n = 5)

Output



# A tibble: 4,200 × 3
  label            tf_text_data tf_text_quantum
  <fct>                   <int>           <int>
1 computer science            0               0
2 computer science            0               0
3 computer science            0               0
4 computer science            1               0
5 computer science            0               0
# ℹ 4,195 more rows




A recipe writes the preprocessing down before it runs: learned on the training data, applied unchanged to the test data
Steps 1 and 2 are the tokens and stop words of weeks 1 and 2; step 3 is week 2’s trimming, and 1,000 columns is a hyperparameter
prep() learns the vocabulary, bake() applies it: 4,200 rows, one column per kept word



Four clicks, one per step; the output belongs to the last. A word seen fewer than twenty times cannot teach the model anything reliable, which is why step 3 exists. Every step is a decision that can change the score, and the only rule is to try.

title: CADC
text:
Specify and fit
splitrecipemodelworkflowfitpredictevaluate


logit_spec <- multinom_reg(penalty = 0.01,    # shrink the weights ...
                           mixture = 1) |>    # ... lasso: many go to zero
  set_engine("glmnet") |>                     # the R package that fits it
  set_mode("classification")

logit_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(rec) |>                          # the recipe from before
  add_model(logit_spec)                       # the model from above

m_logit <- fit(logit_wf, data = train_data)


rec is the recipe from the last four slides, unchanged. The workflow binds it to the model
Logistic regression for three classes: a weight per word per class, summed and turned into three probabilities
The penalty is the answer to Part II: it punishes large weights, so a thousand features cannot memorise 4,200 abstracts


Fitting took 11 seconds on this laptop.

title: CADC

text:
The confusion matrix, three by three
splitrecipemodelworkflowfitpredictevaluate


pred_logit <- predict(m_logit, new_data = test_data) |>
  bind_cols(test_data |> select(id, label, title))

pred_logit |>
  conf_mat(truth = label, estimate = .pred_class)

The model has never seen these 1,050 abstracts. Rows are the truth, columns the verdict; the diagonal is what it got right
The errors sit between statistics and computer science: model, data, learning belong to both


Every off-diagonal cell is a pair of disciplines that share a vocabulary. The matrix shows how often the model fails and where the construct is fuzzy.

The numbers you report

class_metrics <- metric_set(accuracy, precision,
                            recall, f_meas)

pred_logit |>
  class_metrics(truth = label, estimate = .pred_class)

pred_logit |>                         # per true class
  group_by(label) |>
  accuracy(truth = label, estimate = .pred_class)

Three classes, so precision and recall are averaged: macro by default, every class counting equally
Per class, the model finds 92% of the physics abstracts but only 70% of computer science and 63% of statistics. The average hides which construct it cannot separate

title: CADC
text:
What the model gets wrong
splitrecipemodelworkflowfitpredictevaluate
arXiv preprintComparative Study of Virtual Machines and Containers for DevOps DevelopersAbstract. In this work, we plan to develop a system to compare virtual machines with container technology. We would devise ways to measure the administrator effort of containers vs. Virtual Machines (VMs). Metrics that will be tested against include human efforts required, ease of migration, resource utilization and ease of use using containers and virtual machines.filed under: computer sciencethe model: physicsarXiv preprintTherML: Thermodynamics of Machine LearningAbstract. In this work we offer a framework for reasoning about a wide class of existing objectives in machine learning. We develop a formal correspondence between this work and thermodynamics and discuss its implications.filed under: statisticsthe model: computer sciencearXiv preprintOn the generation of the quarks through spontaneous symmetry breakingAbstract. In this paper we present the state of the art about the quarks: group SU(3), Lie algebra, the electric charge and mass. The quarks masses are generated in the same way as the lepton masses. It is constructed a term in the Lagrangian that couples the Higgs doublet to the fermion fields.filed under: physicsthe model: computer science

Every number on the last two slides is made of cases like these. Read some before you report the score.


Three of the 262 test abstracts the logistic regression got wrong. Each card shows where the authors filed the paper; ask the room what the model said before the click. The first is plainly computer science, and the model calls it physics, probably on words like machines and resource. The second borrows its vocabulary from physics on purpose (thermodynamics). The third is physics written in the vocabulary of algebra (group, Lie algebra), which the model has seen mostly in computer science. None of this is visible in an F1 score, and all of it is in the confusion matrix. This is last week’s advice applied to a classifier: read the disagreements.

Swap the algorithm: one object changes

title: CADC
section: Swap again: a support vector machine
text:
Swap again: a support vector machine
splitrecipemodelworkflowfitpredictevaluate


rec_norm <- rec |>
  step_normalize(all_predictors())         # SVMs want scaled inputs

svm_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(rec_norm) |>                  # the recipe, plus one step
  add_model(svm_linear() |>                # a different model
              set_engine("LiblineaR") |>
              set_mode("classification"))

This is what the workflow buys: the comparison is fair, because everything else is held fixed

title: CADC
CADC
text:
Which algorithm?










The three you just ran, plus a tree and a network, on the same 180 points. The line is where the verdict flips; the tint is how sure the model is.


Each model draws its boundary in a different shape. Text has a thousand features instead of two: the same picture, impossible to draw.

title: CADC
text:
Which algorithm, in words









Algorithm
The rule it learns
Strong when
Weak when




Logistic regression
one weight per word, summed
many features; readable weights
meaning lies in combinations


Naive Bayes
word rates per class, multiplied
little data; a fast baseline
words are correlated


Support vector machine
the widest-margin boundary
sparse, high-dimensional text
you need probabilities


Decision tree
yes/no questions on words
mixed feature types
text: brittle, overfits


Neural network
weighted sums, stacked, non-linear
combinations matter; lots of data
little data; nothing readable




For a bag of words, start with Naive Bayes, then try a regularised logistic regression or a linear SVM.


Hvitfeldt, E., & Silge, J. (2021). Supervised machine learning for text analysis in R. CRC Press. https://smltar.com — Chapters 6–7.


The network earns its place in Part IV for one specific reason (features made of features) and nowhere else on a bag of words. Say that here so the comparison figures later do not read as a disappointment.

title: CADC
text:
Sixty-eight years of one idea

  


The same timeline, at the screen the cold open started on. 1958: the perceptron, one layer, and the Navy’s press conference. Then eleven years of promise, then Minsky and Papert (1969) prove that one layer cannot learn exclusive-or (the not good problem in its purest form), and the funding stops. 1986: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams show that networks with a hidden layer can be trained by backpropagation, which is what the room watched happen. One click on: 2012, the same algorithm on GPUs and a million images. The idea did not change between 1958 and 2012; the data and the compute did.

title: CADC
section: From the neuron to the unit
text:
From the neuron to the unit



A biological neuron sums the signals it receives and fires once a threshold is passed. That is where the analogy starts and ends
The artificial unit (McCulloch & Pitts, 1943; Rosenblatt, 1958): each input x is multiplied by a weight w, the products are summed, a bias is added, and an activation function turns the sum into an output
Written out: output = f(w1x1 + w2x2 + … + b): the same weighted sum as last week’s word list, drawn on the right
A network stacks units in layers: the outputs of one layer are the inputs of the next; a unit only talks to the layer before and the layer after












one review, one unit



One unit is a regression. A network is regressions whose inputs are other regressions, and that is the only difference.

PLAYGROUNDMultiply, then add

The figure is deliberately the same picture as week 2’s dictionary slide, one row per input, so say so: nothing new has happened to the arithmetic. What is new is the bias, the bottom row, which shifts the whole sum, and f in the subtitle, which squashes it into (0, 1).
The review is “great food, not bad”, and the sum lands on exactly 0, so the unit answers 0.50: it cannot decide. That is not a coincidence and it is the door into Part IV. not and bad each pull down on their own, and one unit has no way to notice that together they mean the opposite. A hidden unit does. Hold the point until the network explainer, but plant it here.


Rosenblatt, F. (1958). The perceptron: A probabilistic model for information storage and organization in the brain. Psychological Review, 65(6), 386–408. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0042519

title: CADC
text:
The activation function



Without it, a stack of weighted sums is one weighted sum: the hidden layer would add nothing
The logistic curve squashes any sum into (0, 1), a probability: with it, one unit is a logistic regression
tanh has the same S-shape between −1 and +1; the network on the next slide uses it inside
ReLU, zero below zero and the sum itself above, is the workhorse inside large modern networks

title: CADC
text:
The network, taken apart

  


Sixteen clicks: the cold open’s network (same drawing, same starting weights, same run) taken apart on one review, Not good at all, human label negative. The panel says each step in a few words; the numbers on the lines and units are the model’s own. Go back with the ‹ beside the counter or the left arrow key. It follows one hidden unit, C, the whole way.
The opening screen is the neuron again. Click 1: one unit laid over it. With the logistic curve as its activation function, one unit is a logistic regression; say it, it is the bridge to Part III. Click 2 unfolds the network. Click 3: the review goes in as word counts, a 1 on not and good. Click 4: the weights, with C’s lines labelled. Click 5: C adds up, each count times its weight plus its bias, worked out in the panel. Click 6: the activation function squashes the sum (tanh, from the previous slide). Click 7: the other three units do the same. Click 8: the output unit adds up the four numbers the same way. Click 9: the logistic curve turns its sum into p(positive) = .76; the network says positive, the human said negative. The output unit is a logistic regression on A to D. Click 10: the loss, 1.44, large because the answer is wrong and sure. Click 11: every review has a loss, and training lowers their average, .79 now.
Click 12 is the heart of it. Make one weight a little larger and look at the average loss: it falls, so that weight should go up. That question, asked of every weight, is the gradient. Click 13: backpropagation answers it for all 64 weights at once, working back from the output; amber shows which way each should go. Click 14: one step. Every weight moves a little, as far as the learning rate allows; the changes show in the third decimal. Click 15: epoch after epoch, C’s lines grow and the review’s p(positive) falls below .5 at epoch 26; all twenty are right at 65. Click 16: what C learned. It sends −0.80 for Not good at all and +0.38 for Not boring at all, and the only difference between the two is good against boring. Nobody told it to; the weights went where the loss fell.
Tie back to Part II: nothing stops this from continuing until the twenty are memorised. Epochs, the penalty and the number of hidden units are the degree of the polynomial. Nothing in the procedure knows what a word means. It knows which weights lower a number.

title: CADC
section: What a hidden unit can see that a list cannot
text:
What a hidden unit can see that a list cannot

A dictionary gives good +1 whatever stands in front of it; Naive Bayes gives good one learned weight, and the same problem
A hidden unit can learn a weight on not and a weight on good and fire only when both are present: a combination, not a sum
Not good at all is the first text in this course that a model gets right without being told the rule
The cheap alternative from week 1 still stands: put not good in the matrix as a bigram, and the list works again. The network learns the bigram; the tokeniser declares it


This is the specific thing the hidden layer buys: features made of features. Next week’s models do this with many layers, at scale.


Honest caveat for the room: on twenty reviews the network found the not good unit because the corpus was written so that it would. On 4,200 abstracts, with a thousand features and sixteen hidden units, what the units learned is not readable, and the score two slides on is the only evidence that they learned anything.

title: CADC
section: Other ways to wire the units
text:
Other ways to wire the units




































One hidden layer
this week































































































Many hidden layers
deep learning






























Convolutional
a window slides over words





















Recurrent
reads in order, remembers



































































Transformer · week 4
words look at each other


All of them are units with weights, trained the same way, by backpropagation. What differs is how the units are wired.


A look ahead, not a lesson. One hidden layer is what we built. Stack more and it is a deep network: deep learning means no more than many layers. A convolutional network slides a small window over the text, so a unit can learn a phrase such as not good wherever it occurs; the CNN in van Atteveldt et al.’s table at the end of today is one of these. A recurrent network reads word by word and carries what it has read so far, which gives it word order. A transformer, next week’s subject, lets every word look at every other word, in each of many layers; the large language models are transformers.

title: CADC
text:
Fitting a network with tidymodels
splitrecipemodelworkflowfitpredictevaluate


nn_spec <- mlp(hidden_units = 16,       # one hidden layer, 16 units
               epochs = 100,            # passes over the training set
               learn_rate = 0.1,        # the step size
               penalty = 0.01) |>       # the brake on the weights
  set_engine("brulee") |>               # torch, inside R
  set_mode("classification")

nn_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(rec_norm) |>               # scaled inputs, as for the SVM
  add_model(nn_spec)

set.seed(42)                            # the random starting weights
m_nn <- fit(nn_wf, data = train_data)

pred_nn <- predict(m_nn, new_data = test_data) |>
  bind_cols(test_data |> select(id, label))


A multilayer perceptron: 1,000 inputs, 16 hidden units, 3 outputs (about sixteen thousand weights)
Every number in the specification is a hyperparameter; none has a right value in advance
The seed matters now in two places: the split, and the random initial weights


Fitting took 2 seconds. The recipe, the split and the metrics did not change.



Kuhn, M., & Falbel, D. (2023). brulee: High-level modeling functions with torch (R package). https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=brulee

title: CADC
text:
Four algorithms, one test set
splitrecipemodelworkflowfitpredictevaluate



On the test set the network lands among the three models from Part III
On its own training abstracts it reaches .92, the widest gap of the four: sixteen thousand weights for 4,200 abstracts
Where a network pays off is when the input carries structure worth combining, and that is what the next part changes


The representation limits the score more than the algorithm.

title: CADC
text:
From text to numbers, again

  


Week 1’s explainer, opened at its last step. The left shape is what every model so far has read: the document–term matrix, one row per text, one column per word, and any two words as different as any other two. The right shape is where Part V goes: one column per word, a few hundred numbers nobody named, learned so that words used alike get similar numbers. Same idea as in week 1, now with the reason to switch.

title: CADC
section: What a bag of words cannot see
text:
What a bag of words cannot see

Every model so far took the document–term matrix as its input: one column per word, and every column a stranger to every other
fantastic and great share nothing in that matrix. A model that learned great from the training set knows nothing about a test abstract that says fantastic
The matrix is sparse (94 cells in 100 were zero last week) and wide: a thousand columns for a thousand words, and the 1,001st word gets none
Word order is gone, and with it not good; the hidden unit could only rebuild it because both words survived the cut


The representation throws away similarity between words before the model ever sees them. So the fix goes into the representation.

title: CADC
text:
Words as vectors

  


Seven clicks. The numbers are real. Each strip on the right is one word’s fifty GloVe numbers, from blue (negative) to amber (positive). The drawing places the six words in three dimensions: the three directions in which these six words differ most, which keep 94% of their spread. A word is a point; the arrow from the middle of the space is the same thing drawn differently. The box and the dotted lines to its floor are only there so the eye reads depth.
The opening screen and click 1: man, then woman, each with its strip. Click 2: the arrows from the middle go, because what matters is the arrow between the two words: woman minus man, subtracted number by number, and its strip. Click 3: uncle and aunt. In the drawing the same arrow separates them; their strip is similar, not identical. Nobody labelled that direction gender; it is there because the pairs are used the same way in millions of sentences. Click 4: king, and the question. Click 5: subtracting man and adding woman is the same as adding the arrow from before, so put that arrow on king; the strip is the sum over all fifty numbers. Click 6: queen sits next to where it lands, and its strip looks like the sum. One detail to say out loud: over all fifty numbers the nearest word is still king itself (.89), and queen comes next (.86). The Arithmetic slide’s code hides the three inputs for that reason. Click 7: the drawing is a projection, and the sum runs over every number in the strip. The sentence model later in this part uses 768. The Playground’s Where words live does this on 50,000 words.
Data: _scripts/build_vectors_explainer.py. The next four slides are real too.

title: CADC
text:
Where the numbers come from



The distributional hypothesis (Firth, 1957): a word is characterised by the company it keeps
An embedding gives each word k numbers, learned from the text alone, so that words used in similar contexts get similar numbers
GloVe (2014) fits them to a corpus’s co-occurrence counts; word2vec (2013) trains a shallow network to predict a word from its neighbours


glove <- read_delim("data/glove.6B.50d.10k.w2v.txt",
                    skip = 1, delim = " ", quote = "",
                    col_names = c("word", paste0("d", 1:50)))

glove |> filter(word %in% c("king", "queen", "pizza")) |>
  select(word, d1:d6)
dim(glove)

Output



# A tibble: 3 × 7
  word     d1     d2     d3      d4    d5     d6
  <chr> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
1 king  0.505  0.686 -0.595 -0.0228 0.600 -0.135
2 queen 0.379  1.82  -1.26  -0.104  0.358  0.600
3 pizza 0.621 -0.496 -0.696  0.195  1.06   0.142


[1] 10000    51



Ten thousand words, fifty numbers each, from six billion tokens of Wikipedia and news. No column means anything on its own



Mikolov, T., Chen, K., Corrado, G., & Dean, J. (2013). Efficient estimation of word representations in vector space. arXiv. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.1301.3781
Pennington, J., Socher, R., & Manning, C. D. (2014). GloVe: Global vectors for word representation. Proceedings of EMNLP 2014, 1532–1543. https://doi.org/10.3115/v1/D14-1162


A representation learned without anyone assigning meaning: the fourth column of Part I’s table, arriving early. The file is cut down to ten thousand words for the lab.

title: CADC
text:
How close are two words?



Every word is an arrow. Two words are similar when their arrows point the same way
Cosine similarity measures that angle: 1 for the same direction, 0 for a right angle
The length of an arrow plays no part, so a frequent word does not win by being long













Football points almost the same way as basketball; pizza is nearly at a right angle. The neighbour lists on the next slide are sorted by this number.

PLAYGROUNDMultiply, then add

The one idea students need before the next slides. The numbers are real, computed from the fifty-dimensional file, and each arrow is drawn at its true angle to basketball. Only those angles can be read off the drawing: the angle between football and pizza here is not the real one. All arrows have length 1, which is the point: dividing out the length is what stops a frequent word with a long vector from winning everything. For anyone who wants the arithmetic, the Playground’s Multiply, then add ends on it: multiply position by position, add, divide by the two lengths.

title: CADC
text:
Neighbours


wv <- as.matrix(glove[-1]); rownames(wv) <- glove$word
wv <- wv / sqrt(rowSums(wv^2))     # unit length: dot product = cosine

nearest <- function(target, n = 6) {
  sims <- wv %*% target            # cosine with every word at once
  tibble(word = rownames(wv), similarity = sims[, 1]) |>
    arrange(-similarity) |> slice_head(n = n)
}

nearest(wv["basketball", ])
nearest(wv["netherlands", ])

nearest() sorts every word by its cosine with the target
Nobody told the vectors that Belgium is near the Netherlands. Six billion tokens of context did



Output

title: CADC
text:
Arithmetic


analogy <- function(a, b, c, n = 4) {
  target <- wv[a, ] - wv[b, ] + wv[c, ]
  nearest(target, n + 3) |>
    filter(!word %in% c(a, b, c)) |>   # the inputs score high: hide them
    slice_head(n = n)
}

analogy("king", "man", "woman")
analogy("doctor", "man", "woman")

The famous demonstration, with its thumb on the scale in view: without the filter, king itself is the nearest word
The second line is the same arithmetic, and the answer is a measurement of the corpus, not of medicine



Output



# A tibble: 4 × 2
  word     similarity
  <chr>         <dbl>
1 queen          0.85
2 throne         0.76
3 prince         0.75
4 daughter       0.74


# A tibble: 4 × 2
  word     similarity
  <chr>         <dbl>
1 nurse          0.94
2 child          0.86
3 pregnant       0.85
4 mother         0.84



Embeddings inherit the regularities of the text they were trained on: the useful ones and the ones a study would call bias.



Bolukbasi, T., Chang, K.-W., Zou, J., Saligrama, V., & Kalai, A. (2016). Man is to computer programmer as woman is to homemaker? Debiasing word embeddings. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 29.


Two readings of the doctor line, and both matter for the course. As a measurement instrument the vectors are contaminated: a classifier built on them inherits the association. As an object of study they are a measurement of the corpus: Andrich et al. (2023) trained embeddings on five million US news stories and read gendered trait associations off politicians’ names, which is the next slide.

title: CADC
section: Embeddings as the object of study
text:
Embeddings as the object of study



Andrich, Bachl and Domahidi (2023): are US politicians described in gender-stereotyped terms in the news?
Five million news stories, 2010 to 2020; word2vec trained on them, with each of 1,095 politicians as a token of their own
The measure is a cosine: how close is a politician’s vector to words such as competent, honest or caring?




Right of the dashed line: closer to male politicians. Masculine traits and integrity sit closer to men, physical feminine traits closer to women. Most other traits show no difference.



No classifier, no labels: the geometry of the space is the finding. The validation question is whether the geometry measures the construct.


Andrich, A., Bachl, M., & Domahidi, E. (2023). Goodbye, gender stereotypes? Trait attributions to politicians in 11 years of news coverage. Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly, 100(3), 473–497. https://doi.org/10.1177/10776990221142248 Figure 2, cropped (CC BY-NC 4.0).


The cosine from three slides ago, used as a measure. They trained one word2vec model per year, took the mean vector of each group of trait words, and computed its cosine with each politician’s vector. The figure pools the years. The differences are small on the scale of the measure, and over the eleven years some stayed the same (integrity) while others shrank. Their list of trait words was checked with a survey of native speakers, which is the validation step this method needs: nothing guarantees that a direction in the space means what its label says.

title: CADC
text:
From words to sentences


movies <- c("This movie is great, I loved it.",
            "The film was fantastic, a real treat!",
            "I did not like this movie, it was not great.",
            "Today, I went to the cinema and watched a movie.",
            "I had pizza for lunch.",
            "Sometimes, when I read a book, I get completely lost.")

# a sentence-embedding model, run locally through Ollama
emb <- request("http://localhost:11434/api/embed") |>
  req_body_json(list(model = "nomic-embed-text", input = movies)) |>
  req_perform() |> resp_body_json()
E <- do.call(rbind, lapply(emb$embeddings, unlist))   # 6 × 768
E <- E / sqrt(rowSums(E^2))
tibble(sentence = movies, similarity_to_2 = as.numeric(E %*% E[2, ])) |>
  ggplot(aes(similarity_to_2, reorder(sentence, similarity_to_2))) +
  geom_col()











great and fantastic make the nearest pair: different words, similar meaning. The negated sentence is further away than the cinema trip



Averaged word vectors put sentences 1 and 3 almost on the same point. A model that reads the sentence does not.


Thursday’s lab uses exactly this call. The vectors here were computed once and cached so the deck renders offline; the code is what ran. The grey bar is sentence 2 itself. The take’s numbers: with averaged GloVe vectors, sentences 1 and 3 have a cosine of .98, higher than 1 and 2 (.94); with this model it is .71 against .77. The model is Nomic’s open embedding model, 137 million parameters, which runs on a laptop in seconds. What “reads the whole sentence” means, mechanically, is next week’s lecture.

title: CADC
text:
The pipeline with embeddings

  


The one variant whose arrow does not point at step 03. Embeddings replace the representation, not the classifier: the week 3 classifier sits under 03 untouched, and the document–term matrix turns into a matrix of dimensions when the arrow lands. That swap is the whole slide, and it is why the next slide changes one recipe step and nothing else.

title: CADC
CADC
text:
Six models, one test set



The mean of fifty-dimensional word vectors scores below all the bag-of-words models: averaging two hundred words into one point blurs the abstract
The sentence-embedding model comes first: a representation trained to keep what a text means, fed to the same regression
The same 1,050 abstracts for all six rows. Every comparison in this course follows that rule


Four algorithms on the same word counts span 6 points of accuracy. Changing what one logistic regression reads moves it from .69 to .80.













The sentence-embedding row: every abstract embedded with the same local model as the six movie sentences, then the same regularised regression. The embeddings were computed once (five minutes for 5,250 abstracts) and the test-set predictions cached; the metrics are computed live from them. The gap between the two embedding rows is the argument for next week: what the model does while reading is the representation.

title: CADC
section: Tuning: nobody knows the right settings
text:
Tuning: nobody knows the right settings
splitrecipemodelworkflowfitpredictevaluate


nn_tune <- mlp(hidden_units = tune(),    # "decide this by trying"
               penalty = tune(),
               epochs = tune(),
               learn_rate = tune()) |>
  set_engine("brulee") |> set_mode("classification")

nn_tune_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(rec_norm) |> add_model(nn_tune)

grid <- crossing(hidden_units = c(2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128),
                 penalty = c(.0001, .001, .01, .03, .1, .3, 1),
                 epochs = c(5, 100),
                 learn_rate = c(.001, .01, .1))

folds <- vfold_cv(train_data, v = 5, strata = label)   # never the test set

nn_results <- tune_grid(nn_tune_wf, resamples = folds, grid = grid,
                        metrics = metric_set(accuracy))


Hidden units, penalty, epochs, learning rate: every value so far was a guess
A grid search tries the combinations systematically: 294 here, each scored by five-fold cross-validation inside the training set
That makes 1,470 fits, which took ten minutes on twenty processor cores


The test set is not touched. Choosing settings on it would be Part II’s leak.



Five folds, as in the Other designs explainer. The grid is much wider than anyone would search on purpose, including settings that are plainly too weak, so that the next slide shows what goes wrong. It ran before the lecture on a desktop machine (_scripts/tune_week3_mlp.R), and the deck loads the metrics from results/mlp-tune.rds.

title: CADC
text:
Tuning: what the grid says


collect_metrics(nn_results) |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(penalty),
             factor(hidden_units), fill = mean)) +
  geom_tile() +
  facet_grid(epochs ~ learn_rate)

The penalty matters most: too little .72, about right .75, too much .65
Too little training also hurts: at the smallest learning rate, five epochs can stay at chance (.33)
Hidden units hardly matter, and the top settings all sit near .75













Chosen on the training folds, then refitted and scored once on the test set: .77, against .75 for the first guess.


Every tile is one combination, 294 in all, and the outlined tile is the best one (64 hidden units, penalty 0.3, 100 epochs, learning rate 0.001). Read along the columns first: at a penalty of 1 every panel goes pale, because the brake is so strong the weights cannot grow. That is Part II’s underfitting. At the far left there is little brake, and the score is a few points lower, which is its overfitting. Then the top left panel: a small learning rate and five epochs has not finished learning, and some networks stay at the .33 of guessing among three balanced classes. At a learning rate of .1, 5 and 100 epochs give the same tiles, because brulee’s default optimizer, LBFGS, a faster relative of gradient descent, gets there early and training stops. Hidden units hardly matter once there are more than two, which is the same message as the comparison slide: on a bag of words there is little for them to combine. The grid ran on a newer version of torch than the laptop that refits the winner, so the last number can move a little between machines.

title: CADC
text:
What moves the score

The task: sentiment in tweets is harder than discipline in abstracts, whatever the model
The amount of labelled data: more hand-coding beats a cleverer algorithm, nearly always
The representation: counts, n-grams, word vectors, sentence vectors; the largest lever today
Preprocessing: stop words, stemming, trimming; small effects, and not always in the direction you expect
The algorithm: on a bag of words, a point or two between reasonable choices
Tuning: a point or two, on folds and not on the test set


Items 1 and 2 are decided before any code runs. That is what the sketch at the start of every lab is for.


Barberá, P., Boydstun, A. E., Linn, S., McMahon, R., & Nagler, J. (2021). Automated text classification of news articles: A practical guide. Political Analysis, 29(1), 19–42. https://doi.org/10.1017/pan.2020.8

Same table as last week, now with the middle rows in bold. Three things: the ordering is stable (humans, crowd, classifiers, dictionaries), and no dictionary comes close to the worst classifier. title: CADC
section: A lot of data comes as text
text:
A lot of data comes as text

  


COLD OPEN.
Say nothing for the first ten seconds; the field drifts, far away, hundreds of them. Click 1: a slow zoom to a dozen you can read. These are real: tweets from the week 2 corpus, restaurant and film reviews from the labs, two lines from State of the Union addresses. Click 2: labels fly in and attach, slowly at first, then faster than anyone can read. That is what a machine does, and the speed is what the room should notice. Click 3: the camera pushes in on one of them. “862 patients test positive” was labelled positive, because something saw the word and stopped reading. Let the room notice before you say anything, then ask the two questions yourself: how do we get a machine to do this at all, and how would we know when it is wrong? Both come back on the dark slide after the first two figures.

title: CADC
section: The world went digital in about twenty years
text:
The world went digital in about twenty years

  


Hilbert, M., & López, P. (2011). The world’s technological capacity to store, communicate, and compute information. Science, 332(6025), 60–65. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1200970
International Data Corporation. (2024). Global DataSphere and StorageSphere forecasts. IDC. — post-2007 storage.
Epoch AI. (2026). Global AI computing capacity is doubling every 7 months. https://epoch.ai/data-insights/ai-chip-production — AI panel.


The labels need glossing out loud, since none of them are self-explanatory:
Optimally compressed exabytes. They did not count devices or files; they converted everything to the number of bits it would take to store the same content under ideal compression. That is the only way a vinyl record, a VHS tape and a hard disk end up on one axis. One exabyte = a billion gigabytes.
Analog vs digital. Analog is paper, film, vinyl, cassette, VHS. Note the shape: analog capacity does not just lose share, it peaks around 2000 and then shrinks in absolute terms. The blue overtakes it around 2002. The paper itself says only “the early 2000s”; 2002 is what interpolating 25% in 2000 to 94% in 2007 gives, hence the ≈ on the marker. Recent enough that most of the room was alive for it.
General-purpose computing. Machines that can be programmed to do anything: PCs, servers, phones, calculators. Hilbert & López separate these from application-specific computing, the fixed-function chips in a washing machine or a DVD player, which they measured separately and which was much larger in aggregate. Measured in instructions per second, so the axis is log: each gridline is a hundredfold.
Why the compute line is straight. On a log axis a straight line is exponential growth, with a constant doubling time; it looks tame only because the axis is log. If a student asks whether growth slowed: single-thread CPU performance did collapse after Dennard scaling ended around 2005, but aggregate world capacity is core counts times device counts times datacentres, and that kept compounding. AI-specific compute went the other way entirely, doubling every 6–9 months since 2020, far steeper than this line.
The AI line. This one comes from Epoch AI (2026), not Hilbert & López: total AI chip capacity growing ~3.3× a year since 2022, a doubling every 7 months, about 5.2 million operational H100-equivalents by end of 2025. Note that the two right-hand series are in different units: general-purpose is instructions per second, AI accelerators are 8-bit floating-point operations. They share an axis so you can compare shape and order of magnitude, but you cannot read a like-for-like ratio off it. Say that if anyone asks.
The rates. 58% a year for general-purpose computing 1986–2007 is theirs. Carrying that same rate past 2007 is an assumption, and you should say so. Same for the storage figure after 2007: ~12 zettabytes installed by 2025 is an IDC industry estimate. Nobody has repeated their exact inventory since.
Ask before clicking: “how much bigger do you think it gets?” Then click. The 2007 total becomes a sliver you can barely see, which is what the second half of the animation is for.

title: CADC
section: Much of what we know about human behavior
text:
Much of what we know about human behavior


  
    ... is based on what people tell us 
    
      
        
        Self-report measures in surveys
      
      
        
        Responses in experimental research
      
      
        
        Accounts in qualitative interviews
      
    
    Useful for measuring motivations, attitudes, or feelings, but such measures can be biased:
    reported and actual behaviour diverge systematically.
  

  
    ... not based on records of actual behavior
    
      messagespostscommentsreviewsnews articleswiki entriestranscriptsparliamentary debatescode
    
    Communication that was never explicitly elicited for
    research, but is stored and available at scale. How can we use it?
  



Parry, D. A., Davidson, B. I., Sewall, C. J. R., Fisher, J. T., Mieczkowski, H., & Quintana, D. S. (2021). A systematic review and meta-analysis of discrepancies between logged and self-reported digital media use. Nature Human Behaviour, 5(11), 1535–1547. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-021-01117-5
Scharkow, M. (2016). The accuracy of self-reported internet use — A validation study using client log data. Communication Methods and Measures, 10(1), 13–27. https://doi.org/10.1080/19312458.2015.1118446


The left column. Ask how they have measured media use so far; almost every answer is one of these three. That is the discipline’s default, and for good reason: an attitude or a motive is not lying around to be picked up, so you have to ask.
The bias claim. Parry et al. (2021) meta-analysed 106 comparisons of logged versus self-reported digital media use: the association is only about r = .38, and self-reports are mostly over-estimates. The error also correlates with what we study: heavy users misreport differently from light users. Scharkow (2016) found the same with client log data. So the bias has a direction, and averaging will not remove it. If someone objects that self-reports are still fine for attitudes, agree; that is the boundary.
The right column. These are old phenomena that now leave a record. Debates were always spoken, but are now transcribed; complaints always existed, but are now reviews with a timestamp.
Do not oversell it. Someone will point out this record is skewed: not everyone posts, platforms shape what is said, APIs decide what you can see. Agree, and say we return to it in the lab: digital traces have their own validity problem, different from that of self-report and no smaller.
Bridge. The obvious objection: it is text, and you cannot run a regression on a tweet. That is the next slide.

title: CADC
section: An standard question, but too many articles to code
text:
An standard question, but too many articles to code



How did Dutch news cover the housing crisis between 2015 and 2025?

Did the coverage get more negative over the decade?
Did the framing shift from economics to fairness?
Whose voices were quoted: politicians, developers, tenants?

Nothing computational about the question itself: this is the content analysis communication research has been doing since the 1950s
To answer it you would read every article mentioning woningmarkt in four national outlets, 2015 to 2025



  Articles to code100,000
  Minutes to read and code one× 4
  
  Hours≈ 6,700
  Working days≈ 830
  3 years
  one coder, full time, no holidays, reading each article exactly once



Do the arithmetic out loud, slowly. This is the only big number in the deck, and it is there to make “just read them” visibly impossible rather than merely tedious.
Ask what they would do instead. Two answers come up, and both deserve taking seriously:
“Sample it.” A real answer, and it costs you the thing you wanted: the whole decade, and the rare cases. A sample of 500 is perfectly defensible for average tone and useless for “how often were tenants quoted”, because the interesting cases are rare.
“Get more coders.” Also real, also expensive, and it buys a new problem: two coders do not agree with each other. That problem has a name and a number attached, and they meet it in week 2.
Bridge: so either you give up the decade, or you find something that can read 100,000 articles.

title: CADC
section: The two big questions this course will answer
text:
The two big questions this course will answer

How can we analyse all of this text — automatically?
How can we make sure that the analysis is valid?


Say both out loud and say that the second one is the harder of the two. Week 1 is about the first; week 2 turns to the second, and the course stays with it from then on.

title: CADC
text:
Objectives and learning goals


After completion of the course, you will…

identify the data-analytic problem in a communication question, state it precisely enough for a machine, and judge whether a computational method can answer it
describe the text-classification pipeline end to end and name where each decision can go wrong
explain what each method costs and assumes, from word counts to large language models, and when the cheap one is right
treat measurement as a research question and decide when a number is not good enough to publish
run a small text-analysis study in a group, from research question to presentation


Only the third is about specific methods. The others will outlast whatever tool is “current” when you graduate.



  



Read the goals as the exam blueprint, because that is what they are: the exam asks you to frame a problem, to locate a decision in the pipeline, and to judge whether a measurement can be believed. It does not ask you to write code from scratch.
The diagram is the familiar text-mining Venn, rebuilt for this course. It has six steps: one circle arrives per click, and on the last step the middle is labelled “This course” where the original Venn has a field. Worth saying that nobody arrives holding all four circles: you each bring one or two, and the course works where all four overlap.

title: CADC
text:
Skills and methods
With regard to the specific methods taught in R, you will be able to…

import and wrangle text into a tidy table, and turn it into tokens, counts and embeddings
apply dictionaries, supervised classifiers, word embeddings and LLMs to the same texts
build a gold standard, compute coder agreement (Cohen’s κ, Krippendorff’s α), read a confusion matrix, and report precision, recall and F1
obtain data for a project of your own from APIs, archives and existing corpora
make an analysis reproducible from a clean start, document its decisions, and disclose what an AI tool did


Each of these is practised in the labs, the homework or the group project.


Worth saying plainly: nobody is expected to arrive knowing R. The course website has a “Before the first lab” page that walks through the installs and ends with a small setup check; anyone whose laptop cannot run RStudio messages us on Canvas before the first lab.
