title: Few-shot, structured output & sensitivity
text:
03 CLASSIFY Lab A · Few-shot, structured output & sensitivity Week 4 · 105 min
Today a language model does the coding. You write the codebook as a prompt, send it to a model running on your own laptop, and get a label back for every text. Then you do what the lecture called the harder work: find out how much the labels depend on the way you asked, and on the model you asked.
Everything runs locally, through Ollama: no account, no costs, and no text leaves your laptop. The models are small (3 and 8 billion weights), much smaller than the chatbots you know, which makes their weaknesses easier to see and their results reproducible. If your laptop cannot run them, you use the course key for a small model on OpenAI’s servers instead.

title: Few-shot, structured output & sensitivity
text:
Check-in


FIRST 10 MINUTES · ON YOUR OWN

A few short questions about Monday’s lecture, answered on Canvas, without notes or AI.
Not graded, but required: you need at least six of the eight check-ins to pass the course.

title: Few-shot, structured output & sensitivity
section: Part 1 · Film reviews, coded by a model
text:
Part 1 · Film reviews, coded by a model

1 · The first call
This is the lecture’s first example. llm_message() builds the message, chat() sends it to a model (here: Ollama on your laptop), and get_reply() returns the answer as text. The first call takes a little longer, because the model has to be loaded into memory.

library(tidyverse)
library(tidyllm)
library(yardstick)

llm_message("In two sentences: what is a codebook in content analysis?") |>
  chat(ollama(.model = "llama3.2:3b", .temperature = 0)) |>
  get_reply()

# with the course key, in this call and every call below:
# chat(openai(.model = "gpt-5.4-nano", .temperature = 0))

.temperature = 0 makes the model take the most probable word every time, so the same prompt gives the same answer, which is what you want for measurement.
With the course key, write openai(.model = "gpt-5.4-nano", .temperature = 0) instead of ollama(.model = "llama3.2:3b", .temperature = 0), as the comment in the code says. A model on OpenAI’s servers is not perfectly repeatable even at temperature 0: a rerun can change a label now and then.


2 · The data: one construct, two codebooks

reviews <- read_csv("film-reviews.csv")
reviews

reviews |> count(broad)
reviews |> count(narrow)

The two gold columns apply two rules for mixed to the same coding of each review:

broad: mixed whenever a review contains both substantial praise and substantial criticism, even if one side wins;
narrow: mixed only when the review reaches no overall verdict.

Look at the reviews where the two codebooks disagree:

reviews |>
  filter(broad != narrow)



3 · Sketch first: your own codebook


ON PAPER · ON YOUR OWN · 5 MIN

Before you read our prompt:

Your own one-sentence definition of mixed.
Which of the two gold columns your definition is closer to.
How you would know that the model understood your definition, and not its own.




4 · A prompt is a codebook
We write the codebook as a text with a placeholder {text}, and replace the placeholder with one review. This is the broad codebook:

codebook <- "You are coding film reviews for a research project.
Label the review as positive, negative, or mixed.
Use 'mixed' whenever the review contains BOTH substantial praise AND substantial
criticism, even if one outweighs the other.

Review: {text}"

prompt <- str_replace(codebook, stringr::fixed("{text}"), reviews$text[30])
cat(prompt)

llm_message(prompt) |>
  chat(ollama(.model = "llama3.2:3b", .temperature = 0)) |>
  get_reply()

stringr::fixed() tells str_replace() to look for the literal characters {text}.


5 · Structured output, and 48 reviews
A free-text reply has to be parsed. A schema forces the model to answer with one of the allowed labels. code_one() wraps the whole call in a function, and map_chr() runs it on every review.

schema <- tidyllm_schema(
  name  = "coding",
  label = field_fct("the code", .levels = c("positive", "negative", "mixed")))

code_one <- function(text, model = "llama3.2:3b") {
  llm_message(str_replace(codebook, stringr::fixed("{text}"), text)) |>
    chat(ollama(.model = model, .temperature = 0, .json_schema = schema)) |>
    get_reply_data() |>
    pluck("label")
}

labels <- c("positive", "negative", "mixed")

coded <- reviews |>
  mutate(pred = map_chr(text, code_one, .progress = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(across(c(broad, narrow, pred), \(x) factor(x, levels = labels)))

coded |> accuracy(truth = narrow, estimate = pred)

across() turns the three label columns into factors with the same three levels, which yardstick needs to compare them.


THE TRAP

The accuracy looks good. But which codebook did the prompt give the model, and which gold column is the prediction compared with?

Exercise 1: Evaluate the predictions against the gold column that matches the prompt. Report the confusion matrix, the accuracy and Cohen’s κ (kap()). Then count how often the model said mixed, and compare that with the gold. What does the model do with the broad rule?

# your code here



6 · The six lines you report
The lecture ended part IV with what a method section needs. Fill in what you know so far, as comments in your script:

# prompt:      (the codebook above, verbatim)
# model:       llama3.2:3b, via Ollama, run on (date), temperature 0
# validation:  accuracy ... and kappa ... against the broad gold, 48 reviews
# sensitivity: (section 7)
# failures:    (number of replies that were no valid label)
# data:        stayed on my laptop



7 · Sensitivity: change the prompt, change the model
Now add three coded examples to the prompt: the few-shot technique from the lecture.

codebook_few <- "You are coding film reviews for a research project.
Label the review as positive, negative, or mixed.
Use 'mixed' whenever the review contains BOTH substantial praise AND substantial
criticism, even if one outweighs the other.

Review: The effects are dated, but the story still lands.
Answer: mixed

Review: Superb cast, wasted on a script that goes nowhere.
Answer: mixed

Review: Gorgeous from start to finish.
Answer: positive

Review: {text}"

Exercise 2: Run the 48 reviews again with codebook_few. Tip: the easiest way is to set codebook <- codebook_few and run code_one() again, storing the result in a new column pred_few. Compare the accuracy with the zero-shot run, and compute how many reviews changed their label between the two prompts.

# your code here

Exercise 3: Run the zero-shot prompt with a second model (code_one(text, model = "llama3.1:8b"); with the course key, model = "gpt-4o-mini"), or swap results with a pair that has it. Fill in the 2 × 2 table: two prompts × two models, accuracy against the broad gold. What moved the score more: the prompt or the model?

# your code here

title: Few-shot, structured output & sensitivity
section: Part 2 · On your own: do the examples decide the label?
text:
Part 2 · On your own: do the examples decide the label?


ABOUT 30 MINUTES · AI PERMITTED, DISCLOSE IN ONE LINE

Open week04-lab-a-part2.qmd from the lab folder; science-abstracts.csv from week 3 is next to it.

Back to week 3’s abstracts. In week 3 you split them into training and test data: a classifier learns its rules from coded examples, so it has to be tested on abstracts it did not learn from. A language model needs no training data from you. Others trained it, on other texts, and your coded abstracts change nothing in it. So here you do not split the abstracts, as Monday’s slide The steps, with a language model showed. You draw 30 of them, 10 per discipline, as the test set: their labels are the gold standard you validate the model against. Thirty keeps one run to a minute or two.
In Exercise 2 you added three coded examples to the prompt; here you test what the choice of examples does. The examples are part of the prompt: the model reads them along with every abstract, and its weights do not change. They must still come from outside your 30 test abstracts, or the model would see the right answer for an abstract it is tested on. Two prompts give the model the three categories and three coded example abstracts, and differ only in which examples:

Prompt A: one example from each discipline.
Prompt B: three examples from statistics.

Your question: Do the examples in a prompt decide which label the model gives?
Take 30 abstracts (10 per discipline) and, as examples, short abstracts that are not among those 30. The skeleton gives you a function that builds a prompt from three examples. Run both prompts with a schema, and report the accuracy of each, the share of abstracts whose label changed, and how often each prompt answered each discipline. Before you run them, write down which prompt you expect to answer statistics more often, and by how much.

title: Supervised classification
text:
03 CLASSIFY Lab A · Supervised classification Week 3 · 105 min
Last week you wrote the word list yourself. Today an algorithm writes it: you give it texts with a known label (the training set), it learns which words go with which label, and you test the resulting classifier on texts it has never seen (the test set). This is supervised classification, and you build the lecture’s workflow step by step with tidymodels: split, recipe, model, workflow, fit, predict, evaluate. Then you swap the algorithm while the recipe and the evaluation stay the same, and compare the results.

title: Supervised classification
text:
Check-in


FIRST 10 MINUTES · ON YOUR OWN

A few short questions about Monday’s lecture, answered on Canvas, without notes or AI.
Not graded, but required: you need at least six of the eight check-ins to pass the course.

title: Supervised classification
section: Part 1 · Which discipline wrote this abstract?
text:
Part 1 · Which discipline wrote this abstract?

1 · Getting to know the data
The first chunk loads tidyverse, tidymodels (split to evaluation) and textrecipes (the text steps for tidymodels), reads the abstracts and counts them per discipline.

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(textrecipes)

science <- read_csv("science-abstracts.csv") |>
  mutate(label = factor(label))

science |> count(label)

science has one row per paper: id, label (the discipline), title and text (title plus abstract). tidymodels needs label as a factor, a variable with a fixed set of categories, to treat the task as classification. With 1,750 abstracts per discipline, always predicting the same one gives an accuracy of .33, the floor any classifier has to beat clearly.
Before any model reads these texts, read one abstract per discipline yourself (run the chunk a few times to see others). Could you tell them apart? Which words gave the discipline away?

science |>
  group_by(label) |>
  slice_sample(n = 1) |>
  pull(text)



2 · Sketch the pipeline first
In week 2, the hand-coded texts only checked your dictionary. Now they have two jobs: some teach the model, the others test whether what it learned holds for texts it has not seen.


ON PAPER · ON YOUR OWN · 5 MIN

Sketch the lecture’s pipeline for this task, a box per step with arrows between them, and answer these five questions next to it:

Which texts are labelled, and by whom?
How do you split them, and why?
How is a text turned into numbers?
Which model learns from them?
How, and on which texts, do you find out whether it works?

Mark the route of the training texts and of the test texts. Sections 3 to 6 build each box in code.



3 · Split first
splitrecipemodelworkflowfitpredictevaluate
Sections 3 to 6 turn your sketch into the seven steps of the lecture’s workflow. The chips under each heading show where you are: green for the steps the section covers, grey for those already done.








Step
Function
What it does




split
initial_split()
puts part of the labelled abstracts aside as a test set


recipe
recipe(), step_*()
describes how a text becomes numbers


model
multinom_reg()
chooses the algorithm and its settings


workflow
workflow()
joins the recipe and the model into one object


fit
fit()
trains the recipe and the model on the training set


predict
predict()
lets the trained model label the test set


evaluate
conf_mat(), metric_set()
compares those labels with the true ones



The first step puts 20% of the abstracts aside. The model never sees them during training, so they can stand in for the new texts it will classify later.

set.seed(42)                                   # the split is reproducible
split <- initial_split(science, prop = .8,     # 80% training, 20% test
                       strata = label)         # each class keeps its share

train_data <- training(split)
test_data  <- testing(split)

nrow(train_data)
nrow(test_data)
test_data |> count(label)


set.seed(42) fixes the random draw of initial_split(), so you get the lecture’s split.
prop = .8 gives 4,200 abstracts for training and 1,050 for the test.
strata = label draws within each discipline, so each keeps its share: 350 test abstracts per discipline.
training() and testing() take the two sets out of the split.

Leave test_data alone until section 6: a model always looks better on texts it has already seen.


4 · The recipe
splitrecipemodelworkflowfitpredictevaluate
A recipe writes down how a text becomes numbers. It learns what it needs from the training data and applies it unchanged to every later text, the test set included. These are the lecture’s four steps:

rec <- recipe(label ~ text, data = train_data) |>   # predict label from text
  step_tokenize(text) |>
  step_stopwords(text) |>
  step_tokenfilter(text, min_times = 20, max_tokens = 1000) |>
  step_tf(text)


recipe(label ~ text, ...) predicts label (left of the ~) from text (right of it).
step_tokenize() splits each abstract into words, like unnest_tokens() in week 1.
step_stopwords() drops frequent English words such as the and of, which occur in every discipline.
step_tokenfilter() keeps the 1,000 most frequent of the words seen at least 20 times in the training abstracts (3,690 words qualify). Rare words teach the model nothing reliable, and fewer columns fit faster.
step_tf() counts how often each kept word occurs in each abstract (term frequency).

A recipe does nothing until you use it: prep() learns the 1,000 words from the training data, and bake() applies them (new_data = NULL means the data it was prepared on). The result is week 1’s document–term matrix:

rec |> prep() |> bake(new_data = NULL)

It has 4,200 rows and 1,001 columns, mostly zeros: the label plus one count per word, such as tf_text_quantum. The test abstracts are later counted on the same 1,000 words; a word that occurs only in the test set is ignored. You only call prep() and bake() here to look: the workflow in section 5 runs both for you.


5 · Model, workflow, fit
splitrecipemodelworkflowfitpredictevaluate

logit_spec <- multinom_reg(penalty = 0.01, mixture = 1) |>
  set_engine("glmnet") |>
  set_mode("classification")

logit_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(rec) |>
  add_model(logit_spec)

m_logit <- fit(logit_wf, data = train_data)


multinom_reg() is the lecture’s logistic regression for more than two classes: a weight per word per discipline, summed and turned into three probabilities. penalty = 0.01 punishes large weights, so 1,000 words cannot memorise 4,200 abstracts (overfitting); mixture = 1 (the lasso) sets many weights to exactly zero.
set_engine("glmnet") names the R package that does the computing, and set_mode("classification") says the outcome is a category.
workflow() joins recipe and model, so every text passes through the same recipe first.
fit() does the learning; until then, the specification only describes the model. It prepares the recipe on train_data and estimates the weights in about ten seconds. m_logit is the trained classifier.



6 · Predict and evaluate
splitrecipemodelworkflowfitpredictevaluate
Now the test set comes back. predict() runs the 1,050 test abstracts through recipe and model and returns one column, .pred_class, in the row order of test_data; bind_cols() puts the true label next to it. Last week you counted the confusion matrix and computed precision and recall by hand; here conf_mat() and metric_set() do that. conf_mat() shows the truth in the columns and the predictions in the rows, with the hits on the diagonal. With three classes, precision, recall and F1 are averaged over the disciplines (macro).
Exercise 1: Write down which two disciplines you expect the model to confuse most. Then predict the discipline of the abstracts in test_data with m_logit, put the true labels next to the predictions, and compute the confusion matrix and the accuracy, precision, recall and F1. Was your guess right?
Tip: predict(m_logit, new_data = test_data) |> bind_cols(select(test_data, label)), then conf_mat(truth = label, estimate = .pred_class). For the four numbers: class_metrics <- metric_set(accuracy, precision, recall, f_meas), used like conf_mat().

# your code here



7 · Swap the algorithm
splitrecipemodelworkflowfitpredictevaluate
Trying another algorithm now means changing one object, the model. Split and evaluation stay the same, so a difference in the scores comes from the algorithm alone. The lecture’s linear support vector machine (SVM) is sensitive to the scale of its inputs, so its recipe gets one extra step, step_normalize(all_predictors()), which puts every word column on the same scale (mean 0, standard deviation 1). That is why the recipe chip is green too.

svm_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(rec |> step_normalize(all_predictors())) |>
  add_model(svm_linear() |>
              set_engine("LiblineaR") |>
              set_mode("classification"))

m_svm <- fit(svm_wf, data = train_data)

pred_svm <- predict(m_svm, new_data = test_data) |>
  bind_cols(select(test_data, label))

Naive Bayes, the lecture’s “dictionary the data wrote”, learns from the counts how typical each word is of each discipline. In its specification below, usepoisson = TRUE says the inputs are counts, and Laplace = 1 adds one to every count, so a word never seen in one discipline does not rule it out. It needs raw counts, so it takes the original rec without normalisation.
Exercise 2: Build a workflow with the recipe rec and the Naive Bayes model nb_spec from the chunk below, fit it on the training data, and predict the test set. Then make one table that compares the three models on accuracy, precision, recall and F1. Which model would you pick? Is the difference large enough to matter?
Tip: apply class_metrics to each model’s predictions, add the model’s name with mutate(model = "naive bayes"), and stack the three with bind_rows(). To judge the difference, count how many of the 1,050 test abstracts one or two points of accuracy are.

library(discrim)
nb_spec <- naive_Bayes(Laplace = 1) |>
  set_engine("naivebayes", usepoisson = TRUE) |>
  set_mode("classification")

# your code here

title: Supervised classification
section: Part 2 · On your own: beat the paper
text:
Part 2 · On your own: beat the paper


ABOUT 35 MINUTES · IN THE ROOM · NOT HANDED IN · AI PERMITTED

Open week03-lab-a-part2.qmd from the lab folder; ecosent-headlines.csv is next to it. This part stays in the room; this week’s homework is the second part of Thursday’s lab.

You know this data from the lecture: 6,322 Dutch newspaper headlines about the economy, hand-coded as negative, neutral or positive by van Atteveldt, van der Velden and Boukes (2021). Besides id and label, the file has headline as printed (Rabobank voorspelt flinke stijging hypotheekrente); lemmata, the same with every word in its dictionary form (Rabobank voorspellen flink stijging hypotheekrente), so different forms of a word count as one; and set: train for the 6,038 headlines you may learn from, test for the 284 on which the paper reports its results:



Model in the paper
Accuracy




Naive Bayes
.58


Support vector machine
.57


Convolutional neural network
.63


(Best dictionary, week 2)
.46



Your question: Can a classifier you build beat the paper’s machine-learning results on the same test headlines?

The rules

Train only on the headlines with set == "train". The 284 test headlines are your test_data.
Compare settings on a validation part: split the training headlines once more with initial_split().
Use the test headlines once, at the end, for the setting you chose. If you try several settings on them and keep the best, the test set has helped to choose, and its score no longer shows how the model does on unseen headlines.



What you can change
You can change any step of the Part 1 workflow, in any combination. None of these options needs an extra package.
In the recipe:

Use headline instead of lemmata, in recipe() and in every step.
Drop Dutch stop words: step_stopwords(lemmata, language = "nl") after step_tokenize().
Add pairs of neighbouring words (flink stijging): step_tokenize(lemmata, token = "ngrams", options = list(n = 2, n_min = 1)).
Keep more or fewer words with max_tokens and min_times in step_tokenfilter(). Without max_tokens, it keeps only 100.
Weight counts by how rare a word is, like week 2’s tf-idf: step_tfidf() instead of step_tf().

In the model:

Logistic regression with another penalty: smaller uses more words, larger fewer. With too large a penalty, every weight is zero and the model predicts one label for all headlines. Keep max_tokens at 1,000 or below: with 2,000 words, one fit takes minutes instead of seconds.
Naive Bayes (Exercise 2) with another Laplace. It needs counts from step_tf().
The linear SVM (section 7), with step_normalize(all_predictors()) in the recipe. A larger cost lets it follow the training headlines more closely.

Other algorithms, such as a random forest, are listed at tidymodels.org; most need one more package.


How to work
Treat it as a small experiment:

Start with the workflow from Part 1, adapted to lemmata. Train it on the training part and check its accuracy on the validation part. This is your first result.
Change one thing, for example the number of words or the algorithm, and check again. If you change two things at once, you cannot tell which one made the difference. Write each attempt and its accuracy in the table in the skeleton.
Compare every accuracy with the majority baseline: the accuracy you would get by always guessing the most common label, neutral. That guess is right for about four in ten training headlines, so a model has only learned something from the words if it does clearly better.
When you have found your best version, train it once more on all training headlines (training and validation part together), and test it on the 284 test headlines. Do this once, at the very end, and compare the result with the paper.

The headlines come back in week 4, when a language model takes the same test.

title: Dictionary approaches
text:
03 CLASSIFY Lab A · Dictionary approaches Week 2 · 105 min
Today you label texts for the first time. The method is the one from Monday’s lecture: a dictionary is a list of words, each with a category attached, and the computer counts how many words of each category occur in a text. Sum the counts and you have a score; turn the score into a verdict and you have a label for every text. You go through the analysis step by step, as the lecture did, and then you open it up to see which words did the work.

title: Dictionary approaches
text:
Check-in


FIRST 10 MINUTES · ON YOUR OWN

A few short questions about Monday’s lecture, answered on Canvas, without notes or AI.
Not graded, but required: you need at least six of the eight check-ins to pass the course.

title: Dictionary approaches
text:
Part 1 · Ten days of #corona

1 · Getting to know the data

library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)

tweets <- read_csv("corona-tweets.csv")
tweets

Every row is one tweet, with an id, the time it was posted, the text, and how often it was liked and retweeted. User names are replaced by @user.
Before you count anything, read some tweets. slice_sample() draws random rows; pull(text) prints only the text column.

tweets |>
  slice_sample(n = 5) |>
  pull(text)



2 · Sketch the pipeline first


ON PAPER · ON YOUR OWN · 5 MIN


How did the sentiment of #corona tweets change over these ten days?


Input: what is one document?
Output: what does the final plot show on each axis?
Steps: the lecture’s steps, in your own words.
Check: how would you notice that the line is not measuring sentiment?




3 · A dictionary is a table
The Bing dictionary comes with tidytext. It is an ordinary table with two columns: a word and its sentiment.

bing <- get_sentiments("bing")
bing

bing |> count(sentiment)
bing |> filter(word %in% c("virus", "positive", "trump", "like"))

Look closely at the last line. Which of these four words do you expect to cause trouble in tweets about corona?


4 · Tokens, and the join
We split the tweets into words, and then keep only the words that are in the dictionary. inner_join() does exactly that: it keeps the rows that have a match in both tables, and adds the sentiment column.

tokens <- tweets |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text)

hits <- tokens |>
  inner_join(bing, by = "word")
hits

Exercise 1: The dictionary lists death but not deaths, and the tweets say deaths more often. Lemmatise the tokens first with textstem::lemmatize_words(word) inside a mutate(), then join again. How many more hits do you get? Predict first.

# your code here



5 · From words to a verdict per tweet
We count the positive and negative words per tweet, put them side by side, and compute a score: positive minus negative.

scores <- hits |>
  count(id, sentiment) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sentiment, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  mutate(score = positive - negative)
scores

Exercise 2: Join scores back to tweets so that every tweet is kept, and add a column verdict that says "positive" if the score is above 0, "negative" if it is below 0, and "no call" otherwise. Count the verdicts. For how many tweets does the dictionary say nothing? Tip: case_when(score > 0 ~ "positive", score < 0 ~ "negative", TRUE ~ "no call").

# your code here



6 · Sentiment over ten days
This is the code behind the plot in the lecture.

daily <- hits |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(created_at)) |>
  count(date, sentiment) |>
  group_by(date) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))

daily |>
  filter(sentiment == "negative") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = share)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "", y = "Share negative") +
  theme_minimal()



THE TRAP

The question was about the sentiment of tweets. What does this code count?

Exercise 3: Compute the daily share of negative tweets, using your verdicts from Exercise 2 (leave out the no calls). Plot both lines in one plot. Does the difference change what you would conclude?

# your code here



7 · Which words do the work?
A score is a sum, so you can always look at the parts.

hits |>
  count(word, sentiment, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(15)

Exercise 4: Take the top three negative and top three positive words. For each, read five tweets that contain it: tweets |> filter(str_detect(str_to_lower(text), "\\bvirus\\b")) |> pull(text). The \\b means “word boundary”: without it, virus would also find coronavirus, which the tokeniser treats as a different word. Answer in one line per word: does it measure the sentiment of the tweet, or something else?

# your code here

title: Tidy wrangling
text:
02 REPRESENT Lab A · Tidy wrangling Week 1 · 105 min
Monday’s lecture made a simple point about computational communication science: before a computer can analyse anything, a text, a post or a log file has to become a table, with one row per case and one column per variable. This first lab makes you comfortable with that kind of table in R. You learn the five functions from the tidyverse that you will use in every lab of this course, filter(), select(), mutate(), group_by() and summarize(), and the pipe |> that chains them into a pipeline. At the end you turn one of your results into a bar chart with ggplot, one layer at a time.
If you have never used R before, work through chapters 2–5 of R for Computational Social Science before the session. This lab assumes that you can open RStudio and run a line of code.

text:

title: Tidy wrangling
text:
Part 1 · Political news in Europe

1 · Getting to know the data
We first load the tidyverse and then read the data with read_csv(). Because the file sits in the same folder as your script, the file name is enough.

library(tidyverse)

ess <- read_csv("ess-news.csv")
ess

R shows a tibble: the first ten rows, the number of rows and columns, and the type of every column (<dbl> is a number, <chr> is text). You can also click on ess in the Environment tab to browse the whole table.
These are the eight variables, taken from the ESS codebook:








Variable
Meaning
Values




id
respondent number



country
country code
e.g. NL, BE, DE


gender
gender
1 = male, 2 = female


age
age in years
999 = not available


news_min
minutes per day spent on news about politics
7777 = refused, 8888 = don’t know, 9999 = no answer


internet_min
minutes per day on the internet
6666 = does not use the internet, 7777–9999 = missing


pol_interest
interest in politics
1 = very … 4 = not at all; 7–9 = missing


trust_politicians
trust in politicians
0 = none … 10 = complete; 77–99 = missing



Keep this table open; you will need it later in the lab.


2 · Sketch the pipeline first


ON PAPER · ON YOUR OWN · 7 MIN


Do Dutch men and women differ in how much political news they follow?

Before you write any code, and without a laptop, answer these four questions, based on the four lines from the lecture.

Input: which rows and which columns do you need?
Output: what should the final table look like? How many rows, which columns?
Steps: in plain words, what has to happen between input and output?
Check: how would you notice if the answer were wrong?




3 · Rows and columns: filter() and select()
filter() keeps the rows that meet a condition. select() keeps the columns you name. In both, the first argument is the data and the rest says what to do with it.

nl <- filter(ess, country == "NL")
nl

select(nl, gender, news_min)

Note the double ==: a single = gives a value to an argument, a double == asks “is this equal?”. Other comparisons are != (not equal), >, <, >= and <=. You can combine conditions with a comma, which means and.
Exercise 1: Create a table young_nl with Dutch respondents under 30, and keep only the columns gender, age and news_min. How many rows do you expect? Write your guess down first.

# your code here



4 · Pipes
In Exercise 1 you probably stored an in-between result and used it again in the next line. This happens so often that R has a shortcut, the pipe |>. It takes the result on its left and puts it into the first argument of the function on its right. Read it as “and then”:

ess |>
  filter(country == "NL") |>
  select(gender, news_min)

This works because every tidyverse function takes a table and returns a table. From now on we will write most code as a pipe, with one step per line.


5 · New variables: mutate()
mutate() adds a column, or changes an existing one. Here we turn the gender codes into words, which will make every table and plot easier to read.

nl <- ess |>
  filter(country == "NL") |>
  mutate(gender = ifelse(gender == 1, "male", "female"))
nl

ifelse() takes a condition, the value if it is true, and the value if it is false.
Exercise 2: Add a column news_hours to nl that gives the political news use in hours instead of minutes.

# your code here



6 · Groups and summaries
group_by() splits a table into groups. summarize() then shrinks every group to a single row with the summary you ask for. n() counts the rows in a group.

nl |>
  group_by(gender) |>
  summarize(n = n(),
            mean_news = mean(news_min))

Before you read the output: what do you expect? Men more, women more, or no difference?


THE TRAP

The code above runs without an error or a warning, and its answer is wrong. Find out why. Two hints: look at the codebook table again, and run summary(nl$news_min).

Exercise 3: Fix the summary so that it only uses real answers. Does the conclusion about men and women change?

# your code here



7 · All countries in one table
Exercise 4: Compute the average political news use per country, using only real answers. Keep the number of respondents per country as well, and sort the table from most to least news. Call the result countries. Tip: arrange(-mean_news) sorts in descending order.

# your code here



8 · A plot, layer by layer
A table with 22 rows is hard to take in at a glance, and a bar chart makes the ranking easier to see. The tidyverse makes plots with ggplot, which builds a plot from layers that you add one at a time with +. Every plot needs three things:

the data: a table, here countries;
the aesthetics, written inside aes(): which column decides what you see, for example which column goes on the x axis and which on the y axis;
a geom: the kind of mark that stands for one row, such as a bar, a point or a line.

Everything else (the order of the bars, the labels, the colours) is added on top of these three. We build the chart in five steps. Run each chunk and look at what has changed before you go on to the next one.
Start with the data and the aesthetics only:

# step 1: data and aesthetics
ggplot(countries, aes(x = country, y = mean_news))

R draws an empty panel. It already knows which column goes on which axis and has set the scales: country codes along the x axis, minutes along the y axis. It does not know yet what to draw on them.
For that you add a geom. geom_col() draws one bar (a column) per row, as high as the value on the y axis:

# step 2: add a geom
ggplot(countries, aes(x = country, y = mean_news)) +
  geom_col()

The + must stand at the end of a line. If you put it at the start of the next line, R treats the first line as a finished plot and then stops with the error Cannot use + with a single argument.
The bars are in alphabetical order, which tells you nothing about the countries. reorder(country, mean_news) sorts the countries by their average instead:

# step 3: sort the bars
ggplot(countries, aes(x = reorder(country, mean_news), y = mean_news)) +
  geom_col()

A ranking reads more easily from top to bottom, and labels have more room on the side. coord_flip() swaps the two axes. With two-letter country codes this is a matter of taste, but in Part 2 the policies have names such as ban-assault-weapons, which do not fit under a bar.

# step 4: turn the chart on its side
ggplot(countries, aes(x = reorder(country, mean_news), y = mean_news)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip()

The last step changes how the chart looks, without changing what it shows. fill = "steelblue" gives all bars the same colour. labs() sets the axis titles, a title and a caption; note that x and y keep the names they have in aes() even after coord_flip() has moved them, so x = "" removes the title next to the country codes. theme_minimal() replaces the grey background with a plainer one (try theme_classic() or theme_bw() as well).

# step 5: colour, labels and theme
ggplot(countries, aes(x = reorder(country, mean_news), y = mean_news)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = "", y = "Minutes of political news per day",
       title = "Political news use in 22 European countries",
       caption = "Source: European Social Survey, round 10 (2020)") +
  theme_minimal()

Exercise 5: Change one layer at a time, and write down what you expect to see before you run the code. First, replace geom_col(fill = "steelblue") with geom_point(): what stays the same, and what changes? Then go back to bars and colour them by the number of respondents, with geom_col(aes(fill = n)). Why does fill = n have to go inside aes(), while fill = "steelblue" stood outside it?

# your code here

title: Computational Analysis of Digital Communication
text:
MA Communication Science · Period 2


Computational Analysis of Digital Communication

Over eight weeks you learn to turn digital text into evidence you can defend, from counting words to prompting a large language model. This site contains all information and materials for the course “Computational Analysis of Digital Communication (CADC)”, taught at the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam.

Start with Week 1 




THE ROUTE

Word frequenciesWEEK 1 · 1960sDictionariesWEEK 2 · 1990sClassifiersWEEK 3 · 2010sNeural netsWEEK 3 · 2013+Language modelsWEEK 4 · 2023+

The course follows five generations of the same method. Each of the four weeks of methods teaches a new way to classify a text: in week 1 you learn to count words, and in week 4 you learn how to prompt a large language model to do the task.




THE TEXT CLASSIFICATION PIPELINE


01ObtainGet the text02RepresentTurn it into numbers03ClassifyAssign categories04ValidateCheck the results


You will meet this pipeline in every lecture and lab. From week 1 to week 4, only step three changes substantially. Step four matters most: we have to evaluate the model’s performance and interpret the results. The pipeline is a simplified version of what you would encounter in a real-world text classification project.




The Playground
Seven small tools you can work through until you properly understand how an algorithm or concept works. Runs in your browser.

Open the Playground →

title: What counts
text:
Assessment · 2026




An exam, four homework assignments and a group project, plus two things you simply have to do (ungraded). What you may use AI for, and how to say so, is on the AI use page.





  
    40%
    Written exam
    Week 5 · individual · no AI
  
  
    30%
    Homework
    Weeks 1 to 4 · individual · four assignments
  
  
    30%
    Group project
    Weeks 6 to 8 · one grade per group
  


The block widths are the weights. All three must be passed with a 5.5 or higher; a fail in one cannot be compensated by the other two. The final grade is the weighted average, rounded to the nearest half point: 5.5 or higher becomes a 6.0, anything below 5.5 a 5.0. Every rule in full is in the course manual (PDF).




REQUIRED TO PASS



TWO THINGS WITHOUT A GRADE


At least six of the eight check-ins. Each lab opens with a ten-minute check-in, on your own and without AI. It is not graded, only recorded, so a missed lab is a missed check-in. You may miss two labs, with a reasonable justification (illness, family or another serious reason): tell your lab teacher the same week.
All four homework assignments. A homework you do not hand in cannot be averaged away.





THE EXAM · 40%



Week 5 · in the room · on TestVision · no AI



Multiple-choice and open questions on everything from weeks 1 to 4, lectures and labs alike. You read output and say what it means, find the leak in a pipeline, explain why a κ is impossible given a confusion matrix, choose a method and say what you would lose. Your R skills are tested by reading code you are shown, never by writing a script from scratch. Many questions use the data, the code and the traps from the labs: if you did those yourself, you have practised exactly this. The check-ins are your chance to practise similar questions in the room, and to ask your lab teacher for clarification on anything you do not understand.





THE HOMEWORK · 30%



Weeks 1 to 4 · four assignments · individual



Each homework is the second part of that week’s Lab B: started in the room, finished at home, handed in on Sunday as one rendered file with your code, three short reflections and an AI disclosure. Graded Excellent, Good, Sufficient or Insufficient; your homework grade is the mean of the four, not rounded, and must be 5.5 or higher. An Insufficient is not redone: one or two can be made up by the others, three most likely cannot.
How the homework works and how it is graded





THE GROUP PROJECT · 30%



Weeks 6 to 8 · one grade per group



A question of your own, data you obtained yourselves, and a measurement you validated, presented at the mini conference in week 8. A project without a validation section cannot pass, and a failed project cannot be resat.
How the project works and how it is graded





PRACTICALITIES






How it works




Deadlines
Homework is due on the Sunday after the week it belongs to, 23:59, on Canvas. Every date is on the Weeks page.


Late work
Talk to us before the deadline: message the coordinator on Canvas. Without prior agreement, a late homework is graded Insufficient.


Resit
Only the exam has a resit, in the resit exam week in January/February. The homework and the project are coursework and cannot be resat: a failed project means the course is failed.


Language
Anything you write out yourself (homework, open exam questions, the project report) may be in English or Dutch. Multiple-choice questions, check-ins and all course materials are in English; the talk and the poster at the conference must be in English.


Feedback
Check-ins are discussed in the room. Each homework gets a grade and a few lines from your lab teacher. The project gets its feedback live, at the conference.


Questions about a grade
Your lab teacher first, the coordinator second. The formal route is the Examination Board, and it stays open to you.

title: Using AI in this course
text:
AI use · 2026


Using AI in this course

AI tools are everywhere, and we cannot realistically make you work without them. What we can do is decide where they help your learning, and hold you accountable for what you hand in. The rule is the same every week: no AI in Part 1 of a lab, in the check-ins or in the exam; AI with a disclosure in Part 2 of a lab, in the homework and in the project. Wherever AI is permitted, you say how you used it, can account for everything you hand in, and can own the claims in it. This page explains the two lanes, the four categories of AI use, how to disclose them and how I used AI to make the course; the Assessment page explains how the grades are affected.





TWO LANES


We know from our own experience that the competence to use these tools well depends on knowledge you built without them. You cannot judge whether a classifier’s output is any good if you have never worked out what a confusion matrix means on your own. So the course runs two “lanes” on purpose, and always tells you which one you are in.




No AI


Part 1 of every lab, the check-ins and the exam
Part 1 of each lab is guided practice. You work through the exercises yourself, with the lab teacher in the room to ask, and without AI tools: pasting an exercise into a chatbot skips the step the exercise is there to train. This includes code completion in RStudio, such as GitHub Copilot, so switch it off for Part 1. The check-ins and the exam are closed as well: no tools, no model, no notes beyond what is allowed in the room. This is where you build, and where we find out, what you can do yourself (reading output, reading code, judging a design), which is the capability the other lane rests on.




AI permitted, but disclosed


Part 2 of every lab, the homework and the project
From Part 2 of a lab onwards, you may use whatever AI tools help you, as long as you disclose them. Each Part 2 says at the top how: in Lab A usually one line in your file, in Lab B (which is the homework) the full disclosure described below. The project follows the same rules as the homework. Where a tool does the routine work, we ask for the judgement instead: why this decision, why this metric, what you rejected and why, and how you know the output is right. In week 4 you use AI as an instrument anyway, and you may also use it as an assistant or a thinking partner. You may not use it as a surrogate: you may not hand in work that was done solely by AI and that you therefore cannot defend without the output in front of you.






FOUR KINDS OF USE


We sort AI use into acceptable and unacceptable categories by what the tool did to the work, and therefore by what you have to be able to account for.






Category
What it means
What we ask of you




Instrument
The model performs a defined task whose output enters your work: classifying your texts, generating code you run, producing labels you analyse.
Method-level disclosure, written like a methods section: model and version, how the prompt was designed, and validation against your own judgement.


Assistant
Editing, grammar, translation, debugging, help searching. The intellectual content is yours; the tool touched the surface.
Which tool, for what, and what you did with its output: what you kept, what you changed, what you rejected.


Thinking partner
The model works on your own notes, drafts and materials, helping you stress-test ideas that are already yours.
Say what you discussed with it and what came out of it. You must be able to defend every claim without the output in front of you, and the text must be in your own voice.


Surrogate
The model produces the work and you put your name on it.
Not allowed. It falls under the VU fraud and plagiarism regulation, and no disclosure statement makes it acceptable.








HOW TO DISCLOSE



THE TEMPLATE

Every homework ends with a section C · AI disclosure. Write one block for each category you used, and say which parts you wrote without AI. For each use, answer four questions:

Which tool, and when (e.g. ChatGPT, 12 November; Claude in RStudio; GitHub Copilot)?
What for: which step or section, and what you asked it?
What you did with it: what you kept, what you changed, and at least one thing you rejected, with the reason.
How you checked it: how you know the code does what it says, or the claim is right.

If you used it substantially, paste your most important prompts in an appendix at the end of your file, or add a share link to the conversation.
The standard behind all of it: you must be able to reconstruct and defend the reasoning without the output in front of you. If you cannot, the category was Surrogate, whatever the disclosure says.




Example · light use


Only as an assistant
Assistant. ChatGPT (14 Nov), for one error message in step 4 (“object ‘word’ not found”). It explained that I had removed the column with select() two lines earlier. I fixed the order of the steps myself.
Not used for: the reflections, written without AI.




Example · medium use


Assistant and thinking partner
Assistant. Claude (20 Nov), to write the pivot_wider() call in step 6. I kept its code, checked the table against the confusion matrix by hand (the four cells add up to my 50 tweets), and rejected its suggestion to drop the neutral tweets, because my codebook defines neutral explicitly.
Thinking partner. After writing my error types in B2, I asked Claude whether it saw others. It suggested sarcasm; I checked tweets 12, 31 and 40 and it fits only 31, which I added as an example. The error types are mine.
Not used for: B1 and B3. Prompts in the appendix.




Example · homework 4


When the model is your method
Instrument. llama3.2:3b through Ollama, run on 19 Nov on my laptop, temperature 0, with a JSON schema. The prompt is my week 2 codebook, verbatim in step 2; all 50 replies are in my file. Validated against my gold standard (κ = .58, against .71 between my partner and me).
Assistant. ChatGPT (20 Nov), to turn my codebook into a prompt. It added an instruction to “be careful with sarcasm”, which I removed: it is not in my codebook, and the comparison with my partner’s coding would no longer be fair.
Not used for: the reflections.





NOT ENOUGH


AI use: ChatGPT was used for help with the code and to improve the text.

Which code? Which text? What did you keep, what did you change, what did you reject, and how did you check it? A disclosure like this counts as missing.




AI Statement


Because we ask students to disclose their AI use, we lead by example: here is how I used AI to make this course, in the same format. It covers what I prepared as coordinator: this website, the slides, the labs, the Playground tools and the course manual. The standard is the same: I can account for every page and every number in them, and the errors in them are mine (tell us on Canvas when you find one).



Disclosure · Philipp Masur

title: The homework
text:
Weeks 1 to 4 · individual


The homework

One homework a week, four in total. Each one is the second part of that week’s Thursday lab: you start it in the room, with your teacher around, and finish it at home.



WHERE THE TASK IS

The exact task, with every step, is always in Part 2 of that week’s Lab B, and in the file you download there. This page explains how the homework works; the lab tells you what to do.





THE FOUR ASSIGNMENTS





Week
Homework
What you do
The task




1
New Year’s resolutions
Clean, count and compare the words in 5,000 resolution tweets, and find out where counting words misleads you
Lab B, Part 2


2
Is the dictionary right?
Score the Bing dictionary against the gold standard you coded with your partner: confusion matrix, precision, recall, and the tweets it gets wrong
Lab B, Part 2


3
Word counts or embeddings?
A classifier that finds one category of resolution tweets, on word counts and on embeddings, and what accuracy hides
Lab B, Part 2


4
Your own measurement
Your week 2 codebook as the prompt for a language model, compared with the dictionary and your partner: which measurement would you defend?
Lab B, Part 2





Homework 2 and 4 use the gold standard you and your partner code in week 2. Keep that file safe.




HOW A HOMEWORK WEEK WORKS


  Th
  
    Thursday · in Lab B
    Start in the room
    The lab folder you download for Lab B contains the homework file: a
    skeleton with every step as a heading. Use the end of the session to get the
    first steps running while your teacher can still help.
  



  Fr
  
    At home
    Finish the steps, then think about your results
    Complete the code, write the three reflections and the AI disclosure, and
    render the file to HTML. If it does not render, it cannot be graded: render
    early, not at 23:55.
  



  Su
  
    Sunday 23:59 · on Canvas
    Hand in the HTML file
    One rendered HTML file per homework. Your lab teacher grades it and adds a
    few lines of feedback. The exact dates are on the Weeks
    page.
  




WHAT A HOMEWORK FILE CONTAINS



  
    A · Code
    Every step, run and rendered
    The skeleton gives you the steps; the code under each one is yours. It must
    run and render. It is not graded for style.
  

  
    B · Reflections
    Three short answers about your results
    About 100 words each, and about your own output: quote
    the texts (with their id) and give your numbers. This is the part that counts
    most.
  

  
    C · AI disclosure
    What a tool did, and what you did
    One block per kind of use, following the
    template and examples. Also needed if
    you used no AI at all: then say so.
  





WHAT A GOOD REFLECTION LOOKS LIKE


Both examples are reflections on a made-up homework question. Here, a student wrote a short dictionary of insults to find uncivil comments among 50 reader comments under a news article about a local tax plan, and compared its verdicts with the labels they and their partner had coded by hand. The reflection question asks to reflect on the quality of the dictionary approach.




Too general

“Dictionaries cannot understand context, so some comments were classified wrongly. Sarcasm and irony are especially hard to detect. A larger dictionary or a machine-learning model would probably give better results.”
It could have been written before running any code. It quotes no comment and gives no number, and there may not be a single sarcastic comment among this student’s errors.



About your own output

Comment 12 says: “Calling the mayor an idiot, like half this thread does, doesn’t make your argument any stronger.” The dictionary flagged it because of ‘idiot’, but my partner and I coded it as civil, since the writer is objecting to the insult. My word list cannot tell whether a word is aimed at someone or only mentioned.
In comment 31 (“I’m so stupid, I read the headline and thought the tax was going up”) the matched word is ‘stupid’. The writer is talking about themselves, so nobody is insulted, and we coded this one as civil as well.
The third error goes the other way. Comment 44 (“Can’t wait to hear what the 🤡 in charge comes up with next”) mocks the mayor, and we both coded it as uncivil, but the dictionary found nothing. The insult is an emoji, and my list contains only words. Of the three uncivil comments it missed, two use an emoji or a misspelling such as ‘id1ot’.
Most of my errors look like comments 12 and 31. The dictionary flagged 10 comments, only 4 of which are uncivil in our coding, and 5 of the other 6 use an insult without aiming it at anyone else. For a study of incivility, this means that a thread where people push back against insults gets a higher score than a thread with the same insults and no pushback, so part of what the dictionary counts is talk about incivility.




WHAT MAKES THE SECOND ONE GOOD


Each comment is quoted with its id, with what the dictionary did and how the two coders labelled it. A reader can check every claim against the output.
Each explanation gives the reason for that particular error: the insult was only mentioned, it was aimed at the writer, or it was not a word.
It keeps the comment the dictionary missed apart from the ones it flagged by mistake, because they go wrong for different reasons.
The last paragraph counts how often the main error occurs, with numbers from the student’s own output, and says what it does to the measurement. Explaining why the results look as they do is what the grading table asks for in an Excellent.





HOW IT IS GRADED









Grade
What it looks like




Excellent · 10
Everything below, and the reflections explain why something happened in your results, not only that it happened


Good · 8
The file renders, every step is done, the reflections refer to your own output (specific texts, specific numbers), and the AI disclosure is complete


Sufficient · 6
The file renders and the steps are done, but the reflections stay general, or a step is incomplete


Insufficient · 4
The file does not render, steps or reflections are missing, or there is no AI disclosure





Your homework grade is the mean of the four, not rounded, and counts for 30% of the final grade; it must be 5.5 or higher. An Insufficient is not redone: one or two can be made up by the others, three most likely cannot. All four must be handed in to pass the course. You may write in English or Dutch. Late work, deadlines and the rest are on Assessment.

title: How this course works
text:
MA Communication Science · Period 2 · 2026




Digital communication leaves more text behind than anyone can read: political messaging, news, social posts, support logs, open survey answers. This course is about turning that text into numbers so a computer can analyse it, and about finding out whether those numbers measure what you think they do.


New here? Start with Before the first lab (about an hour). How you are graded is on Assessment, what you may use AI for on AI use, and every date and room on Weeks. All rules in one document: the course manual (PDF).





WHAT YOU WILL LEARN



  
    01
    
    Spot the data-analytic problem inside a communication question, state it
    precisely enough that a machine could attempt it, and judge whether a
    computational method can answer it at all.
  

  
    02
    
    Describe the text-classification pipeline end to end (obtain, represent,
    classify, validate) and name the point where each decision can go wrong. In
    R: import text, wrangle it into a tidy table, turn it into tokens, counts and
    embeddings.
  

  
    03
    
    Word counts, dictionaries, classic machine learning, word embeddings, large
    language models: what each costs and assumes, and when the cheapest one is
    good enough. In R: apply each of them to the same texts.
  

  
    04
    
    Build a gold standard, compute coder agreement, report precision, recall
    and F1 honestly, read a confusion matrix, and decide when a number is not good
    enough to publish.
  

  
    05
    
    Make an analysis reproducible from a clean start, document the decisions
    behind it, and disclose what a tool did and where your own judgement shaped
    the outcome.
  

  
    06
    
    Develop a research question, run a small text-analysis study in a group,
    and present your findings to the room.
  





HOW A WEEK WORKS


Eight weeks in three parts: four weeks of methods, the exam in week 5, and three weeks on a project of your own. In the four weeks of methods, every week has the same rhythm.



Monday · lecture



Each week opens with a research problem and works toward a method that could solve it. The arc runs from counting words in the 1960s to prompting a language model today. Lectures are not mandatory, but the exam is built on them.




Tuesday & Thursday · labs · mandatory



You work in RStudio on real data, in a group of about twenty. You predict what a chunk will output before you run it, find planted bugs, and on Thursday start the week’s homework with your teacher in the room. Each lab opens with a short check-in.




Sunday · homework



Your code, its output, three short reflections on your own results, and an AI disclosure. Four in total, one each Sunday of weeks 1 to 4.
How the homework works





WHAT WE EXPECT FROM YOU



Bring your own laptop to every lab, with R, RStudio and the course packages installed and the setup check passed.
Run everything yourself. Reading along teaches you less than it seems to, and the exam tests what you only learn by doing it.
Say something. Labs run on discussion: about a coding decision, a metric, a result that looks too good.
Say how you used AI. The rules are on the AI use page, and they are more permissive than you probably expect.





WHO TEACHES IT

Coordinator, lecturer & lab teacherThe Monday lecture, and two of the six parallel lab groups.Writes the lectures, sets the exam, and answers anything that is not about a specific lab. Contact through Canvas.Labs in Dutch or EnglishLab teacherTwo of the six parallel lab groups.Labs in EnglishLab teacherTwo of the six parallel lab groups.Labs in Dutch

Your lab teacher is your first stop for anything that happens in a lab: code that won’t run, a result you don’t trust, a homework you’re stuck on. Which lab group you are in comes from Canvas before week 1; the groups are on the Weeks page. Project supervisors are allocated in week 6.




WHERE THINGS LIVE



  
    Canvas
    
    Announcements, readings behind a paywall, lab folders with course data,
    submissions, check-ins and grades. If it has a deadline, it is submitted
    there.
  

  
    This site
    
    Weeks, slides, labs, the playground and the schedule, released week by
    week.
  

  
    Asking
    
    Lab questions to your lab teacher, in the lab if at all possible: they get
    answered fastest and help five other people at the same time. Everything else
    to the coordinator, via Canvas.

title: Text wrangling & exploration
text:
02 REPRESENT Lab B · Text wrangling & exploration Week 1 · 105 min
On Monday you saw how a text becomes numbers in three moves: split it into tokens, count them, and arrange the counts in a document–term matrix. Today you make those three moves yourself in R, first with the three sentences from the lecture, where you can check every number by eye, and then with more than two centuries of State of the Union speeches.
The package that does the text work is tidytext, which turns a text into a table with one row per word. From then on, everything you learned on Tuesday works on text too: filter(), mutate(), group_by() and summarize() for the counts, and ggplot for the plots. You built your first bar chart on Tuesday; today you make the same kind of chart from word counts yourself.

title: Text wrangling & exploration
text:
Check-in


FIRST 10 MINUTES · ON YOUR OWN

A few short questions about Monday’s lecture and Tuesday’s lab, answered on Canvas, without notes or AI.
Not graded, but required: you need at least six of the eight check-ins to pass the course.

title: Text wrangling & exploration
text:
Part 1 · From text to numbers

1 · Three sentences, one matrix
These are the three sentences from the lecture. We store them in a small table with one row per document.

library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)

texts <- tibble(
  doc  = c("A", "B", "C"),
  text = c("The new law is good news.",
           "The new law is not good news.",
           "A disaster, this law."))
texts

unnest_tokens() splits the text into tokens. The first argument is the name of the new column (word), the second the column that holds the text. It also lowercases everything and removes punctuation.

tokens <- texts |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text)
tokens

Now we count how often every word occurs in every document, and turn the result on its side with pivot_wider(): one row per document, one column per word. This is the document–term matrix from the lecture.

tokens |>
  count(doc, word) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = word, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)

count(doc, word) is a shortcut for group_by(doc, word) |> summarize(n = n()). values_fill = 0 writes a 0 where a word does not occur in a document.
Exercise 1: Look at the matrix. Which two documents are most similar in their numbers? Do they mean the same? Write one sentence about what the matrix has thrown away.
Exercise 2: Tokenising is a decision. Check ?unnest_tokens and tokenise the three sentences into word pairs (bigrams) instead of single words. Which bigram would help you tell sentence A and B apart?

# your code here



2 · Sketch the pipeline first


ON PAPER · ON YOUR OWN · 5 MIN


What did Obama and Trump talk about in their State of the Union speeches?

This is the question for the rest of Part 1. The data is the sotu package: the full text of all 240 State of the Union addresses from 1790 to 2020, one row per address, with the president, the year and the party. Answer the four questions below without a laptop.

Input: which texts, and what is one document?
Output: what should the final table or plot look like?
Steps: what has to happen between input and output?
Check: how would you notice that the answer is misleading?




3 · The State of the Union corpus
The sotu package contains all State of the Union speeches from 1790 to 2020. The text and the information about each speech (president, year, party) are stored separately, so we first put them into one table.

library(sotu)

speeches <- as_tibble(sotu_meta) |>
  rename(doc_id = X) |>
  mutate(text = sotu_text)
speeches



4 · Tokens and counts

sotu_words <- speeches |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text)
sotu_words

sotu_words |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE)

The information about each speech (president, year, party) rides along on every row, so you can group by president later.
Exercise 3: The most frequent words are the, of and and. Remove them with the stop-word list that comes with tidytext (stop_words) and anti_join(), and show the 20 most frequent remaining words. Before you run it: which words do you expect at the top?

# your code here



5 · The counts as a bar chart
On Tuesday you built a bar chart of the countries in five steps: data and aesthetics, a geom, sorting, turning the chart on its side, and labels. The same steps work for text. The data is now a table of word counts, the words take the place of the countries, and the counts take the place of the averages. This chunk makes the table:

top_words <- clean_words |>
  count(word, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(15)
top_words

Exercise 4: Plot top_words as a bar chart, with the most frequent word at the top, readable labels and a title. Build it step by step as on Tuesday, and run the code after each step. Which column goes in aes() as x, and which as y?

# your code here



6 · Obama and Trump

two_presidents <- clean_words |>
  filter(president %in% c("Barack Obama", "Donald Trump"))

two_presidents |>
  filter(word %in% c("america", "jobs", "applause")) |>
  count(president, word)



THE TRAP

From this table you might conclude that Obama talked much more about america than Trump did. That conclusion is not supported by the table. Why not? Count the speeches per president before you answer.

Exercise 5: Make the counts comparable. Compute, for each president, how often each word occurs per 1,000 words that president spoke (after stop-word removal). Then plot the ten most frequent words per president side by side. Tip: group_by(president) before a mutate() computes the total per president; slice_max(share, n = 10) keeps the top ten per group; facet_wrap(~president) draws one panel per president. reorder() sorts the words across both presidents at once, so within a panel the bars come out of order; sort within each president with reorder_within(word, share, president) in aes() and add scale_x_reordered() as a layer.

text:
Part 2 · Homework 1: New Year’s resolutions


START IN THE ROOM · FINISH AT HOME · AI PERMITTED, DISCLOSE IT

Open week01-lab-b-part2.qmd from the lab folder; resolution-tweets.csv is next to it. Use the rest of the session to get through the first steps with your teacher around, and finish the rest at home.

At the turn of the year 2014/15, about 5,000 people in the US tweeted their New Year’s resolution with the hashtag #NewYearsResolution. Crowd workers sorted every tweet into a category (Health & Fitness, Personal Growth, Humor, …), and we know the gender and US region of the person who tweeted.
Your question: What do people resolve to do, and do women and men, or different kinds of resolutions, use different words?
The skeleton takes you through eight steps, all with the tools from today:

Load the data.
Look at it: how many tweets per category and per gender, and ten tweets read in full.
Tokenise and clean: stop words, plus your own list of words to remove.
The 15 most frequent words, as a bar chart.
Women and men: the top words per 1,000 words, side by side.
Two categories of your choice, compared in the same way.
Word pairs: what do people want to stop doing? (bigrams, as in Exercise 2)
Words in context: read five tweets for each of three top words.

Then three short reflections on your own results, and your AI disclosure.


HANDING IN HOMEWORK 1


What: the skeleton, completed and rendered to HTML: your code, its output, the three reflections (B) and your AI disclosure (C).
Where and when: on Canvas, by Sunday 23:59 (the date is on the schedule). Required to pass the course.
How it is graded: Excellent, Good, Sufficient or Insufficient: what each means. The reflections count most: they must be about your output, with specific texts and numbers.
AI disclosure: follow the template and the examples.

title: Validation lab
text:
04 VALIDATE Lab B · Validation lab Week 2 · 105 min
On Tuesday the dictionary gave every tweet a verdict. Nothing you did told you whether those verdicts were right. For that you need what the lecture called a gold standard: texts coded by humans, following a codebook, with a known level of agreement between the coders. Today you build one yourself, in pairs, and then learn to compare a machine’s verdicts with it: the confusion matrix, accuracy, precision, recall and F1.
Every method in weeks 3 and 4 is judged the way you learn today, and the gold standard you build comes back in week 4.

title: Validation lab
text:
Check-in


FIRST 10 MINUTES · ON YOUR OWN

A few short questions about Monday’s lecture and Tuesday’s lab, answered on Canvas, without notes or AI.
Not graded, but required: you need at least six of the eight check-ins to pass the course.

title: Validation lab
section: Part 1 · A gold standard, by hand
text:
Part 1 · A gold standard, by hand

1 · The codebook comes first


ON PAPER · IN PAIRS · 10 MIN

Together with your partner, and before you look at any tweet, write a short codebook:

Three labels, pos = positive, neg = negative and neu = neutral, each defined in one sentence.
Formulate a rule for a tweet that contains both praise and criticism.
Also find a rule for a tweet that only reports a fact (“500 new cases today”). This should help you decide on ambiguous cases.


Take ten minutes at most. You will have to code by these rules.




2 · Draw your tweets
Use your pair number as the seed, so that you and your partner draw the same 50 tweets, and other pairs draw different ones. We first remove exact duplicates: on Tuesday you saw that some tweets were posted dozens of times.

library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)

tweets <- read_csv("corona-tweets.csv")

set.seed(1)                                    # change 1 to your pair number
sample_50 <- tweets |>
  distinct(text, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  slice_sample(n = 50) |>
  select(id, text)

cat(paste0(1:50, ". ", sample_50$text), sep = "\n\n")

cat() prints the tweets as plain, numbered text, which is easier to read than a table.


3 · Code on your own
Fill in your 50 labels in the order the tweets are numbered. Do not talk to your partner and do not look at their screen. Once you have coded a tweet, do not go back and change it.

coder_a <- c(
  "", "", "", "", "", "", "", "", "", "",      # tweets 1-10
  "", "", "", "", "", "", "", "", "", "",      # tweets 11-20
  "", "", "", "", "", "", "", "", "", "",      # tweets 21-30
  "", "", "", "", "", "", "", "", "", "",      # tweets 31-40
  "", "", "", "", "", "", "", "", "", ""       # tweets 41-50
)

When you are both done, send your partner your coder_a <- c(...) lines. Paste theirs into your script and rename it to coder_b. Then put everything in one table:

coded <- sample_50 |>
  mutate(coder_a = coder_a,
         coder_b = coder_b)

coded |> count(coder_a)
coded |> count(coder_b)



4 · Agreement and Cohen’s κ
The simplest measure is the share of tweets on which you agree:

p_o <- mean(coded$coder_a == coded$coder_b)
p_o

As the lecture showed, this number cannot be read on its own: two coders who guess at random, each with their own label frequencies, also agree sometimes.
Exercise 1: Compute the agreement you would expect by chance (p_e) and Cohen’s κ, using the formula from the lecture: for each label, multiply the two coders’ shares, and add up the products. Before you run it: will κ be higher or lower than p_o?

# your code here



5 · Read the disagreements

disagreements <- coded |>
  filter(coder_a != coder_b)

cat(paste0(disagreements$id, " (", disagreements$coder_a, " / ", disagreements$coder_b, "): ",
           disagreements$text), sep = "\n\n")

Each entry shows the tweet’s id, your label and your partner’s label, and then the tweet. Read every disagreement out loud with your partner. For each one, decide: was it a slip, or a case the codebook did not cover? Count the second kind, and change the codebook so that it covers them.


6 · Your gold standard
Agree on one label for every tweet you disagreed on, using your improved codebook. Start from coder A’s labels. Write one line for each tweet you changed, with its id and the label you agreed on:

gold <- coded |>
  mutate(label = case_when(id == 1234 ~ "neg",     # replace with your own: one line per tweet,
                           id == 567  ~ "neu",     # its id and the label you agreed on
                           TRUE       ~ coder_a)) |>
  select(id, text, coder_a, coder_b, label)        # keep both coders: Homework 2 needs them

gold |> filter(coder_a != coder_b) |> select(id, coder_a, coder_b, label)   # check your decisions
gold |> count(label)
write_csv(gold, "gold-corona.csv")

Keep gold-corona.csv safe. You need it for the homework, and it comes back in week 4, when a language model codes the same tweets with your codebook.


7 · A dictionary against a gold standard
Before you test Tuesday’s dictionary on your own tweets, practise on the lecture’s data: 1,000 restaurant review sentences, each labelled positive or negative by a human. This is the lecture’s code: Bing verdicts, computed as on Tuesday.

bing <- get_sentiments("bing")
yelp <- read_csv("yelp-sentences.csv")

scores <- yelp |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text) |>
  inner_join(bing, by = "word") |>
  count(id, sentiment) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sentiment, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  mutate(score = positive - negative)

verdicts <- yelp |>
  left_join(scores, by = "id") |>
  mutate(verdict = case_when(score > 0 ~ "positive",
                             score < 0 ~ "negative",
                             TRUE      ~ "no call"))

called <- verdicts |>
  filter(verdict != "no call")

called |> count(label, verdict)                # the confusion matrix
mean(called$label == called$verdict)           # accuracy



THE TRAP

A report says: “The dictionary is right 84% of the time.” Is that what this code shows? Look at how many sentences called contains.

Exercise 2: Take the four numbers from the confusion matrix and compute, by hand in R, the precision, recall and F1 for the class positive. Then compute the accuracy on all 1,000 sentences, counting a no call as wrong. Which accuracy would you report?

# your code here

title: Validation lab
section: Part 2 · Homework 2: is Tuesday’s dictionary right?
text:
Part 2 · Homework 2: is Tuesday’s dictionary right?


START IN THE ROOM · FINISH AT HOME · AI PERMITTED, DISCLOSE IT

Open week02-lab-b-part2.qmd from the lab folder. Part 1 saved your gold-corona.csv in the same folder (if that is not the case, create it!), with your labels, your partner’s labels and the resolved gold label. Try to reach the confusion matrix (step 5) before the session ends. That way, your teacher can still help. Then finish at home.

Your question: How well does the Bing dictionary measure the sentiment of #corona tweets, judged against your own gold standard?
Your gold standard has three labels; the dictionary has positive, negative and no call. You first count a no call as neu. Later you decide which accuracy you would report: with these tweets or without them. Be careful: there is more than one defensible answer.
That decision and your explanation of the errors are what you have to explain. What each step has to show is described in the skeleton script. You and your partner share the gold standard, but the decision, the code and the reflections should be your own!
The skeleton takes you through eight steps:

Load your gold standard and the dictionary.
Describe your gold standard: how often does each label occur, and also compute p_o and κ with your partner’s codings. Then run gold |> filter(coder_a == coder_b, label != coder_a), which should return no rows. If it returns a row, redo section 6 of Part 1.
Score the 50 tweets with Bing (using the code we created and used on Tuesday).
Produce a verdict per tweet, in the codes of your gold standard (we used pos, neg, and neu!). Tweets the dictionary cannot judge (score NA or 0) get the verdict neu.
Now, we test the dictionary’s performance. Create the confusion matrix, with the gold labels in the rows and the dictionary verdicts in the columns.
Compute accuracy on all 50 tweets, and also precision and recall for each class.
Remove the tweets the dictionary cannot judge, and compute the accuracy again. How many tweets are left?
Go back to all 50 tweets, with the verdicts from step 4. Describe and evaluate the errors: identify every tweet the dictionary got wrong, with its id, text, gold label, verdict and the words it matched.

Then write three reflections on your own results, and your AI disclosure. B1 says which of the two accuracies you would report, and why. B2 explains three errors and names their types. B3 judges whether Bing is good enough for a study like Tuesday’s, with your accuracy, p_o and the weakest class. The skeleton lists the points each one has to cover.

title: Word embeddings
text:
02 REPRESENT Lab B · Word embeddings Week 3 · 105 min
On Tuesday every word was a column of its own. For a document–term matrix, movie and film are as different as movie and pizza. The last part of the lecture showed another way to turn words into numbers: word embeddings, where every word is a list of numbers, learned from how the word is used in billions of sentences, so that words used in similar contexts get similar numbers.
In this lab you work with such embeddings directly. You look up which words are close to each other, do arithmetic with meanings, find out what “close” means, and finally feed embeddings to Tuesday’s classifier instead of word counts.
