title: Word embeddings
text:
Part 1 · Words as vectors

1 · Loading the word vectors
We use the GloVe vectors from the lecture. The file is downloaded once.

library(tidyverse)

if (!file.exists("glove.6B.50d.10k.w2v.txt"))
  download.file("https://cssbook.net/d/glove.6B.50d.10k.w2v.txt",
                "glove.6B.50d.10k.w2v.txt")

glove <- read_delim("glove.6B.50d.10k.w2v.txt", skip = 1, delim = " ",
                    quote = "", col_names = c("word", paste0("d", 1:50)))
glove

glove |> filter(word %in% c("king", "queen", "pizza"))

Every row is a word, every column a dimension. No single dimension means anything you could name; only the pattern across all 50 does.


2 · Sketch the pipeline first


ON PAPER · ON YOUR OWN · 5 MIN


Does describing an abstract by the average meaning of its words classify it better than counting its words?

You answer this question at the end of Part 1.

What goes into the classifier now, instead of word counts?
Which output stays the same as on Tuesday?
Which step of Tuesday’s pipeline changes, and which stay the same?
What would a fair comparison with Tuesday need?




3 · Neighbours
To find words that are close to each other, the lecture used cosine similarity: how much two vectors point in the same direction, from −1 to 1. The code below first scales every vector to length 1 (so that frequent words with long vectors do not win everything), and then defines a small function nearest() that returns the words closest to a target. You do not need to understand the matrix arithmetic inside; use the function.

wv <- as.matrix(glove[-1])
rownames(wv) <- glove$word
wv <- wv / sqrt(rowSums(wv^2))                 # every vector gets length 1

nearest <- function(target, n = 6) {
  sims <- wv %*% target                        # cosine with every word at once
  tibble(word = rownames(wv), similarity = sims[, 1]) |>
    arrange(-similarity) |>
    head(n)
}

nearest(wv["basketball", ])
nearest(wv["netherlands", ])

Exercise 1: Look up the neighbours of three words: one from communication research (e.g., media, news, campaign), one with two meanings (e.g., apple, bank, mouse), and one of your own choice. What happens with the word that has two meanings?

# your code here



4 · Arithmetic with meanings
Because words are vectors, you can add and subtract them. The lecture’s analogy() computes a − b + c and returns the nearest words (leaving out the three input words).

analogy <- function(a, b, c, n = 4) {
  target <- wv[a, ] - wv[b, ] + wv[c, ]
  nearest(target, n + 3) |>
    filter(!word %in% c(a, b, c)) |>
    head(n)
}

analogy("king", "man", "woman")
analogy("paris", "france", "netherlands")

Exercise 2: Find one analogy that works and one that fails. Then run analogy("doctor", "man", "woman"). What does the result tell you about the text the embeddings were learned from?

# your code here



5 · Close, but not the same
A colleague wants to improve last week’s sentiment dictionary: “Take every word on the list and add its five nearest neighbours. More words, more hits.”

nearest(wv["terrible", ])
nearest(wv["good", ])



THE TRAP

The neighbours of terrible look perfect. Before you agree with the colleague, check how close good is to the word the dictionary counts as its opposite.

Exercise 3: Compute the cosine similarity of good and bad, positive and negative, and increase and decrease. Tip: for two vectors of length 1, the cosine is sum(wv["good", ] * wv["bad", ]). Why are opposites so close? What would happen to the colleague’s dictionary?

# your code here



6 · Embeddings as features
splitrecipemodelworkflowfitpredictevaluate
Now back to Tuesday’s task and its workflow. Only the recipe changes, which is why only the recipe chip is green: the lecture’s recipe replaces the word counts by the average word vector of each abstract. step_word_embeddings() looks up every word and averages the vectors. The split, the model and the evaluation stay as on Tuesday.

library(tidymodels)
library(textrecipes)

science <- read_csv("science-abstracts.csv") |>
  mutate(label = factor(label))

set.seed(42)                                   # the same split as Tuesday
split <- initial_split(science, prop = .8, strata = label)
train_data <- training(split)
test_data  <- testing(split)

rec_glove <- recipe(label ~ text, data = train_data) |>
  step_tokenize(text) |>
  step_word_embeddings(text, embeddings = glove, aggregation = "mean")

glove_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(rec_glove) |>
  add_model(multinom_reg(penalty = 0.01, mixture = 1) |>
              set_engine("glmnet") |>
              set_mode("classification"))

m_glove <- fit(glove_wf, data = train_data)

Exercise 4: Predict the test abstracts and compute the accuracy. On Tuesday, the same model on word counts reached .75. Is the embedding version better or worse? Give two reasons why.

section: Part 1 · The row the paper could not add
text:
Part 1 · The row the paper could not add

1 · One gold set for every method
The paper’s 284 test headlines are the gold standard. To keep the language model runs short, we draw 100 of them, once, and every method is scored on exactly these 100.

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(textrecipes)
library(discrim)
library(tidyllm)

labels <- c("negative", "neutral", "positive")

eco <- read_csv("ecosent-headlines.csv") |>
  mutate(label = factor(label, levels = labels))

train <- filter(eco, set == "train")

set.seed(4)
gold <- eco |>
  filter(set == "test") |>
  slice_sample(n = 100)

gold |> count(label)



2 · Sketch first: what makes a comparison fair?


ON PAPER · ON YOUR OWN · 5 MIN


Which texts must every method be scored on?
Which number(s) will you compare, and why those?
What else, besides accuracy, belongs in the table? Think of the lecture’s Seconds, hours, and what they cost.
How would you notice that one method’s score is misleading?




3 · Row 1: the classifier from week 3
The first row is the Naive Bayes classifier from the solution of week 3’s Lab A, Part 2 (the 2,000 most frequent lemmata), trained on the training headlines and scored on the 100 gold headlines. We also time it.

t0 <- Sys.time()

rec <- recipe(label ~ lemmata, data = train) |>
  step_tokenize(lemmata) |>
  step_tokenfilter(lemmata, max_tokens = 2000) |>
  step_tf(lemmata)

nb <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(rec) |>
  add_model(naive_Bayes(Laplace = 1) |>
              set_engine("naivebayes", usepoisson = TRUE)) |>
  fit(train)

gold <- gold |>
  mutate(pred_nb = predict(nb, gold)$.pred_class)

time_nb <- Sys.time() - t0
time_nb



4 · Row 2: a language model, with a schema
The prompt states the paper’s codebook in a few sentences. It is shorter than the prompt of the study on Monday’s slides, so expect other numbers than that figure. The model gets no training data at all.

codebook <- "You are coding headlines from Dutch newspapers for economic sentiment,
as in a content analysis of economic news. Codebook: positive = the headline
indicates that the economy or economic conditions are good or improving;
negative = bad or worsening; neutral = the headline makes no evaluation of
economic conditions, or is not about the economy. The headline is in Dutch.
Code the following headline.

Headline: {text}"

schema <- tidyllm_schema(name = "coding",
  label = field_fct("the code", .levels = labels))

code_schema <- function(text) {
  llm_message(str_replace(codebook, stringr::fixed("{text}"), text)) |>
    chat(ollama(.model = "llama3.2:3b", .temperature = 0, .json_schema = schema)) |>
    get_reply_data() |>
    pluck("label")
}
# with the course key, here and in section 5:
# chat(openai(.model = "gpt-5.4-nano", .temperature = 0, ...))

t0 <- Sys.time()
gold <- gold |>
  mutate(pred_llm_schema = map_chr(headline, code_schema, .progress = TRUE),
         pred_llm_schema = factor(pred_llm_schema, levels = labels))
time_llm_schema <- Sys.time() - t0



5 · Row 3: the same prompt, in free text
This row uses the same model and the same prompt, but the model answers in its own words. We then have to find the label in the reply. The parser below takes the label word that appears first, and returns NA if there is none, so that an unreadable reply stays visible instead of silently becoming a label.

code_text <- function(text) {
  llm_message(str_replace(codebook, stringr::fixed("{text}"), text)) |>
    chat(ollama(.model = "llama3.2:3b", .temperature = 0)) |>
    get_reply()
}

t0 <- Sys.time()
gold <- gold |>
  mutate(reply = map_chr(headline, code_text, .progress = TRUE),
         pred_llm_text = str_extract(str_to_lower(reply), "negative|neutral|positive"),
         pred_llm_text = factor(pred_llm_text, levels = labels))
time_llm_text <- Sys.time() - t0

sum(is.na(gold$pred_llm_text))                 # replies without a label
gold |> select(headline, reply) |> head(3)



6 · The table
Exercise 1: Build one table with a row per method (Naive Bayes, LLM with schema, LLM in free text) and columns for accuracy, Cohen’s κ and the time it took. Add a row for the majority baseline (always predicting the most common class), and put the paper’s numbers next to it: best dictionary .46, SVM .57, CNN .63, crowd coding .77, one trained human coder .82, three coders .88. Then look at count() of every prediction column. Is any method leaning on one class?
Tip: accuracy(gold, truth = label, estimate = pred_nb) works for one column; write it three times, or use pivot_longer() on the prediction columns and group_by().

# your code here



7 · What to report
A colleague summarises the table for a paper:

scores |>
  slice_max(accuracy, n = 1)
# "Our LLM approach reaches an accuracy of ..."



THE TRAP

This sentence is not false. What is wrong with it?

Exercise 2: Write the sentence(s) you would publish instead. Use the lecture’s list: the prompt, the model and version, the validation, the sensitivity (both formats), the failures, and where the text went.

title: Which Harry?
text:
Playground

 Week 4 · LLMs as instruments


Which Harry?

A word enters a language model as the same vector in every sentence. Whatever it comes to mean in a particular sentence, it gets from the words around it. This tool measures that process in BERT’s real attention weights.



What to do · 12 min

Open layer 3, head 1 on the Harry sentences, then switch to bank and look again.
Compare with head 11 of the same layer.
Untick ignore [CLS] and [SEP] and average the heads.
Read the similarity panel at the bottom.



What you take away

What attention actually shows, and the standard way of over-reading it.
That a word’s meaning is built up layer by layer, and that the result is a vector, not a picture.



Interactive: try the switches. Open full screen

What to notice
The grid shows every attention head BERT has: twelve layers of twelve heads. Up is later in the computation: each layer rewrites every word using the layer below, so order matters. Across is not a sequence: the twelve heads in one layer run simultaneously, never see each other, and are combined at the end of the layer. “Head 7” is a slot number, not a stage. The shading shows how much each head looks at the word that settles the meaning; about 70% of it sits in the bottom half.
Start with layer 3, head 1. Harry puts 100% of its attention on Potter in one sentence and 100% on Kane in the other. That looks like the model working out which Harry it is dealing with.
Now switch to bank, same layer, same head. It points at the full stop. The head was never reading meaning: it reads the token immediately to the right, which in the Harry sentences happened to be the surname. This is the commonest way of over-reading an attention map, and worth having been caught by once.
Head 11 of the same layer finds the disambiguating word. It follows money and water for bank, and Potter for Harry, wherever they sit in the sentence. It is not perfect either; the work is spread across 144 heads.
Untick “ignore [CLS] and [SEP]” and average the heads. At the middle layers, 70–80% of all attention is parked on two bookkeeping tokens with no content. That is documented behaviour, not a quirk of these sentences: heads with nothing to do have to put their weight somewhere. Most published attention pictures leave it out without saying so.
There is no final attention picture. At the top of the grid with heads averaged you get what looks like nothing: most weight on [CLS] and [SEP]. Nothing has gone wrong: layer 12 is only the last mixing step, head 12 is a slot rather than an endpoint, and by that depth the word has long since been placed. What a transformer puts out is a vector for each word.
The bottom panel follows that vector. Take the word’s vector in sentence A and in sentence B and measure how alike they are, at the input and after each layer. They begin as literally the same vector (1.00), because the model has read the same string twice, and end at about 0.62, two different things. Those final vectors are what any classifier you build on top receives. The dashed control word drifts too, because everything becomes context-specific with depth; the claim is the gap between the lines, not the fall of either.

Attention shows you what the model looked at. It does not show you why it answered as it did.

Used in Week 4 · LLMs.

title: Two coders, one codebook
text:
Playground

 Week 2 · Measurement & validation


Two coders, one codebook

Build-a-dictionary hands you twenty human-coded texts and asks how well your word list matches them, and every tool after it does the same. This tool asks where those twenty codes came from and whether they were worth trusting.



What to do · 12 min

Code all twenty reviews yourself. Do not skip ahead; there is no answer key.
Compare with the second coder and read the items you disagreed on.
Add a decision rule to the codebook and re-check the agreement.
In part 3, hold agreement fixed and raise the majority category.



What you take away

How to read raw agreement against Cohen’s κ, and why only the second is reportable.
That a gold standard is something people build, from rules that could have been written otherwise.



Interactive: try the switches. Open full screen

What to notice
Code them before you read on. It takes a minute. What you learn comes from the items where you and the second coder disagree.
Every item you disagreed on has the same shape. The review praises one thing and criticises another, and the codebook never said what to do about that. One of you went with the reviewer’s verdict, the other with the presence of both elements. Both readings are defensible, so a careful colleague can still disagree with you.
Two numbers; report the second. Raw agreement counts the items you matched on. Cohen’s κ subtracts the agreement two coders would reach by guessing, given how often each of you used each category. When they diverge, the raw figure is flattering you.
Look at the worst category, not the average. Expect ~70% on positive and negative and near zero on mixed. The overall figure is a weighted average dominated by the easy, common classes, so it hides exactly the category your instrument cannot measure. This is what macro-averaging is for, and why “we achieved 85% agreement” means nothing on its own.
Add a decision rule and the two coders converge to κ = 1.00. A codebook is an instrument you build and can revise. The rule made the coders agree; it did not make the coding correct. A different rule would have produced a different gold standard from the same twenty reviews, and every model you later validate against it inherits that choice.
An agreement figure without a base rate beside it tells you nothing. In part 3, hold agreement at 90% and push the majority category to 95%: κ falls to roughly zero or below. Two coders who never read a word and guessed at random, in proportion to the 95/5 split, would agree about 91% of the time (.95² + .05² ≈ .905).
Used in Week 2 · Dictionaries, and it is the reference set for build-a-dictionary.

title: Build-a-dictionary
text:
Playground

 Week 2 · Dictionaries


Build-a-dictionary

A dictionary approach is just a word list and a counting rule. Here is the word list. Twenty short texts have been coded by a human; your job is to get your list to agree with them.



What to do · 10 min

Run the starter word list and read the five metric tiles; hover each for its formula.
Add and remove words, and watch precision and recall move in opposite directions.
Turn on match word stems.
Try to reach F1 = 1.00, then look at what coverage says.



What you take away

What precision, recall, F1, accuracy and coverage each measure, and where each one misleads.
Why negation and silence defeat any word list, however long.



Interactive: try the switches. Open full screen

What to notice

Hover any of the five tiles for what it means, the formula in confusion-matrix terms, and the arithmetic with your current numbers. Every figure in the formula is a cell in the table below it, so you can check the sum yourself.
The starter list scores badly, and precision and recall fail differently. Precision falls when your words fire on the wrong texts; recall falls when they don’t fire at all.
A text your dictionary says nothing about is not scored as correct. That is why accuracy starts at 15% rather than the flattering figure you would get by filing every silence under “negative”.
“Not good at all” is coded negative but contains good. Negation is invisible to a bag of words; it stays wrong however many words you add.
Coverage is the tile most people ignore. “It exists.” and “Nothing about this works.” contain no sentiment vocabulary, so the dictionary says nothing. Treat that silence as missing data, not as a neutral verdict.
Turn on match word stems and love catches loved. That one switch raises recall noticeably: last week’s preprocessing choices still matter here.
Pushing F1 up by adding words you can see in the texts is fitting your instrument to your sample; on the next 20 texts it would not hold. This is why you need a held-out validation set.
With enough words you can reach 100% precision and 100% recall and still leave four texts with no verdict. Accuracy and coverage will say so; F1 will not.


Any word list will produce a number. Only a comparison with the human codes can tell you whether that number measures what you claim.

Used in Week 2 · Dictionaries.

title: Let the data write the dictionary
text:
Playground

 Week 3 · Naive Bayes


Let the data write the dictionary

A Naive Bayes classifier is a dictionary whose weights were learned from data instead of declared by you. It uses the same bag of words and the same metrics as last week, and every step is arithmetic you can check by hand.



What to do · 12 min

Read the learned word weights on the left.
Drag the training slider from 400 down to 10 and watch test and train pull apart.
Move the threshold slider from −1 to +1.
Tick only the ones it got wrong and read a few.



What you take away

How a classifier learns a dictionary from labelled data.
What overfitting looks like as a number, and why a bag of words cannot fix some errors.



Interactive: try the switches. Open full screen

What to notice

The bars on the left are a word list nobody wrote. Compare them with the eight words you typed into build-a-dictionary. The model counted how often each word appears in positive versus negative training texts and turned the ratio into a weight.
Very, throughout, plot and long sit near zero. The model worked out on its own that long carries no sentiment, something a hand-written list cannot express, because a dictionary only says “in” or “out”.
Drag the training slider from 400 down to 10. Test accuracy falls from ~89% to near chance while training accuracy stays high. That gap is the most important number on screen: the model memorising the texts it was shown.
Every tile shows test / train. Only the test figure may go in a paper.
Set smoothing α to 0 and the warning appears: a word seen in only one class makes the other class impossible, so one word decides the whole text. Smoothing pretends every word was seen α extra times in both classes, which stops the model dividing by a count of zero.
The threshold slider sets the precision/recall trade-off. At −1 you catch nearly every positive text but a third of your calls are wrong; at +1 every call is right but you miss a quarter. No setting maximises both, and which end you want depends on your research question.
Tick only the ones it got wrong and read them. “Never boring for a moment” is scored negative; “Well acted, but pointless” positive. More data will not fix these: word order was thrown away at the tokenising step.
In that first example, hover never and moment: no weight at all, because neither appears twice in the training texts. The one word that would rescue the sentence is not in the vocabulary. Every word with a small number above it is one you can add up yourself to reach the total.
P(positive) reaches 99.9% on texts it gets wrong. Naive Bayes is famously overconfident: it treats every word as independent evidence and multiplies. Report the verdict, not that probability.


Neither the dictionary nor the classifier tells you whether the label you are predicting was worth predicting. That judgement is still yours.

Used in Week 3 · Classifiers.

title: The prompt is the instrument
text:
Playground

 Week 4 · LLMs as instruments


The prompt is the instrument

An LLM will label anything you ask it to. Whether the labels measure what you claimed depends, it turns out, on wording you might have thought was incidental.



What to do · 15 min

Part 1: compare two prompt wordings on the same texts, and click a disagreement.
Part 2: bring in the human codes, then switch codebook and watch the slopegraph.
Part 3: read the grid down, across, and within a row.



What you take away

That the wording of a definition moves your results more than the prompting technique does.
Why a score is a property of your codebook as much as of your model.



Interactive: try the switches. Open full screen

What to notice
Three parts, each answering one question. You can stop after the first and still have the point.

1. Do two wordings give different answers?

Two prompts, same 48 texts, same model. The only difference is how each defines mixed. The big number is the count of texts on which the two sets of labels disagree; scores come in part 2.
Read the texts underneath: “Slow, but worth it”, “Well acted, but pointless”. Reviews that praise one thing and criticise another are where a definition has to do work.
Click one to see the same prompt re-run three times at temperature 0.8. Sometimes the three runs give three different answers, and a method that answers differently each time is not yet a measurement instrument.



2. Which one is right?

Only now do the human codes appear. Two numbers per prompt: how often it agreed, and Cohen’s κ, which subtracts the agreement you would get by guessing. Report the second.
Switch the codebook and watch the slopegraph. Lines that cross are prompts that swap places depending on which definition the humans used. The model is the same throughout; only the standard you hold it to has changed.
Both codebooks come from the same hand-coding of each review, on three factual questions. Neither is the true one. With a fuzzy construct, accuracy is a property of your codebook as much as of your model.



3. All 36 combinations at once

Read down for the effect of the definition, across for the technique, and the spread inside one row for the effect of the model.
Every prompt that defines mixed narrowly beats every broad one under the narrow codebook, and loses under the broad one. In practice: match your prompt to your codebook.
Note how little the technique columns differ compared with the definition rows. Few-shot and chain-of-thought are what people fiddle with; the definition is what moved the numbers.


The earlier tools asked whether the measurement was any good. Here the question is whether you had defined the thing you were measuring closely enough for that question to have an answer.

Used in Week 4 · LLMs.

title: Privacy
text:
How this site handles data


Privacy

This site collects nothing from you. Your grades, submissions and attendance are kept in Canvas.





THIS SITE

This site is static: plain pages, built once and served as files. It sets no cookies, runs no analytics or tracking script, and has no login. Viewing it does not create an account or a profile. It is hosted on GitHub Pages, which may keep its own standard server logs (e.g. IP address, requested page) to operate the service; that logging is GitHub’s, governed by GitHub’s privacy statement, not by the course.



WHERE YOUR DATA LIVES

Anything with your name on it (submissions, check-in results, grades, attendance) is handled in Canvas, not here, under Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam’s own privacy policy.



DATA USED IN THE TEACHING MATERIALS

Some datasets shown or analysed in the slides and labs contain text written by other people: tweets, reviews, news headlines. None of it is about you or was collected from this course’s students. Where the course team collected data itself (the corona-tweets set), usernames were removed and @-mentions blanked, and the set is shared only with enrolled students, inside the week 2 lab folders on Canvas. Full sources and licences for every dataset are on the License & data sources page.



QUESTIONS



CONTACT

For anything about this site or the data it uses, reach the course coordinator through Canvas, the same route as any other course question.

title: Before the first lab
text: Every lab runs on your own laptop, in R and RStudio. The first half of this page is a checklist to work through at home before Tuesday of week 1. The second half is a reference for the moments when the computer gets in the way instead of R: a download you cannot find, a zip that will not open, a file R says does not exist, a key you cannot type. The last section installs a language model on your laptop, before week 4.

title: Before the first lab
text:
Before Tuesday of week 1


1



Two minutes


Check your laptop
A Windows laptop (Windows 10 or 11) or a Mac works. A Chromebook, an iPad, or a work laptop on which you are not allowed to install software will not run RStudio. If that is your situation, send us a message on Canvas before week 1 and we will find a solution together.





2



About twenty minutes


Install R, then RStudio
R is the program that runs your code. RStudio is the program you work in; it starts R for you. Both are free. Install R first.

WindowsmacOS



Go to cran.r-project.org, click Download R for Windows, then base, then the download link at the top.
Open the downloaded .exe file and click through, keeping every default. If Windows asks whether the app may make changes to your device, click Yes.
Go to posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop and download RStudio Desktop for Windows. Open it and keep every default.
Open RStudio from the Start menu: press Win, type RStudio, press Enter.




Check which chip your Mac has: the Apple menu (top left) > About This Mac. It says either Chip: Apple M… or Processor: … Intel.
Go to cran.r-project.org and click Download R for macOS. With an Apple chip, take the installer whose name ends in arm64.pkg; with Intel, the one ending in x86_64.pkg. The wrong one installs fine and then causes trouble later, so check twice.
Open the .pkg file and click through.
Go to posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop and download RStudio Desktop for macOS. Open the .dmg file and drag the RStudio icon into the Applications folder in that window. Then eject the RStudio disk in the Finder sidebar.
Open RStudio from Applications, or press Cmd + Space, type RStudio, press Enter. If macOS asks whether you are sure you want to open an app downloaded from the internet, click Open.




Done when the console (the pane at the bottom left) shows a line starting with R version 4., and typing 1 + 1 there and pressing Enter prints [1] 2.





3



Two minutes


Change three settings in RStudio
Open Tools > Global Options.

Under General, untick Restore .RData into workspace at startup, and set Save workspace to .RData on exit to Never. Every session then starts empty, so your code has to work from top to bottom on its own, which is what happens when someone else runs it.
Under Code, tick Use native pipe operator, |>. The shortcut Ctrl + Shift + M (Cmd + Shift + M on a Mac) then types the pipe the labs use.

Click OK.





4



Ten to twenty minutes, on a good connection


Install the course packages
Packages add functions to R. This installs every package the labs use, so no lab has to start with a download. Copy the command (the button at the top right of the box does that) into the RStudio console and press Enter:
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidytext", "sotu", "textstem",
                   "tidymodels", "textrecipes", "glmnet", "discrim",
                   "naivebayes", "LiblineaR", "stopwords", "tidyllm",
                   "rmarkdown"))
A lot of red text scrolls past. That is normal: R prints its progress in red. It is finished when the > prompt is back at the bottom of the console.
If R asks Do you want to install from sources the packages which need compilation?, type no and press Enter. If it asks whether to use a personal library, answer yes both times. What these questions mean.





5



Five minutes · this is also a rehearsal of every lab


Make a course folder and run the setup check
Make one folder for the course, for example cadc inside Documents. Every lab comes as a zip file, and every zip gets extracted into this folder.

Download the setup check (button below) and extract it into your course folder. On Windows: right-click the zip > Extract All. On a Mac: double-click it, then move the folder that appears into your course folder. More on zip files.
In the extracted folder, open setup-check.qmd in RStudio. If a double-click opens it in another program, use File > Open File in RStudio instead.
Click the green ▶ at the top right of the grey code box.

The check looks at your R version, your packages and the folder you are working in, and says [ok], [note] or [fix] for each. A [fix] line also says what to do. Done when nothing says [fix], and clicking Render at the top of the editor opens a web page with the same report.
If you get stuck, bring the check’s output to the first lab, or paste it into your message when you ask for help. It tells us most of what we need to know.
Download the setup check





6



A few hours, spread over the week before


Meet the console before the first lab
Work through chapters 2 to 5 of R for Computational Social Science. It runs in the browser, so this step works even before step 2. The first lab assumes you can open RStudio and run a line of code.
Open r4css





7



Five minutes


Can you do these ten things?
In the first labs, most time is lost on things around R: a file in the wrong folder, a zip that was never extracted, or a key nobody can find. If you hesitate on any of these, read the section it links to.

Find a file you just downloaded, without searching the whole computer. (Downloads)
Extract a zip file into a folder you chose. (Zip files)
See whether a file ends in .csv, .qmd or .zip. (File extensions)
Say which folder your course files are in, and whether it syncs to the cloud. (Where your files live)
Copy the full path of a file. (Paths)
Explain why read_csv("data.csv") works in one place and not in another. (R and your folders)
Run one code chunk of a .qmd file, then one single line. (RStudio in five minutes)
Type |, ~, {, [ and " on your own keyboard. (Keyboard)
Switch from your browser to RStudio without the mouse, and take a screenshot of part of the screen. (Keyboard)
Stop R when it seems stuck, and tell what a + in the console means. (When something goes wrong)

title: Before the first lab
text:
Downloads
Your browser saves files to the Downloads folder unless you told it otherwise. To find the file you just downloaded, click the download icon (an arrow) at the top right of the browser, then Show in folder (Windows) or the magnifying glass (Mac). On Windows, Ctrl + J opens that list in most browsers.

Downloading the same file twice gives week01-lab-a (1).zip. Delete the old one, or you will not know which one you extracted.
Downloads is a place files pass through. Do not work in it: move what you need into your course folder.

title: Before the first lab
text:
Zip files
A zip file packs several files into one, so a lab can be one download. Before you can use the files, they have to be extracted.

WindowsmacOS


Double-clicking a zip shows what is inside, but extracts nothing. Code you open from there cannot find its data, and whatever you save is lost (the explainer under Paths shows why). Instead:

Right-click the zip > Extract All…
Click Browse and choose your course folder, then Extract.

It worked when you see an ordinary folder, without a zipper on its icon.


Double-click the zip in Finder. It is extracted into a folder of the same name, next to the zip. Move that folder into your course folder.
Safari extracts zips by itself after downloading, so you may find a folder in Downloads rather than a zip. That folder is what you need.

title: Before the first lab
text:
File extensions
The last part of a file name, after the dot, says what kind of file it is: .csv is a table, .qmd a Quarto document, .zip a packed folder. Windows and macOS hide it by default, which makes ess-news.csv and ess-news.zip look alike. Make them visible:

WindowsmacOS


In File Explorer, open View > Show and tick File name extensions (Windows 11). On Windows 10, open the View tab and tick File name extensions.


In Finder, open Finder > Settings > Advanced and tick Show all filename extensions.



Two traps this prevents:

Renaming without seeing the extension turns data into data.csv.csv, and R cannot find data.csv.
Saving a .csv from Excel. Opening one in Excel to look at it is fine. Saving it is not: on a Dutch or German computer Excel writes semicolons instead of commas and decimal commas instead of points, and it can change dates and long numbers. Look at data in RStudio instead (View(ess), or click the table in the Environment pane).

If double-clicking a .qmd opens the wrong program, open it from RStudio with File > Open File. To make RStudio the default: on Windows, right-click the file > Open with > Choose another app > RStudio, Always; on a Mac, select the file, press Cmd + I, choose RStudio under Open with and click Change All.

title: Before the first lab
text:
Where your files live
Keep one folder for the course, for example Documents/cadc, and extract every lab into it. After two weeks it looks like this:
cadc/
├── setup-check/
├── week01-lab-a/
│   ├── week01-lab-a-part1.qmd
│   ├── week01-lab-a-part2.qmd
│   ├── ess-news.csv
│   └── guns-polls.csv
├── week01-lab-b/
└── week02-lab-a/

Cloud folders. On many laptops Documents and Desktop are synced to OneDrive (Windows) or iCloud Drive (Mac). That is fine, with one setting: synced files can live only in the cloud until you open them, and R cannot always read those. Right-click your course folder and choose Always keep on this device (OneDrive) or Keep Downloaded (iCloud).
Names. File and folder names without spaces and special characters save typing and mistakes: week01_notes.qmd, not Week 1 notes (final!).qmd.

title: Before the first lab
text:
Paths
A path is the address of a file: the route through the folders to get to it. Click through the six steps below; it is the one idea on this page that most “file not found” errors come down to.
Click through, or use the arrow keys. Open full screen
Copying the path of a file:

WindowsmacOS


Select the file in File Explorer and press Ctrl + Shift + C (Windows 11), or hold Shift, right-click the file and choose Copy as path. You get something like:
"C:\Users\sam\Documents\cadc\week01-lab-a\ess-news.csv"
R reads a \ as the start of a special character, so pasting that gives Error: '\U' used without hex digits in character string. Replace every \ with /:
read_csv("C:/Users/sam/Documents/cadc/week01-lab-a/ess-news.csv")


Select the file in Finder and press Option + Cmd + C. Or right-click it, hold Option, and choose Copy … as Pathname. You get something like:
/Users/sam/Documents/cadc/week01-lab-a/ess-news.csv



In the labs you will rarely need a full path, and you should not hand one in: a line with C:/Users/sam/... in it runs on Sam’s laptop and nowhere else. Keep the data next to the .qmd and use the file name alone. A data file in a subfolder is data/ess-news.csv; .. means one folder up.

title: Before the first lab
text:
R and your folders
R looks for files in one folder at a time, the working directory.

In a .qmd file, the working directory is the folder the .qmd is in, both when you run a chunk and when you click Render.
In the console, it is a separate folder, usually your home folder. A line you type in the console therefore looks somewhere else than the same line in a chunk.
To check: getwd() prints the working directory, list.files() the files in it.
Avoid setwd("C:/Users/..."). It works on one computer only, and inside a .qmd it lasts for one chunk. Move the files instead.

Try it once. Open setup-check.qmd, add a chunk at the end (Ctrl + Alt + I, on a Mac Cmd + Option + I), and run:
writeLines("Hello from R", "hello.txt")
Find hello.txt in File Explorer or Finder, and in RStudio’s Files pane at the bottom right. Then type the same line into the console, press Enter, and find out where that copy went (getwd() tells you). Delete both files afterwards.
A shortcut that prevents typos: type read_csv(" and press Tab. RStudio lists the files in the working directory; type the first letters and press Tab again. If the file is not in the list, R will not find it either.

title: Before the first lab
text:
Installing software
What you might see, and what to do.
R asks Do you want to install from sources the packages which need compilation? (Yes/no/cancel). Answer no. The newest version of a package is sometimes not yet prepared (“compiled”) for your system. Yes means your computer has to compile it, which needs extra tools you probably do not have. No gives you the previous, ready-made version, which is fine.
R asks Would you like to use a personal library instead?. Answer yes, and yes again when it offers to create one. Packages then go into a folder of your own.
R warns Rtools is required to build R packages (Windows). Ignore it. You only need Rtools to compile packages, see above.
Error: there is no package called ‘tidytext’. The package is not installed. Run install.packages("tidytext") once.
Error: could not find function “read_csv”. The package is installed but not loaded in this session, or the name has a typo. Run the library(...) line at the top of the file. Installing happens once per computer; library() once per session.
Mac: RStudio is gone after a restart, or there is an RStudio disk in the Finder sidebar. You ran it from the download instead of installing it. Drag RStudio into Applications, then eject the disk.
Mac: the setup check says you have the Intel version of R. Download the installer ending in arm64.pkg from CRAN, install it over the old one, restart RStudio and install the course packages again.
Your R is more than a year old. Install the current version the same way as the first time, then run the package line from step 4 again: packages belong to one R version. RStudio updates itself through Help > Check for Updates.

title: Before the first lab
text:
RStudio in five minutes
RStudio has four panes. Top left is the editor, where your .qmd file is open. Bottom left is the console, where R runs things and prints the results. Top right, Environment lists the objects you have made. Bottom right, Files shows the working directory, and Plots and Help appear there too.
A .qmd file mixes text with grey code chunks. Three ways to run code:

One line: put the cursor on it and press Ctrl + Enter (Cmd + Enter on a Mac). The cursor moves to the next line, so you can step through a chunk.
One chunk: click the green ▶ at its top right.
Everything above: the small grey ▼ next to the ▶ runs all chunks before this one. Use it when R says an object does not exist because you skipped a chunk.

Render runs the whole file from the top in a fresh session and makes a web page of it. If a file renders with an error but worked when you ran it chunk by chunk, it depended on something you did in the console.
What the console is telling you:

> means R is ready.
+ means R is waiting for you to finish a command, usually a missing ) or ". Press Esc to start over.
A small red stop sign at the top right of the console means R is busy. Wait, or press Esc to interrupt it.

When things behave oddly, restart R (Session > Restart R) and run the file again from the top.

title: Before the first lab
text:
Keyboard
The shortcuts that save the most time in this course. The first rows of each table matter most.
Everywhere








What it does
Windows
macOS




Switch between programs
Alt + Tab
Cmd + Tab


Open a program or find a file
Win, then type
Cmd + Space, then type


Screenshot of part of the screen
Win + Shift + S
Cmd + Shift + 4 (then Space for one window)


Copy, cut, paste
Ctrl + C, X, V
Cmd + C, X, V


Undo
Ctrl + Z
Cmd + Z


Select all
Ctrl + A
Cmd + A


Find
Ctrl + F
Cmd + F


Select text
Shift + arrow keys
Shift + arrow keys


Jump one word
Ctrl + ← / →
Option + ← / →


Start or end of the line
Home / End
Cmd + ← / →


Close a tab or window
Ctrl + W
Cmd + W


Quit a frozen program
Ctrl + Shift + Esc
Cmd + Option + Esc



In RStudio








What it does
Windows
macOS




Run the line (or the selection)
Ctrl + Enter
Cmd + Enter


Run the chunk
Ctrl + Shift + Enter
Cmd + Shift + Enter


Complete a name or file name
Tab
Tab


Previous command (in the console)
↑
↑


Cancel a half-typed command
Esc
Esc


Insert a code chunk
Ctrl + Alt + I
Cmd + Option + I


Type the pipe |>
Ctrl + Shift + M
Cmd + Shift + M


Type <-
Alt + -
Option + -


Comment lines in or out
Ctrl + Shift + C
Cmd + Shift + C


Save
Ctrl + S
Cmd + S


Render
Ctrl + Shift + K
Cmd + Shift + K


Restart R
Ctrl + Shift + F10
Cmd + Shift + 0



Characters R needs that your keyboard may hide
On a US or UK keyboard, |, ~, {, [ and \ are printed on the keys. On other layouts they sit behind a modifier key:








Character
German, Windows
German, Mac




|
AltGr + <
Option + 7


~
AltGr + +
Option + N, then Space


{ }
AltGr + 7 / 0
Option + 8 / 9


[ ]
AltGr + 8 / 9
Option + 5 / 6


\
AltGr + ß
Option + Shift + 7



For any other layout: on Windows, open the On-Screen Keyboard (press Win, type it) and hold AltGr to see what appears; on a Mac, turn on Show Input menu in menu bar under System Settings > Keyboard > Text Input, choose Show Keyboard Viewer from that menu, and hold Option.
The US-International trap. Many laptops in the Netherlands use the US-International layout. On it, ", ', `, ~ and ^ wait for the next key to make é or ë, so typing read_csv("ess can give read_csv(ëss. Press Space after the quote to get the quote itself, or switch to the plain US layout (ABC or U.S. on a Mac), which has no such keys.

title: Before the first lab
text:
When something goes wrong
Read the last line of the error first. It usually names the problem:



R says
What it usually means




object 'ess' not found
The line that makes ess has not run yet in this session, or the name has a typo. Run the chunks above (the grey ▼).


could not find function "..."
The package is not loaded: run the library() line. Or a typo.


'ess-news.csv' does not exist in current working directory
R is looking in another folder than the file is in. See Paths.


there is no package called '...'
Not installed yet. See Installing software.


unexpected symbol, unexpected ')'
A typo: often a missing comma or bracket on that line or the one before.


unexpected input
Often curly quotes, see below.



Curly quotes. Code copied from a PDF, Word or slides often turns " into “ and ”, which R does not accept. Retype the quotes in RStudio, or copy code from the course website with the copy button at the top right of each code box.
Restart and run again. Session > Restart R, then run the file from the top. Many puzzling errors come from leftovers of an earlier attempt.
Asking for help. Say what you ran, what you expected, and paste the error as text, not a photo of your screen. For a screenshot, use Win + Shift + S or Cmd + Shift + 4, then Space. If it is about installing, add the output of the setup check.

title: Before the first lab
section: Before Tuesday of week 4: a language model on your laptop
text:
Before Tuesday of week 4: a language model on your laptop
In week 4 a language model codes texts for you. It runs on your own laptop, in a free program called Ollama, so the texts you code never leave your computer. Setting it up takes about half an hour, most of it waiting for a download. Do it at home, on a good connection, before the first lab of week 4.
If your laptop is too old or too small for this, there is a second route: a course key for a small model on OpenAI’s servers. Step 1 tells you which route is yours.


1



Five minutes


Check your laptop
Your laptop needs all three of these:

System: macOS 14 (Sonoma) or newer, or Windows 10 (version 22H2 or newer) or Windows 11.
Memory: at least 8 GB. With 16 GB or more you can also run the larger second model that Lab A compares.
Disk space: at least 7 GB free: about 4 GB for Ollama, 2 GB for the model, and some room to spare.


WindowsmacOS


Open Settings > System > About. Installed RAM is the memory. Under Windows specifications, Edition says Windows 10 or 11, and for Windows 10 Version must be 22H2. For the free disk space, open File Explorer and click This PC: it shows how much of the C: drive is free.


Open the Apple menu (top left) > About This Mac. It shows the macOS version (it must be 14 or higher), the Memory and the chip. For the free disk space, open System Settings > General > Storage. A Mac with an Intel processor works, but slowly: Ollama can use only its processor there, not its graphics chip.



If your laptop does not meet all three, skip Ollama: you will use the course key instead, which comes on Canvas on Tuesday morning.





2



Five minutes


Install Ollama

WindowsmacOS



Go to ollama.com/download and click Download for Windows. You get a file OllamaSetup.exe.
Open it and click Install. Ollama installs into your own account, so it does not need administrator rights.
When the installation is finished, Ollama runs in the background. Its icon, a small llama, sits in the system tray at the bottom right of the screen (click the small ^ arrow there if you do not see it). If a chat window opens, close it: the labs do not use it.




Go to ollama.com/download and click Download for macOS. You get a file Ollama.dmg.
Open it and drag the Ollama icon into the Applications folder in that window. Then eject the Ollama disk in the Finder sidebar.
Open Ollama from Applications. If macOS asks whether you are sure you want to open an app downloaded from the internet, click Open.
Ollama asks whether it may install its command line tool. Allow it, and type your Mac password when asked. Step 4 needs this tool.
A small llama appears in the menu bar at the top right of the screen. If a chat window opens, close it: the labs do not use it.




Done when you see the llama icon. It means Ollama is running.





3



Five minutes


Open a terminal
The model is downloaded with a command typed into a terminal. A terminal is a window in which you give your computer instructions by typing them instead of clicking: you type one line, press Enter, and the computer answers in text. It does nothing except what you type, and this page asks you to type four lines.
RStudio has a terminal built in, so you do not need another program:

Open RStudio. In the bottom-left pane, next to the Console tab, click the Terminal tab. If there is no such tab, choose Tools > Terminal > New Terminal.
A line with a blinking cursor appears, ending in $, % or > depending on your computer. This is the prompt: the terminal is waiting for a command.

Console and Terminal are two different things. The Console runs R code; the Terminal runs commands for your computer. A terminal command typed into the Console gives Error: unexpected symbol, and R code typed into the Terminal gives an error too. Look at which tab is selected before you type.
Windows: if RStudio was open while you installed Ollama, close RStudio and open it again first. Otherwise its terminal does not know the new command yet.
You can also use the terminal of your system instead of RStudio’s: on a Mac, press Cmd + Space, type Terminal and press Enter; on Windows, press Win, type PowerShell and press Enter. The commands are the same.





4



Ten minutes, mostly waiting


Download the model
Type this line into the terminal and press Enter:
ollama pull llama3.2:3b
Ollama now downloads a model of 2 GB and shows a progress bar. It is finished when the last line says success and the prompt is back. Then type this line to list the models you have:
ollama list
It should show llama3.2:3b with a size of 2.0 GB. Ask it a first question:
ollama run llama3.2:3b "What is a codebook? Answer in one sentence."
The first time, the model has to be loaded into memory, which can take half a minute. Then an answer appears, and the prompt comes back.
With 16 GB of memory or more, also download the larger model (4.9 GB). Lab A compares the two:
ollama pull llama3.1:8b
What you might see:

ollama: command not found (Mac) or 'ollama' is not recognized (Windows): the terminal does not know Ollama yet. On Windows, restart RStudio. On a Mac, open the Ollama app again and allow the command line tool. Or skip the terminal: run tidyllm::ollama_download_model("llama3.2:3b") in the RStudio Console, which downloads the same model.
could not connect to ollama app, is it running?: Ollama is not running. Open it from Applications or the Start menu and wait for the llama icon.
The download stops or fails: run the same ollama pull line again. It continues where it stopped.






5



Two minutes


Send the first question from R
In the labs, R sends the texts to Ollama with the package tidyllm, which you installed in week 1. Run these lines in the RStudio Console (not the Terminal):
library(tidyllm)

llm_message("What is a codebook? Answer in one sentence.") |>
  chat(ollama(.model = "llama3.2:3b")) |>
  get_reply()
Done when a sentence comes back. If R says there is no package called ‘tidyllm’, run install.packages(c("tidyllm", "yardstick")) first. If it says it cannot connect, Ollama is not running: look for the llama icon.
Ollama has to be running whenever you use it from R. Before each lab, check that the llama icon is there, and open Ollama if it is not.




If your laptop cannot run the model: the course key
If your laptop does not meet step 1, or the model does not answer in step 5, use the course key. It gives you a small model on OpenAI’s servers, gpt-5.4-nano, and you do not need to install anything. The labs’ code changes in one place. The key is posted on Canvas on Tuesday morning of week 4; the steps below take five minutes.

Get the key from that announcement on Canvas. The course pays for it; use it for the labs and the homework only. It stops working after the Homework 4 deadline.
Save it where R can find it. In the RStudio Console, run file.edit("~/.Renviron"). A file opens in the editor; it may be empty. Add this line, with the key after the =, without quotes or spaces:
OPENAI_API_KEY=paste-the-key-here
Press Enter at the end of the line, so that the file ends with an empty line. Save the file and restart R (Session > Restart R). R reads this file every time it starts, also when you render.
Check it. In the Console, nchar(Sys.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY")) > 0 should print TRUE.
Send the first question:
library(tidyllm)

llm_message("What is a codebook? Answer in one sentence.") |>
  chat(openai(.model = "gpt-5.4-nano")) |>
  get_reply()
In the labs, wherever the code says ollama(.model = "llama3.2:3b", …), write openai(.model = "gpt-5.4-nano", …) and keep everything after the model name. Where a lab asks for a second model, use gpt-4o-mini.

Two rules come with the key:

Never put the key in a script or a .qmd file. Homework is handed in with its code, and anyone who opens the file can read and use a key in it. The .Renviron file stays on your laptop.
Your texts leave your laptop. With the key, every text you code is sent to OpenAI. Say so where your report says where the text went, as the lecture’s slide Before the first call asks.

title: CADC
text:
Week 2 · Lecture


Counting, dictionaries
& measurement validity


  
    Dr. Philipp K. Masur
    Computational Analysis of Digital Communication · Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

title: CADC
text:
Three tweets, one word list

  


Six clicks. Three real tweets from the corpus the Tuesday lab uses (#corona, November 2021). Before clicking anything, ask the room to call each one: positive or negative. Then click: the words on the list light up, the score accumulates, the list gives its verdict, and finally the human verdict appears beside it.
The third tweet is the one to dwell on. It contains three words from the positive list (work, works, work) and a tone every reader recognises as hostile. The list counts the words correctly and still gets the tweet wrong, and nothing in the count would have told you.
Do not explain precision or κ here. The point is only: a number came out, and you have no idea yet whether to believe it. Say that the second half of the lecture is about how you find out.

title: CADC
section: Last week you learned to count
text:
Last week you learned to count

A text became a row of the document–term matrix: one column per word, a count in every cell, and importantly: the order of the words gone
That is a representation, but not yet a classification: counting itself does not provide a label (e.g., negative or migration)
A measurement or classification adds two things a count lacks: a claim about meaning, and a check that the claim holds
This week supplies the “oldest way” of making such a claim, and the general approach of checking it (validation)


Counting → measuring is the step from step 02 of the pipeline to steps 03 and 04.

title: CADC
section: The second question is always relevant
text:
The second question is always relevant

How can we analyse all of this text — automatically?
How can we make sure that the analysis is valid?


Callback to week 1. Week 1 answered the first with a pipeline. From today the second sits in every lecture, every lab and every homework. It is also where the exam questions live.

title: CADC
text:
This lecture

  
    I
    From counting to measuring
    Reminder: How to count words, and what a count can and cannot say
  
  
    II
    Dictionaries
    The first automated classification: a word list and a counting rule
  
  
    III
    Validation
    Gold standards, agreement, the confusion matrix, and the numbers you need to report
  
  
    IV
    Dictionaries in research
    Two studies, and when a word list is the right tool
  
  
    V
    This week
    Labs, the gold set you build on Thursday, and homework 2
  


Thirty seconds. Part III is the long one and the one the exam draws on; say so, and say that the break falls just before it.

title: CADC
section: Reminder: How to count words in a corpus
text:
Reminder: How to count words in a corpus


library(sotu)

sotu_speeches <- as_tibble(sotu_meta) |>
  rename(doc_id = X) |>
  mutate(text = sotu_text)

sotu_speeches |>
  select(doc_id, president, year, text)

Every State of the Union address, 1790 to 2020: 240 texts
One row per speech, metadata beside the text
The shape you already know from last week’s lab B



Output



# A tibble: 240 × 4
  doc_id president          year text                            
   <int> <chr>             <int> <chr>                           
1      1 George Washington  1790 "Fellow-Citizens of the Se..."  
2      2 George Washington  1790 "\n\n Fellow-Citizens of the..."
3      3 George Washington  1791 "\n\n Fellow-Citizens of the..."
4      4 George Washington  1792 "Fellow-Citizens of the Se..."  
5      5 George Washington  1793 "\n\n Fellow-Citizens of the..."
6      6 George Washington  1794 "\n\n Fellow-Citizens of the..."
7      7 George Washington  1795 "\n\nFellow-Citizens of the ..."
# ℹ 233 more rows



A speech is 8,000 words on average. Two hundred and forty of them is two million tokens.



Kahle, D. (2020). sotu: United States presidential State of the Union addresses (R package, version 1.0.2). https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=sotu

title: CADC
section: Reminder: The corpus as a matrix
text:
Reminder: The corpus as a matrix


sotu_dtm <- sotu_speeches |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text) |>
  count(doc_id, word) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = word,
              values_from = n, values_fill = 0)

dim(sotu_dtm)

mean(sotu_dtm[-1] == 0)     # share of empty cells

sotu_dtm |>
  select(doc_id, freedom, war, tax, terror) |>
  filter(doc_id %in% c(1, 74, 153, 222, 235))

Last week’s matrix, again built the same way: 240 rows, one column per distinct word (plus the id)
Too wide to print, so we look at four columns (freedom, war, tax, terror) for five speeches
The same word can be frequent in one speech and absent in another: that variation is what the next slides use



Output



[1]   240 30586


[1] 0.9411686


# A tibble: 5 × 5
  doc_id freedom   war   tax terror
   <int>   <int> <int> <int>  <int>
1      1       0     1     0      0
2     74       3    20     1      0
3    153      10    31     0      0
4    222      10    12     7     13
5    235       1     4     3      1



Ninety-four cells in a hundred are zero. Every count on the next slides is a column sum or a row sum of this matrix.



Callback, not new content: the same pivot_wider as the three-sentence matrix in week 1, on a real corpus. Two things to point at: the size (thirty thousand columns for 240 texts, which is why nobody prints a DTM) and the sparsity figure. The terror column is the one the keyword-in-context slide comes back to.

title: CADC
section: The most frequent words are the least interesting
text:
The most frequent words are the least interesting



All tokens



# A tibble: 8 × 2
  word       n
  <chr>  <int>
1 the   165601
2 of    106402
3 and    68063
4 to     68037
5 in     43429
6 a      31342
7 that   24113
8 for    21701




After anti_join(stop_words)



# A tibble: 8 × 2
  word           n
  <chr>      <int>
1 government  7597
2 congress    5808
3 united      5156
4 people      4298
5 country     3641
6 public      3419
7 time        3188
8 american    2988




Stop words carry grammar, not content: the, of, and are a fifth of the corpus
Removing them is common practice, but not is on most lists, and week 1’s sandbox showed what that costs


Every cleaning step is a decision about which words are allowed to count.

title: CADC
text:
Trimming the long tail


sotu_tokens |> distinct(word) |> nrow()

sotu_tokens |>
  count(word) |>
  filter(n >= 100) |>
  nrow()

Output



  types_total types_100plus 
        30585          2108 




Thirty thousand distinct words, and most occur a handful of times: names, numbers, misspellings
Two thousand words account for almost all of the two million tokens
Dropping rare terms makes the matrix smaller and models more stable, but it also loses the rare event we may be looking for


This distribution has a name, Zipf’s law, and it appears in nearly every language and corpus.

title: CADC
text:
Stemming or lemmatising


sotu_tokens |>
  filter(word %in% c("nations", "governing", "better",
                     "countries", "was")) |>
  distinct(word) |>
  mutate(stem  = SnowballC::wordStem(word),
         lemma = textstem::lemmatize_words(word))

A stem is cut by rule: fast, language-agnostic, sometimes not a word
A lemma is looked up: the dictionary form, so was becomes be
For a word list (and thus for the dictionary approach) you want lemmas: the list contains country, not countri



Output



# A tibble: 5 × 3
  word      stem    lemma  
  <chr>     <chr>   <chr>  
1 was       wa      be     
2 nations   nation  nation 
3 better    better  good   
4 countries countri country
5 governing govern  govern

title: CADC
section: One sentence, two kinds of normalising
text:
One sentence, two kinds of normalising

  Sentencethestatesweregoverningtheircountriesbetter
  ↓ SnowballC::wordStem() cuts the ending by rule
  Stemmedthestateweregoverntheircountribetter
  ↓ textstem::lemmatize_words() looks the word up
  Lemmatisedthestatebegoverntheircountrygood


The stemmer leaves were and better alone and clips countries to a non-word. The lemmatiser returns be, good and country.


Read the three rows top to bottom. Row two: the stemmer only strips endings, so states becomes state but were stays were, and countries becomes countri, which is not a word. Row three: the lemmatiser looks every word up, so were is be, better is good, countries is country. Same functions as the previous slide, now on a whole sentence.

title: CADC
section: The same counts, as a cloud and as bars
text:
The same counts, as a cloud and as bars























Both show absolute frequency in the whole corpus. The cloud looks good, but only the bars let you compare the words.


Same table of counts, two pictures. In the cloud you can see that government is bigger than country, but not by how much, and the placement of the words carries no information at all: the layout is random, and long words look bigger than short ones. In the bars the order and the distance are readable. Either way the biggest words are generic (government, congress, united, people), so they say little about any particular speech. That is the motivation for the next slides: weight the counts by how unevenly a word is spread.

title: CADC
text:
How tf-idf weights a word



Raw counts reward words every speech uses, like government and congress
So counts alone cannot show which words set one president apart
tf is the share of a president’s words that a word makes up
idf is ln(4 ÷ presidents who use the word): 0 if all four use it, 1.39 if only one does
tf-idf is tf × idf: high only for a word that is frequent here and rare elsewhere


america is Obama’s most frequent word and scores zero, because all four presidents say it.



Four words in Obama’s speeches



# A tibble: 4 × 6
  word            n       tf presidents   idf   tf_idf
  <chr>       <int>    <dbl>      <int> <dbl>    <dbl>
1 isil            9 0.000438          1 1.39  0.000608
2 industry       24 0.00117           2 0.693 0.000810
3 afghanistan    23 0.00112           3 0.288 0.000322
4 america       204 0.00994           4 0     0       




Work along one row. america: 204 mentions, about 1 percent of Obama’s words, but all four presidents use it, so idf is ln(4/4) = 0 and the product is zero. isil: nine mentions, 0.04 percent of his words, but only Obama uses it, so idf is ln(4/1) = 1.39 and it outranks america. The unit of comparison is the president (all of a president’s speeches pooled), which is why the fraction has a 4 in it. Next slide: the one call that computes this.

title: CADC
section: What makes a president’s speeches distinctive
text:
What makes a president’s speeches distinctive
sotu_tfidf <- sotu_tokens |>
  filter(president %in% c("Barack Obama", "Donald Trump",
                          "George W. Bush", "William J. Clinton")) |>
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") |>
  count(president, word) |>                    # term frequency, per president
  bind_tf_idf(word, president, n)              # ... weighted by how few presidents use the word

All speeches of one president are pooled into a single document, so the idf compares four presidents
Raw counts would put america, people and congress on top for everyone
bind_tf_idf() adds tf, idf and tf-idf as columns next to the counts


The first weighting you meet. It sees only how unevenly a word is spread, not what it means.


Silge, J., & Robinson, D. (2017). Text mining with R: A tidy approach. O’Reilly. Chapter 3.

title: CADC
section: What makes a president’s speeches distinctive
text:
What makes a president’s speeches distinctive


sotu_tfidf |>
  group_by(president) |>
  slice_max(tf_idf, n = 8) |>
  ggplot(aes(tf_idf,
      reorder_within(word, tf_idf, president))) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ president, scales = "free_y")

Each panel is one president’s most distinctive words
The crises and the enemies show up before any policy does
applause is not a word Trump said: it is the transcript’s stage direction, and tf-idf cannot tell the difference


Distinctive is not the same as important.

title: CADC
text:
The vocabulary follows the history



One row per word, one column per decade of speeches
The darker the tile, the closer the decade is to the word’s own peak
The diagonal is the history: treaties, slavery, gold, the Soviets, terrorists, jobs


Counting alone already shows what each era talked about.













Each row is the share of a decade’s words that one word makes up, scaled to the word’s own highest decade, so a dark tile means “this word at its most frequent”. The words were picked by hand, because they are easy to place in history; the weighting from the previous slides would find the same kind of words automatically. Nothing here is interpreted yet: the plot says what each era talked about, not what it thought.

title: CADC
section: What a count can tell you, and what it cannot
text:
What a count can tell you, and what it cannot



A count can say


Which words a corpus uses, and how unevenly
Which words set one document apart from the rest
How the vocabulary shifts over time



A count cannot say


Whether a speech is hopeful or fearful
Whether a tweet is about the vaccine, or against it
Anything that needs the researcher’s concept rather than the corpus’s words



To get from words to a concept, somebody has to decide which words the concept consists of. That is a dictionary!


Bridge. terror appearing 400 times after 2001 is a fact about attention. Whether the speeches became more fearful is a claim about meaning, and a count does not make claims. Part II is about the oldest way of making one.

title: CADC
text:
The first automated content analysis

  


Stone, P. J., Dunphy, D. C., Smith, M. S., & Ogilvie, D. M. (1966). The General Inquirer: A computer approach to content analysis. MIT Press.


The same timeline as last week, opened at its third screen (1958 to 1986). The node to dwell on is 1966, now its own event: the General Inquirer. Stone, Dunphy, Smith and Ogilvie at Harvard put word lists on a mainframe and counted psychological and sociological categories across texts. That is the method of this lecture, sixty years old, and the same year ELIZA showed that pattern matching can fool a reader. One click forward, on the 1990s screen, LIWC (2001) is labelled as the point where this 1966 idea went mainstream in psychology, the version most of the room has met in a paper. Nothing about the method changed in between except the size of the lists and the speed of the machine.

title: CADC
text:
What a dictionary approach is



A dictionary is a list of words per category: positive = {good, safe, hope, …}; negative = {bad, threat, war, …}
A counting rule: how many words from each list occur in a text, usually per thousand words
A decision rule: a text is positive if positive words outnumber negative ones, about migration if any migration word occurs
The book is written before the machine sees a text, by the researcher, so the method is deductive


“If word X occurs, the text means Y”: step 03 of the pipeline, and the simplest classifier this course will use.



  



Four clicks, one per bullet. The book opens with two category pages and empty lines; click 1 fills the word lists; click 2 brings in a text and lights the one word the book knows, with the count; click 3 turns the count into a label. The text is B from last week’s three sentences — “not good news” — so the book’s verdict is wrong, and the class has already seen why. Either say it now or hold it for the negation slide; the figure does not say it for you.
Tie it to the 03 · Classify table from week 1: rule based, meaning from the researcher in advance. Everything else in the course moves the meaning somewhere else: into labelled data or a training corpus. The dictionary is the case where you can read every rule, because somebody wrote the book.

title: CADC
section: A dictionary is arithmetic on the matrix
text:
A dictionary is arithmetic on the matrix


# week 1's three sentences, as a document–term matrix
dtm <- texts |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text) |>
  count(doc, word) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = word, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)

# the dictionary: a weight for every column it knows, 0 otherwise
weights <- c(good = 1, news = 1, disaster = -1)

dtm |>
  mutate(score = good * 1 + news * 1 + disaster * -1) |>
  select(doc, good, news, disaster, score)

A word list is a technically just a vector of weights over the matrix’s columns: +1, −1, or 0 for the words it does not know
The score of a text is its row multiplied by that vector: a weighted row sum
Text B scores +2, like text A. not has a column and a zero weight; give it a negative one and “not a disaster” is punished just as hard.












Same matrix as last week. The list only decides which columns count, and with what sign.


PLAYGROUNDMultiply, then add

The one slide that ties the three weeks together, so give it a minute. Week 1 built the matrix. Week 2 hand-declares a weight per column. Week 3’s Naive Bayes learns those same weights from labelled texts, and the Playground’s Let the data write the dictionary shows them side by side. Week 4 leaves the matrix altogether. Text B is the whole argument for that progression.

title: CADC
text:
The pipeline with a dictionary

  


Same row as last week, pixel for pixel. What changes is under step 03: the declared list, then a worked count on one sentence, then the traps: not good, sick as praise. Step 04 is still there and still needs the hand coded subset. Do not skip the last click: it is the reason Part III exists.

title: CADC
text:
Keyword in context


sotu_tokens |>
  group_by(doc_id) |>
  mutate(
    before = str_c(lag(word, 3), lag(word, 2),
                   lag(word, 1), sep = " "),
    after  = str_c(lead(word, 1), lead(word, 2),
                   lead(word, 3), sep = " ")) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(str_starts(word, "terror"),
         year %in% c(1850, 1883, 1918, 1987, 2011)) |>
  transmute(year, kwic = str_c(
    before, " [", word, "] ", after))

Before we put a word on a list, we should understand how it is used
Each hit comes with the three words on either side
A keyword-in-context listing is the cheapest validity check one can run



Output



# A tibble: 5 × 2
   year kwic                                              
  <int> <chr>                                             
1  1850 source of constant [terror] and annoyance to      
2  1883 puritan amphitrite and [terror] have been launched
3  1918 from the german [terror] and whom we              
4  1987 we yield to [terrorist] blackmail and now         
5  2011 the hands of [terrorists] because of a            



In 1883 terror is a navy monitor, a hit no dictionary should count.

title: CADC
section: A dictionary is nothing but a table
text:
A dictionary is nothing but a table


library(textdata)
nrc <- lexicon_nrc()

nrc |> slice_sample(n = 6)

nrc |> count(sentiment, sort = TRUE)

One row per word–category pair; a word can sit in several categories
The NRC lexicon as example: about 6,000 English words in eight emotions and two polarities, rated by crowd workers



Output



# A tibble: 6 × 2
  word       sentiment
  <chr>      <chr>    
1 caries     disgust  
2 abnormal   disgust  
3 armed      fear     
4 autopsy    sadness  
5 elated     joy      
6 visitation negative 


# A tibble: 10 × 2
  sentiment     n
  <chr>     <int>
1 negative   3316
2 positive   2308
3 fear       1474
4 anger      1245
# ℹ 6 more rows




Mohammad, S. M., & Turney, P. D. (2013). Crowdsourcing a word–emotion association lexicon. Computational Intelligence, 29(3), 436–465. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8640.2012.00460.x


The word crowdsourcing in the title matters: the categories are not a theory, they are the votes of Mechanical Turk workers in 2011 on whether abandon feels like fear. When students use NRC on a Dutch parliament, or on tweets, the gap between that room and their corpus is the first threat to validity.

title: CADC
section: Feature engineering for a word list
text:
Feature engineering for a word list


# tokens as they are
sotu_tokens |>
  inner_join(nrc, by = "word") |> nrow()

# tokens reduced to their lemma first
sotu_tokens |>
  mutate(word = textstem::lemmatize_words(word)) |>
  inner_join(nrc, by = "word") |> nrow()

Output



       raw lemmatised 
    552320     698513 




The list says nation; the text says nations, this would lead to no match
Lemmatising the text first finds a quarter more hits!
Stemming would find fewer: the stem nation matches, but govern does not match government in the list
Do not remove stop words before a sentiment list: no, not, never are the words you will need in a moment


Last week’s preprocessing decisions are this week’s measurement error.

title: CADC
section: The dictionary analysis, step by step · 1
text:
The dictionary analysis, step by step · 1


sotu_emotions <- sotu_speeches |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text)                  # 1 · tokens


Same call as last week: the speech becomes two million rows
Metadata rides along on every row, so the president and the year are still there at the end

title: CADC
section: The dictionary analysis, step by step · 2
text:
The dictionary analysis, step by step · 2


sotu_emotions <- sotu_speeches |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text) |>               # 1 · tokens
  mutate(word = lemmatize_words(word))       # 2 · lemmas


Normalise the text to the form the list uses, not the other way round
A list of stems would need stemmed text; a list of lemmas needs lemmatised text

title: CADC
section: The dictionary analysis, step by step · 3
text:
The dictionary analysis, step by step · 3


sotu_emotions <- sotu_speeches |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text) |>               # 1 · tokens
  mutate(word = lemmatize_words(word)) |>    # 2 · lemmas
  inner_join(nrc, by = "word") |>            # 3 · join
  count(doc_id, president, year, sentiment)  # 4 · count

sotu_emotions

inner_join keeps only the tokens the list knows; left_join would keep every token and put NA in the category
The join is the whole classifier. Everything else is bookkeeping



Output



# A tibble: 2,400 × 4
  doc_id  year sentiment        n
   <int> <int> <chr>        <int>
1      1  1790 anger           10
2      1  1790 anticipation    55
3      1  1790 disgust          4
4      1  1790 fear            20
5      1  1790 joy             40
6      1  1790 negative        23
7      1  1790 positive       159
8      1  1790 sadness          6
# ℹ 2,392 more rows

title: CADC
section: Emotion in two hundred and forty speeches
text:
Emotion in two hundred and forty speeches


sotu_emotions |>
  group_by(doc_id) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(share, sentiment)) +
  geom_jitter(height = .2, alpha = .3) +
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "point")

One dot per speech; the marker is the median
Presidents are trusting and positive by profession; fear and disgust are rare on this stage
The spread is the interesting part: some speeches are three times as fearful as others


A share of matched words, not a share of all words: silence is not counted here.

title: CADC
text:
Emotion over two centuries


sotu_emotions |>
  filter(sentiment %in%
           c("fear", "trust", "anger")) |>
  group_by(doc_id) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, share, colour = sentiment)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ sentiment, nrow = 1)

Trust words fall away after 1950; anger words rise after 1990; fear is flat, with spikes in 1812, the 1860s and the 1940s
Each dot is one speech; the smooth line is a loess fit through them


Before you believe the trend: what else changed in 230 years?













The obvious reading is “presidents got angrier and stopped trusting”. The fear spikes are wars, which is reassuring, because the instrument sees something. Two rival readings for the trends, both about the instrument rather than the presidents: the lexicon was rated in 2011, so 1790’s vocabulary matches it worse; and the genre changed: written reports until 1913, then speeches to a chamber, then to a television audience. None of this is visible in the line. That is the argument for Part III.

title: CADC
section: What a dictionary score leaves open
text:
What a dictionary score leaves open

Whether died in “three people died in the crash” is a negative opinion or a negative fact
Whether the texts with no word on the list are neutral, or just use other words
Whether “great, another delay” is positive, as the list says, or sarcastic, as you read it
Whether a list built from product reviews in 2004 or rated in 2011 is about the same thing as your construct


A dictionary returns a number for every text. Whether the number measures anything cannot be read off the number.


Hu, M., & Liu, B. (2004). Mining and summarizing customer reviews. Proceedings of the 10th ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining, 168–177. https://doi.org/10.1145/1014052.1014073


These are general limits of dictionaries, not of one data set. The emotion lines on the last two slides have all four: the lexicon was rated in 2011, many speeches have words it does not know, and anger in a war speech can be a fact about the enemy. Every bullet is a construct-validity question, and every one is answerable only by comparing the list’s verdicts with a human’s. Break here for five minutes, then open Part III with the gold standard.

title: CADC
section: Where a gold standard comes from
text:
Where a gold standard comes from

Draw a sample of texts the instrument will be judged on — random, or stratified so rare cases are in it
Write a codebook: the categories, and a rule for every case the coders will argue about
Two or more people code the sample independently, without seeing the instrument’s output
Measure their agreement; where it is poor, the codebook is the problem, not the coders
Only then compare the instrument against the human codes


Gold is a metaphor. What you have is the best reading humans can agree on, under rules you wrote.


Krippendorff, K. (2019). Content analysis: An introduction to its methodology (4th ed.). Sage. Chapters 11–12.


Point back to the week 1 slide Content analysis, by hand: this is steps 1, 2, 3 and 5 of that list. Thursday’s lab is exactly this procedure on the review corpus, and the sample they code becomes the reference set for weeks 3 and 4 — say that now so the lab does not feel like an exercise.

title: CADC
text:
Two coders, twenty reviews

  

PLAYGROUNDTwo coders, one codebook

The twenty reviews and both coders come from the Playground’s Two coders, one codebook: same texts, same codebook, so a student who did the tool on Sunday recognises them.
Five screens. Screen 1: both rows of labels. Screen 2: the thirteen agreements tick, 65%. Ask: is 65% good?
