Screen 3 is the one to slow down on. Chance means: coder B keeps the same labels, but in a random order. Some reviews still match, here 7; averaged over many shuffles it is 6.55 of 20, 33%. The sum under it is the same number by hand: B used + eleven times, so of A’s seven + reviews B would give + to 7 × 11 / 20, and likewise for − and ±. Coder A used mixed seven times, coder B never did, so that term is zero.
Screen 4: κ on a ruler. Chance already gets you to 6.55, perfect is 20, so there are 13.45 agreements left to earn. The coders earned 6.45 of them: 6.45 / 13.45 = .48. In shares that is (.65 − .33) / (1 − .33), the formula on the next slide.
Screen 5: a hundred items, 90 negative for both coders, each coder labels ten items positive and they share one. They agree on 82 items, and shuffled labels agree on 82 as well, so the gain over chance is 0 and κ is 0.00. Higher raw agreement than the reviews (82% against 65%) and nothing measured.
The disagreements all have one shape: praise and criticism in one sentence, and a codebook that never said what to do about it. That is what the Two coders tool has them fix.

title: CADC
text:
Cohen’s κ



Agreement between two coders, corrected for the agreement they would reach by luck
po: the share of items both coders label the same, here 13 of 20 = .65
pe: the agreement luck gives when each coder keeps their own label shares, here .33
1 is perfect agreement, 0 is no better than luck


Formula

κ = (po − pe) / (1 − pe) = (.65 − .33) / (1 − .33) = .48

coded <- tibble(item = 1:20, coder_a, coder_b)

library(yardstick)        # part of tidymodels
coded |> kap(coder_a, coder_b)

Output



# A tibble: 1 × 3
  .metric .estimator .estimate
  <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
1 kap     multiclass     0.480



The twenty reviews of the explainer: 65% agreement is a κ of .48.



Three steps, in the order of the explainer. po is the plain percent agreement, the thirteen ticks. pe is what the shuffle gave: for each label, coder A’s share times coder B’s share, added up over the labels (.35 × .55 + .30 × .45 + .35 × 0 = .33). κ is how far the coders got from .33 towards 1, the ruler.
In practice nobody computes this by hand: kap() from yardstick (installed with tidymodels) takes the two columns. It treats the first as “truth”, but κ is symmetric, so the order does not matter. Thursday’s lab computes pe and κ by hand once, so the formula is not a black box.


Cohen, J. (1960). A coefficient of agreement for nominal scales. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 20(1), 37–46. https://doi.org/10.1177/001316446002000104

title: CADC
text:
Krippendorff’s α



Disagreement between coders, compared with the disagreement expected by luck
Do: the share of items the coders disagree on, here 7 of 20 = .35
De: how often two codes drawn at random from all codes pooled differ, here .64
Works for any number of coders, with missing codes, and for ordinal or interval scales


Formula

α = 1 − Do / De = 1 − .35 / .64 = .46

codes <- c(coded$coder_a, coded$coder_b)
n_c <- table(codes)                 # 18, 15, 7
N   <- length(codes)                # 40

D_o <- mean(coded$coder_a != coded$coder_b)
D_e <- 1 - sum(n_c * (n_c - 1)) / (N * (N - 1))
round(1 - D_o / D_e, 2)

Output



[1] 0.46



.46 against κ’s .48. They differ because only one coder used mixed.



α counts disagreement instead of agreement. Do is the seven crosses of the explainer. De has a simple reading: put all forty codes of both coders on one pile, draw two at random, and ask how often their labels differ. Of the 1,560 ordered pairs in the pile, 558 carry the same label, so two random draws differ 64 per cent of the time. The coders disagreed 35 per cent of the time, so α = 1 − .35 / .64.
The code is the two-coder, no-missing-data case. For more coders or missing codes the general version builds a coincidence matrix; the R package irr does that with kripp.alpha().
Why α and κ differ: κ builds chance from each coder’s own habits, α from the pooled pile. A’s seven mixed codes inflate A’s share for κ and are diluted in the pile for α.


Krippendorff, K. (2011). Computing Krippendorff’s alpha-reliability. University of Pennsylvania. https://repository.upenn.edu/asc_papers/43

title: CADC
section: κ and α side by side
text:
κ and α side by side









Cohen’s κ
Krippendorff’s α




Coders
exactly two
any number


Missing codes
not allowed
handled


Level of measurement
nominal (weighted κ for ordinal)
nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio


Chance model
each coder’s own marginals
all values pooled


Conventions
none the author endorses; the .41 / .61 / .81 bands are folklore
≥ .80 reportable; ≥ .667 for tentative conclusions


In this course
the lab, because you are two
the group project, because α is what journals ask for




Report the number, the number of coders, the number of units, and the category frequencies. Without the last, no coefficient can be read.


Landis, J. R., & Koch, G. G. (1977). The measurement of observer agreement for categorical data. Biometrics, 33(1), 159–174. https://doi.org/10.2307/2529310

title: CADC
text:
Agreement is not correctness

Two coders can agree perfectly and both be wrong: agreement measures shared reading, not truth
The codebook decides what the gold standard is: a different rule for “praise and criticism” produces a different gold set from the same texts
Every instrument validated against that set inherits the rule, silently
So the codebook is part of the measurement, and it goes in the methods section


A gold standard is something people made. Reliability tells you they made it consistently; nothing tells you they made it right.


This is the sentence the Two coders tool ends on. Adding a decision rule sends κ to 1.00 and changes nothing about whether the coding is correct. Thursday’s lab asks for exactly this: the codebook is written, and the rule for praise and criticism decided, before anyone codes a tweet.

title: CADC
section: Now the machine, against a thousand labelled sentences
text:
Now the machine, against a thousand labelled sentences


yelp <- read_csv("data/yelp-sentences.csv")

yelp |> slice_sample(n = 6)

yelp |> count(label)

One thousand single-sentence restaurant reviews, each with a human label, half positive and half negative
The labels play the role of the gold standard; the Bing word list plays the instrument



Output



# A tibble: 6 × 2
  text                               label   
  <chr>                              <chr>   
1 I love the fact that everything... positive
2 I don't think I'll be running b... negative
3 I can take a little bad service... negative
4 Third, the cheese on my friend'... negative
5 An absolute must visit!            positive
6 I work in the hospitality indus... negative


# A tibble: 2 × 2
  label        n
  <chr>    <int>
1 negative   500
2 positive   500




Kotzias, D., Denil, M., de Freitas, N., & Smyth, P. (2015). From group to individual labels using deep features. Proceedings of the 21st ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining, 597–606. https://doi.org/10.1145/2783258.2783380

title: CADC
section: Scoring the sentences · 1 · a score per sentence
text:
Scoring the sentences · 1 · a score per sentence


scored <- yelp |>
  unnest_tokens(word, text) |>         # 1
  inner_join(bing, by = "word") |>     # 2
  count(id, sentiment) |>              # 3
  pivot_wider(names_from = sentiment,  # 4
              values_from = n,
              values_fill = 0) |>
  mutate(score = positive - negative)  # 5

print(scored, n = 5)

One row per word of each sentence
Keep only the words on the Bing list, each with its sentiment
Count the positive and the negative words per sentence
Back to one row per sentence, with 0 where a sentiment is missing
The score: positive words minus negative words



Output



# A tibble: 782 × 4
     id positive negative score
  <dbl>    <int>    <int> <int>
1     1        2        0     2
2     2        1        0     1
3     3        0        1    -1
4     4        2        0     2
5     5        1        0     1
# ℹ 777 more rows



782 of the 1,000 sentences contain a word on the list. The other 218 are not in scored at all.



The same recipe as the speeches, line by line. Follow sentence 1, “Wow… Loved this place.”: step 1 splits it into four words, step 2 keeps wow and loved (both positive on the Bing list), step 3 counts two positive words, step 4 adds a zero for negative, step 5 gives a score of 2.
The header of the output is the point to stop at: 782 rows, not 1,000. inner_join() drops every word the list does not know, and a sentence with no known word drops out entirely. The next slide brings them back.

title: CADC
section: Scoring the sentences · 2 · from score to verdict
text:
Scoring the sentences · 2 · from score to verdict


verdicts <- yelp |>
  left_join(scored, by = "id") |>     # 1
  mutate(verdict = case_when(         # 2
    score > 0 ~ "positive",
    score < 0 ~ "negative",
    TRUE      ~ "no call"))           # 3

verdicts |>
  filter(id %in% c(1, 2, 12, 18, 32)) |>
  select(text, score, verdict)

count(verdicts, verdict)

Back to all 1,000 sentences: the 218 without a listed word get NA as score
The decision rule: above 0 is positive, below 0 is negative
Everything else is “no call”: 60 ties and the 218 with NA



Output



# A tibble: 5 × 3
  text                                   score verdict 
  <chr>                                  <int> <chr>   
1 Wow... Loved this place.                   2 positive
2 Crust is not good.                         1 positive
3 Would not go back.                        NA no call 
4 Waitress was a little slow in service.    -1 negative
5 This was like the final blow!              0 no call 


# A tibble: 3 × 2
  verdict      n
  <chr>    <int>
1 negative   224
2 no call    278
3 positive   498



Every sentence now has two labels: the human’s and the list’s. Validation is the comparison.



Read the five example sentences. “Wow… Loved this place.” is positive, as it should be. “Crust is not good.” is also positive: the list sees good and nothing else, which is the negation slide coming up. “Would not go back.” has no word on the list, so its score is NA and it gets no call. “Waitress was a little slow in service.” is negative through slow. “This was like the final blow!” has one positive (like) and one negative (blow) word, a tie, so no call either.
left_join() instead of inner_join() is the important choice here: it keeps the sentences the list could not score, so we can count them later instead of silently losing them.

title: CADC
text:
The confusion matrix

  


Eight clicks, and the same twenty reviews again, now with a word list’s verdict beside the human label. Click 1: the list’s verdicts. Click 2: the reviews sort into four cells: human label down the side, verdict along the top. Click 3: the names — true positive, false positive, false negative, true negative. Say them in the order “the verdict was positive, and that was true / false”.
Clicks 4 to 7: each metric lights the cells it uses. Accuracy: the diagonal over everything. Precision: of the verdicts that said positive, how many were. Recall: of the texts that were positive, how many the list found. F1: their harmonic mean. The two errors are Never boring and Long, but never dull, both negation, and Beautiful to look at, and nothing else and I wanted to like it, both praise words in a negative sentence.
Real numbers are on the next slide; this one is for the shape.

title: CADC
section: The confusion matrix, on the real data
text:
The confusion matrix, on the real data


called <- verdicts |>
  filter(verdict != "no call") |>
  mutate(across(c(label, verdict), factor,
                levels = c("positive", "negative")))

with(called, table(human = label, list = verdict))

722 sentences the list was willing to judge
397 positive sentences it called positive; 210 negative ones it called negative
101 negative sentences called positive: the cell with the negations in it
Only 14 positive sentences missed


Rows are the truth, columns the verdict. Every number you report from now on is a ratio of these four cells.

title: CADC
text:
Accuracy, precision, recall, F1


class_metrics <- metric_set(accuracy, precision,
                            recall, f_meas, kap)

called |>
  class_metrics(truth = label, estimate = verdict)

Output



# A tibble: 5 × 2
  .metric   .estimate
  <chr>         <dbl>
1 accuracy      0.841
2 precision     0.797
3 recall        0.966
4 f_meas        0.873
5 kap           0.664




Accuracy: share of all verdicts that were right: (TP + TN) / all
Precision: of the sentences called positive, the share that were: TP / (TP + FP)
Recall: of the positive sentences, the share the list found: TP / (TP + FN)
F1: the harmonic mean of the two, which punishes a lopsided pair
κ: accuracy corrected for chance, exactly as between two coders


Recall .97 and precision .80: the list finds nearly every positive sentence, and calls a fifth of the negative ones positive too.


PLAYGROUNDBuild-a-dictionary

title: CADC
text:
Which number do you report?

A moderation filter for hate speech wants recall: a missed case does harm; a wrongly flagged one costs a human review
A sample of “tweets about the vaccine” for a study wants precision: every false positive pollutes the sample
F1 when the two errors cost about the same and you need one number to compare instruments
Accuracy only with the base rate beside it; the next slides show why
All of them per class: a positive-class F1 says nothing about the negative class


The right metric follows from what an error costs in your study. Decide that in the specification, not after seeing the results.

title: CADC
text:
Sentences the list cannot call


no_call <- verdicts |>
  filter(verdict == "no call") |>
  mutate(why = if_else(is.na(score),
                       "no listed word", "tie"))

count(no_call, why, label)

No call means the list has nothing to say: none of the words is on the list, or the positive and negative words cancel out
“Would not go back.” has no listed word; “This was like the final blow!” is a tie, like against blow



Output



# A tibble: 4 × 3
  why            label        n
  <chr>          <chr>    <int>
1 no listed word negative   144
2 no listed word positive    74
3 tie            negative    45
4 tie            positive    15



278 of 1,000 sentences: 218 without a listed word, 60 ties
They are not neutral: the human labels say 189 of them are negative and 89 positive


No call is still an outcome. Before you report a number, decide what happens to these 278 sentences.



Define the term before the numbers. A sentence gets no call in two ways: the list knows none of its words (218 sentences, “Would not go back.”), or it knows some, and they cancel out (60 sentences, like plus blow). The human labels show that silence is not neutrality: two thirds of these sentences are negative. Many are negative complaints phrased without any evaluative word, “Would not go back”, “They never brought a salad we asked for”.

title: CADC
section: Three ways to count the no-call sentences
text:
Three ways to count the no-call sentences







Rule
Sentences
Precision
Recall
F1




Leave them out
722
0.80
0.97
0.87


Count as negative
1,000
0.80
0.79
0.80


Count as positive
1,000
0.63
0.97
0.76






Coverage, the share of texts an instrument says anything about, is a validity number too. Report it.



Leave them out: the list is judged only where it found words, which flatters it
Count as negative: the 89 positive reviews among them become misses, so recall falls
Count as positive: the 189 negative ones become false alarms, so precision falls
Negative is the usual default, because the question is whether the list finds the positive reviews, and saying nothing does not find them. It remains a decision, and the paper has to state it



Precision and recall here are for the positive class. Each rule moves the same 278 sentences into a different cell of the confusion matrix: out of the matrix, into the “said negative” column, or into the “said positive” column. Leaving them out gives the best numbers and describes only 722 of 1,000 sentences. Counting them as negative is the convention when the instrument is meant to detect positive texts: no evidence for positive counts as not positive, and the cost shows up in recall. Counting them as positive is just as possible and moves the cost to precision. Thursday’s lab adds a fourth option for the tweets: call them neutral. Whatever the rule, the methods section has to name it and report the coverage, 722 of 1,000.

title: CADC
text:
Where it goes wrong: negation


verdicts |>
  filter(str_detect(text, "\\bnot\\b|n't"),
         verdict == "positive", label == "negative") |>
  select(text)

The word list has no entry for not: good scores +1 whether or not it is negated, and the matrix cannot say what the not was attached to
Fifty-eight of the 101 false positives contain not or n’t
Fixes exist (flip the sign of the next word, count bigrams, use a list with negated entries), and each is a new decision to validate



Output



# A tibble: 8 × 1
  text                                                
  <chr>                                               
1 Crust is not good.                                  
2 Honeslty it didn't taste THAT fresh.)               
3 This place is not worth your time, let alone Vegas. 
4 did not like at all.                                
5 There is not a deal good enough that would drag m...
6 It was not good.                                    
7 REAL sushi lovers, let's be honest - Yama is not ...
8 The waiter wasn't helpful or friendly and rarely ...



“Not good at all” from the Playground, a thousand times over.

title: CADC
section: More than two classes: macro and micro
text:
More than two classes: macro and micro


with(three, table(human = gold, list = verdict))

per_class <- three |>
  group_by(verdict) |>
  summarise(precision = mean(gold == verdict))
per_class

round(c(macro = mean(per_class$precision),
        micro = mean(three$gold == three$verdict)), 2)

Per class: of the reviews the list called positive, all were right (1.00); of those it called mixed, .65
Macro averages the three precisions: every class counts equally
Micro pools all reviews first: every review counts equally, and for precision that is simply accuracy



Output



          list
human      positive negative mixed
  positive       11        1     3
  negative        0       14     4
  mixed           0        2    13


# A tibble: 3 × 2
  verdict  precision
  <fct>        <dbl>
1 positive     1    
2 negative     0.824
3 mixed        0.65 


macro micro 
 0.82  0.79 



Report per class, and say which average you used. A single macro figure hides the class your instrument cannot see.



48 hand-coded film reviews in three classes, and an instrument’s verdicts on them. The instrument here is a language model prompted with the codebook (you meet it in week 4). It is used only because the course has a three-class gold set for it (data/prompt-lab/). The point is the arithmetic, not the model.
Read the table by column: the list called 11 reviews positive and all 11 were positive; it called 20 mixed and 13 of those were. Precision per class is the share correct within each column, which is what group_by(verdict) computes. Macro is the plain mean of the three, (1.00 + .82 + .65) / 3 = .82. Micro counts every correct review once, 38 of 48 = .79. yardstick gives the same with precision(three, gold, verdict, estimator = "macro") or "micro".

title: CADC
text:
Class imbalance













The same dictionary, used on corpora where positive texts are more or less common
Its accuracy stays at 80% everywhere, so it looks equally good in all of them
When positive texts are rare, most of what it flags is wrong: at 5% positives, only 17% of the flagged texts are positive
A useless rule, “always say negative”, would even beat it on accuracy


When a class is rare, accuracy says almost nothing. Look at precision and recall.



Nothing about the instrument changes along the x-axis: it always catches 79 per cent of the positive texts and correctly rejects 80 per cent of the negative ones (the dictionary’s numbers from a few slides back). What changes is how many positive texts there are to catch.
Walk the vertical line at 5 per cent. In a corpus of 1,000 texts, 50 are positive and the list flags 40 of them. Of the 950 negative texts it wrongly flags 20 per cent, 190. So it flags 230 texts, and only 40 of those are right: precision 17 per cent. Accuracy still reads 80 per cent, because most of the 950 negative texts are correctly left alone. A lazy instrument that calls every text negative reaches 95 per cent accuracy and finds nothing.
This is the situation of most real measurement tasks in communication research: hate speech, misinformation, a rare frame. The thing you look for is rare.

title: CADC
text:
How sure are you?












Bars: 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, from 1,000 resamples of each size drawn from the 1,000 coded sentences. Dots: median F1.



The same dictionary, checked against hand-coded samples of different sizes
With 50 coded texts, its F1 could be anywhere between .65 and .91: from unusable to good
With 1,000 coded texts, it is pinned between .77 and .82
The smaller the validation sample, the less a validation score tells you


A validation set of 50 is a rumour about your instrument. Code more, or report the interval.



The dictionary and the corpus stay the same; only the number of hand-coded texts changes. To see what a small validation sample would have told us, we draw many random samples from the 1,000 coded sentences (with replacement, a bootstrap) and compute F1 in each. The spread of those values is the uncertainty you live with when you code only that many texts.
With 50 texts the same instrument could look unusable or good, depending on which 50 you happened to code. With 1,000 the estimate is pinned down. This is the practical answer to “how many texts should we hand-code”: enough that the interval is narrow for the decision you have to make.

title: CADC
text:
Do dictionaries measure sentiment?



Dutch economic news, 2015; three-class sentiment, hand-coded gold standard
The same texts measured by trained coders, crowd workers, three classifiers, and fourteen dictionaries
Agreement with the gold standard as Krippendorff’s α, the way you would report your own coders


No dictionary reaches α = .35. The worst human reaches .75. That is the gap this week is about.












Redrawn from Table 2. Blue: humans, orange-red: machines.



van Atteveldt, W., van der Velden, M. A. C. G., & Boukes, M. (2021). The validity of sentiment analysis: Comparing manual annotation, crowd-coding, dictionary approaches, and machine learning algorithms. Communication Methods and Measures, 15(2), 121–140. https://doi.org/10.1080/19312458.2020.1869198


The paper the course keeps returning to. Two things to take from it. First, the ordering: humans, then crowd, then supervised learning, then every dictionary, and it does not matter which dictionary. Second, the dictionaries were not built for this corpus: Dutch economic news, scored by lists made for English product reviews or finance filings. The next two lectures move up this chart; week 4’s language models land above the classifiers and near the crowd.

title: CADC
section: Example 1 · Who gets to speak in pandemic news
text:
Example 1 · Who gets to speak in pandemic news



940,000 posts about COVID-19 from 78 news outlets on Facebook, Instagram and Twitter, seven countries, all of 2020
Question: which sources does pandemic news quote — politicians, doctors, scientists, citizens?
Half of all sources are political, in every country; health sources second, citizens a distant third
Elite orientation survives a health emergency


A construct that is a word list: a source is a name, a title, an institution.












Redrawn from Table 2 (global column). Mellado et al. (2021).



Mellado, C., Hallin, D., Cárcamo, L., Alfaro, R., Jackson, D., Humanes, M. L., … Ramos, A. (2021). Sourcing pandemic news: A cross-national computational analysis of mainstream media coverage of COVID-19 on Facebook, Twitter, and Instagram. Digital Journalism, 9(9), 1271–1295. https://doi.org/10.1080/21670811.2021.1942114

title: CADC
section: Example 1 · How the dictionary was built
text:
Example 1 · How the dictionary was built

Eleven source categories, each broken into positions, names, institutions, organisations, nicknames and acronyms
Each national team translated and extended the list for its own country and language
10,102 entries, a dictionary of who is speaking
Built from the corpus and the coders’ knowledge, then applied to all 940,000 posts


This is where dictionaries are strongest: a closed, enumerable category, where the presence of a name is the measurement.


Ask what validation looks like here. Precision is nearly free: a match on “Fauci” is a health source. Recall is the problem: every source you did not think of is missed, and the missing ones are systematically the less famous. That is the recall trap of every hand-built list.

title: CADC
section: Example 2 · Migration on politicians’ Facebook pages
text:
Example 2 · Migration on politicians’ Facebook pages

24,578 migration-related posts by 1,702 members of parliament in six European countries, 2013–2017
Two questions: how visible is migration on each party’s page, and how negative is the tone?
Every post machine-translated into English, then scored with the Lexicoder Sentiment Dictionary: positive words minus negative words, per word
Hypothesis: parties of the right talk more, and more negatively, about migration


Two dictionary decisions stacked: a translation model and a word list, and the paper’s validity rests on both.


Heidenreich, T., Eberl, J.-M., Lind, F., & Boomgaarden, H. (2020). Political migration discourses on social media: A comparative perspective on visibility and sentiment across political Facebook accounts in Europe. Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies, 46(7), 1261–1280. https://doi.org/10.1080/1369183X.2019.1665990
Young, L., & Soroka, S. (2012). Affective news: The automated coding of sentiment in political texts. Political Communication, 29(2), 205–231. https://doi.org/10.1080/10584609.2012.671234

title: CADC
text:
Example 2 · Sentiment by ideological position



Not what was hypothesised: the tone is most negative at both ends of the left–right scale
Moderate parties in the middle are mildly positive; the extremes on either side are negative
The visibility finding is the same shape: extremes post about migration more, whatever their side


The finding stands or falls with the list’s ability to read a translated Facebook post. The paper says so in its limitations.












Redrawn from Figure 2. Values read from the published figure, approximate. Heidenreich et al. (2020).

title: CADC
section: When a word list is the right tool
text:
When a word list is the right tool



For


Transparent: every rule can be read, and shared
Cheap: no training data, runs on a laptop in seconds
Deterministic: the same text gets the same label tomorrow
Excellent for closed categories — names, actors, topics with a fixed vocabulary



Against


Low validity for anything that lives in context: sentiment, frames, irony
Silent on texts that use other words; blind to negation
A list built for one corpus and decade measures something else on another
Encodes its makers’ vocabulary, and their biases, as the construct



Each point on the right calls for a validation result, and no point on the left excuses you from producing one.

title: CADC
text:
Building your own

Define the category in words a coder could apply: the codebook first
Read keyword-in-context listings for candidate words; keep the ones that mean what you think they mean
Add spellings, inflections and lemmas; decide what to do with negation
Score a hand-coded sample; read the false positives and drop the words that cause them
Read the false negatives and find the words you missed
Repeat on a fresh sample — a list tuned on the texts it is scored against will not hold


The Playground’s build-a-dictionary is steps 4 to 6 on twenty texts, with precision and recall updating as you type.

PLAYGROUNDBuild-a-dictionary

Step 6 is the one students skip, and it is the week 3 idea in miniature: fitting to the sample you evaluate on. Adding nasty because you saw it in a negative sentence is fine; adding it because it fixed your F1 on those twenty texts is overfitting a word list.

title: CADC
text:
Conclusion: what a dictionary is



A dictionary stores what people know about words: which words signal a category
Applying it means looking words up, the way you look up an entry in a reference book
So it is only as good as that knowledge: who wrote the list, for which texts, and when
That is why it has to be validated on your own texts, against human judgement


A dictionary hands human knowledge about words to the computer. Validation checks whether that knowledge fits your texts.




The Encyclopædia Britannica, one of the largest reference works in English: knowledge written down by people, to be looked up.



Photo: TSTPL Pedia (2007). Britannica Micropedia Ready Reference Index 1–7. Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:HK_Britannica_Micropedia_Ready_Reference_Index_1-7.JPG


The one sentence to leave the room with before the week overview. Everything in Part II was lookup: a list of words that people judged to be positive, fearful or about migration, applied to new text. Like an encyclopedia, the list holds knowledge that people wrote down for others to look up, and like an encyclopedia it is written at a time, for a purpose, by particular people. Part III was about checking whether that knowledge fits the texts at hand. Week 3 changes who writes the list: the computer learns the word weights from labelled examples instead.

title: CADC
section: What you can do after this week.
text:
What you can do after this week.

Turn a corpus into counts, weight them, and say what a count can and cannot claim
Apply a dictionary as a join, and name the preprocessing decisions that change its result
Build a gold standard: sample, codebook, independent coders, agreement
Compute and read κ and α, and say why raw agreement is not reportable
Read a confusion matrix and choose between accuracy, precision, recall and F1 for a given cost of error
Say what class imbalance, silence and sample size do to those numbers


Everything in Part III applies unchanged to the classifier in week 3 and the language model in week 4. Only the instrument changes.

title: CADC

Week 4 · Lecture


Large language models
as research instruments


  
    Dr. Philipp K. Masur
    Computational Analysis of Digital Communication · Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

title: CADC
text:
The machine, running

  


Seven clicks, and the numbers are real: the ten most probable next tokens at every step were produced by Llama 3.1 8B on this laptop, through Ollama, and packed into the page. Nothing runs in the browser.
The opening screen is the machine idle: thirty-two layers, a prompt waiting at the bottom. Say the one sentence that is the whole lecture: given the text so far, a language model produces a probability for every token in its vocabulary. Click 1: the prompt goes up the tower and the first distribution appears. “Delicious” won with nine percent — nine other words were nearly as likely. Click 2: it runs. Watch the sentence assemble on the left while the bars change on the right; every token is one full pass through the model. Click again to skip to the end, or let it finish. Click 3 stops: seventeen tokens, seventeen distributions, nothing “written”. At temperature zero the top token is taken every time.
Click 4 is the turn: the same operation with a classification prompt. The instruction is the codebook, the review is the text, and the first token of the answer is the label. Click 5, a borderline review: positive at 94 percent. Click 6, a review the model is unsure about: positive 79, “mixed” 13 — a label the codebook did not offer. What you report is one word. What the model computed is the chart. Do not explain transformers here; Part II opens the tower.

title: CADC
text:
We may hope that machines will eventually compete with men in all purely intellectual fields. But which are the best ones to start with? […] It can also be maintained that it is best to provide the machine with the best sense organs that money can buy, and then teach it to understand and speak English. […] We can only see a short distance ahead, but we can see plenty there that needs to be done.
Alan Turing, 1950


Seventy-six years later the machine speaks English. This lecture is about what it is doing when it does, and what that is worth to a content analysis.


Turing, A. M. (1950). Computing machinery and intelligence. Mind, 59(236), 433–460. https://doi.org/10.1093/mind/LIX.236.433 — closing paragraph.


Last week’s cold open ended on the 1958 press conference. Turing is eight years earlier and more careful: not “will be conscious” but “compete in intellectual fields”, and the proposal is exactly the one the field took — teach it English. The last sentence is the register for today: plenty to be done, and most of it is validation.

title: CADC
section: What if you could just ask?
text:
What if you could just ask?




Her (Spike Jonze, 2013). Theodore talks to an operating system that reads his mail, sorts it, and answers back.



Three weeks of wrangling, word lists, splits, recipes and grid searches — for one label per text
In 2013 this was science fiction: a machine you describe the task to, in your own words, and it does it
Since late 2022 it is a product, and since 2024 it runs on the laptop
The question for a researcher is not whether it works. It is how can we know that it does what it is supposed to do?


This week the instruction replaces the training. The validation does not.



Jonze, S. (Director). (2013). Her [Film]. Annapurna Pictures. Still reproduced for teaching.

title: CADC
text:
… and it does work


library(tidyllm)

abstract <- sci_test$text[1]      # one of last week's held-out abstracts

llm_message(str_c(
  "Which discipline is this abstract from: physics, computer science ",
  "or statistics? Answer with the field only.\n\n", abstract)) |>
  chat(ollama(.model = "llama3.1:8b", .temperature = 0)) |>
  get_reply()

No recipe, no training set, no fitted object: a question in English and a model that runs locally
The answer arrives in about two seconds



The abstract



The Reduced PC-Algorithm: Improved Causal Structure
Learning in Large Random Networks We consider the
task of estimating a high-dimensional directed
acyclic graph, given observations from a linear
structural equation model with arbitrary noise
distribution....



Output



Statistics


human label: statistics 



Right, on the first try. Whether it is right on the next thousand is Part V.



This call executes when the deck is built: the reply on the right is what the model said this morning, not a mock-up. One abstract proves nothing, and the deck will say so repeatedly. But the room should see how little code it takes before it sees how much validation it takes.

title: CADC
text:
Last week ended here

A classifier learns its weights from labelled texts; the gold standard we coded is what it learns from and is scored on
Changing what the model sees moved the score more than changing the algorithm: a bag of words at .75, a sentence embedding at .80
The sentence-embedding model was trained by somebody else, on text we never saw, to keep what a sentence means — and it beat everything trained on our own data alone
Van Atteveldt et al. (2021): classifiers beat every dictionary and reach no human. The table had one row missing


This week the model that read the sentence also writes the label. The gold standard does not change.

title: CADC
text:
This lecture

  
    I
    What changed since 2013
    Three advances, the timeline's last screen, the pipeline with one box fewer
  
  
    II
    Inside a transformer
    The architecture built in eight clicks; the two Harrys, measured
  
  
    III
    The models
    What an LLM is, who makes them, how big, and where your text goes
  
  
    IV
    LLMs as instruments
    The prompt as codebook; structured output; what moves the score
  
  
    V
    Four generations, one gold set
    Dictionary, classifier, embeddings and language models on the same texts
  
  
    VI
    What to do with it
    Images, rules, bias, and the last homework
  


Thirty seconds. Parts II and III are the architecture and the landscape, kept to twenty minutes together; the plan’s own critique of the old deck was that they took the hour. The break falls after Part III. Part IV is the long one and is where the lab work starts; Part V is the payoff.

title: CADC
text:
Three advances

Representation. From counts to word vectors to contextual vectors: a word’s numbers now depend on the sentence it is in
Pre-training and transfer. A model trained once, on an enormous corpus, for a general task — then reused for our task, with a little fine-tuning or none at all
Scale. The same architecture, thousands of times larger, trained on most of the written web; abilities nobody trained for appeared along the way


The three compound. The instrument we get is a model that reads a text and can be told, in words, what to do with it.


Kroon, A., Welbers, K., Trilling, D., & van Atteveldt, W. (2024). Advancing automated content analysis for a new era of media effects research: The key role of transfer learning. Communication Methods and Measures, 18(2), 142–162. https://doi.org/10.1080/19312458.2023.2261372

title: CADC
section: The last screen of the timeline
text:
The last screen of the timeline

  


The timeline opens at its sixth screen. Every deck so far has moved one screen to the right; this is the end of the axis, and the room is living in it. Two points: the distance from 2017 (attention) to 2022 (a chat product used by a hundred million people in two months) is five years; and the timeline’s next node is not written yet.

title: CADC
section: The pipeline with a language model
text:
The pipeline with a language model

  


The one variant that takes a box away. Step 02 is drawn dashed: no document–term matrix, no embedding you compute, because the model reads the text itself. Two arrows arrive at step 03 — the text and the prompt — which is exactly what an API call contains. Step 04 is untouched. Say it now and again in Part V: the method changed; the validation did not.

title: CADC
text:
Attention is all you need

Until 2017 the models that read sequences did so one word at a time, carrying a memory forward — slow to train, and forgetful over long distances
Vaswani et al. (2017), at Google, dropped the recurrence: every word looks at every other word at once, through a mechanism they called attention
The consequences: training could be parallelised, so models could be made much larger; and distant words could influence each other directly
The paper was about translation. The architecture — the transformer — is the backbone of BERT, GPT, Llama, Claude, Gemini and everything else in this deck


One architecture, 2017, cited a hundred and fifty thousand times. Everything since is that block, stacked and scaled.


Vaswani, A., Shazeer, N., Parmar, N., Uszkoreit, J., Jones, L., Gomez, A. N., Kaiser, Ł., & Polosukhin, I. (2017). Attention is all you need. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 30, 5998–6008.

title: CADC
section: How a word’s vector picks up its context
text:
How a word’s vector picks up its context

  


Eight clicks; the pictures do the work. Click 1: the sentence, with arcs for who modifies whom — angry and blue belong to the dog, red and haired to the man. Click 2: last week’s static embeddings, one vector per word, and above each content word a picture of what that vector “sees” on its own: a dog, but no particular dog; blue, but nothing that is blue. The numbers are illustrative. Click 3: the position is added in — one to ten — without it the model would have a bag of words. Click 4: attention. Every word looks at every other, faintly; the strong lines are where the weight goes — angry and blue into dog, red and haired into man. Click 5: the updated vectors, and the pictures change: E4 now sees a blue angry dog and E10 a red-haired man. Same words, different vectors. Clicks 6 to 8: the same idea as a movement in space — E(dog) is a point; fold in blue and it moves; fold in angry and it moves again; every layer moves it once more. That is all “contextual embedding” means, and the next slide shows the machinery that does it.

title: CADC
text:
Inside a transformer

  


Eight clicks; keep it to eight minutes. Tokens (1): the pieces the model has a number for. Embeddings (2): last week’s word vectors, looked up in a table, and Harry’s is the same vector whoever Harry is. Position (3): a second vector for where the word stands; without it, a bag of words. Attention (4) is the new idea: Harry asks every other token how relevant it is, and the weights are real (BERT, layer 4, head 0, measured: 96 percent on Potter). Update (5): Harry takes a weighted share of what the others carry, and its vector changes; on the right, the real curve: the two Harrys start identical and drift apart layer by layer.
Feed-forward (6): attention moved information between tokens. Now each vector goes through a network like week 3’s on its own, the same network for every token. On the right, Harry’s vector, which now carries Potter. Each hidden unit responds to a pattern in the vector; the lit one responds to Harry together with Potter. The network’s output is added to the vector, so Harry and Potter stay and wizard and Hogwarts join them. Much of what a model learned in pre-training is stored in these units (Geva et al., 2021; Meng et al., 2022). BERT has 3,072 of them in every block, Llama 3.1 8B has 14,336. The word labels are illustrative; real dimensions do not come with names.
Many layers (7): attention plus feed-forward is one block; BERT stacks twelve, the model in the cold open thirty-two. Why more than one: a block gathers once and looks up once, and every block works on what the blocks below added. In an early block Harry picks up Potter and then wizard. Only in a later block can the castle look at Harry, find a wizard there and become Hogwarts; with a single block the castle would only see the plain Harry. Roughly, lower blocks work out which pieces belong together, middle blocks add what the model knows, and upper blocks prepare what comes next (Tenney et al., 2019, for BERT). The three bands simplify a gradual change.
The next token (8): after the top block, the vector of the last token, the full stop, gets one score for each of the 128,256 tokens in Llama’s vocabulary. A softmax turns the scores into probabilities that sum to one. Week 3’s logistic regression did the same for three classes; here there are 128,256. After the full stop the model expects a new sentence (The 10%, But 8%, He 7%), and no token gets more than ten percent.
Two models on one drawing, on purpose: the attention and the curve are BERT’s, because it reads in both directions and its heads are legible; the bars are Llama’s, because it predicts the next token. Query, key and value are named in words; the matrices are in the reading.

title: CADC
section: Which Harry? Measured DATA · BERT-BASE-UNCASED · TWO SENTENCE PAIRS
text:
Which Harry? Measured DATA · BERT-BASE-UNCASED · TWO SENTENCE PAIRS

  
    One name, two people
    Harry Potter cast a spell in the castle.
    Harry Kane scored a goal in the stadium.
  
  
    One word, two meanings
    She deposited the money by the bank.
    She watched the water by the bank.
  




At the input, the word has the same vector in both sentences: one table, one row per token
After each layer the two vectors drift apart, as the words around them are folded in. By layer 11 the two Harrys are further apart than two unrelated words
The grey line is a control: a word that means the same in both sentences also drifts, but less


A contextual vector is a word vector that has read its sentence. That is what week 3’s embeddings could not do.












bert-base-uncased, 12 layers. Measured by the Playground’s Which Harry? tool; the same data.


PLAYGROUNDWhich Harry?

The Playground tool lets students click any head of any layer; this is its summary figure. The bank pair is the textbook case of lexical ambiguity; Harry is the case the old deck used. Note the control: even a word with one meaning is rewritten by its context, which is the point — nothing in the output is a word vector any more, everything is a sentence vector read at one position.
If there is time, tie it to week 2’s failures. The same mechanism tells the dog bit the man from the man bit the dog (position plus attention), resolves it in the trophy did not fit in the suitcase because it was too big (a Winograd schema: the answer sits several words away), and lets not rewrite good before any classifier sees it. None of it was taught; it falls out of predicting the next word well. For honesty: most attention heads are not interpretable, and the Playground tool says so; what can be measured is that the vectors separate.

title: CADC
section: Two ways to read a sentence
text:
Two ways to read a sentence



Encoder · reads in both directions


  
  classifier: negative
  
  
  transformer blocks · ×12
  
  
  
  
  the
  film
  was
  not
  good

BERT · Google, 2018RoBERTa · MetaXLM-R · multilingualDeBERTa · MicrosoftModernBERT · 2024nomic-embed · week 3

Every word’s vector has read the whole text, including what follows it, so not sees good: what a classifier needs
110 to 600 million weights and one pass per text, with nothing to write. Fine-tuned on a few thousand coded texts, it often beats a prompted LLM (Bucher & Martini, 2024)



Decoder · reads left to right


  
  next token: good
  
  
  transformer blocks · ×32
  
  
  
  the
  film
  was
  not
  ?

GPT · OpenAILlama · MetaGemma · GoogleQwen · AlibabaMistralClaude · Anthropic

Predicting the next token, again and again, is all that writing text takes. An answer, a translation and a label are all continuations of a prompt
Any task without training, because the task goes into the prompt. The price is billions of weights and a full pass for every token it writes



Bucher, M. J. J., & Martini, M. (2024). Fine-tuned “small” LLMs (still) significantly outperform zero-shot generative AI models in text classification. arXiv:2406.08660.


The same block, used two ways. Point at the arcs. In the encoder, not draws on every other word, on both sides, so its vector already contains good when the classifier on top reads it. In the decoder, not may only look back; the position after it is empty, because predicting it is the whole job. That one restriction is what makes a decoder a text generator: write a token, append it, predict the next.
Then the trade. For generation the decoder is enough, and for almost everything else, since any task can be written as a prompt and continued. For classification at scale an encoder is the efficient choice: hundreds of millions of weights instead of billions, one pass per text instead of one per generated token, and fine-tuned on our coded sample it often beats zero-shot prompting (Bucher & Martini, 2024, across several classification tasks). Week 3’s sentence embeddings came from an encoder. The table on the next slide sums up the differences.

title: CADC
text:
Encoder and decoder









Encoder · BERT (2018)
Decoder · GPT, Llama, Claude (2018 →)




Reads
the whole text, both directions
left to right, one token at a time


Pre-trained to
fill in a masked word
predict the next token


Produces
a vector per token, or per text
the next token — and so, text


Used in research for
fine-tuned classifiers, embeddings
prompting, generation, chat


Size
110 million to a few billion weights
3 billion on a laptop to trillions in a data centre




Same block, two directions. The encoder is the better classifier per weight; the decoder is the one you can talk to.


Devlin, J., Chang, M.-W., Lee, K., & Toutanova, K. (2019). BERT: Pre-training of deep bidirectional transformers for language understanding. Proceedings of NAACL-HLT 2019, 4171–4186. https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/N19-1423


BERT is where the Playground’s attention data comes from, and where the “fine-tune a pre-trained model on your coded sample” line of research lives (Kroon et al., the Balluff et al. media-capture study of the old deck). The rest of this lecture is about decoders, because that is what a prompt talks to. Say clearly that “LLM” in practice means decoder.

title: CADC
section: From a base model to a chatbot
text:
From a base model to a chatbot

  


Five clicks, and the last two are the ones worth the time. Card 1 is pre-training: predict the next token, on trillions of tokens of web pages, books, code and transcripts. Nobody labels anything; the text is the label, every next word a right answer, hence “self-supervised”. To predict well the model has to represent grammar, facts, style, who Harry is and what not good means, as side effects of the objective. Everything a model knows about your construct it learned this way, from text nobody chose for your study. Months, tens of thousands of chips, paid for once by the vendor, and what comes out only continues text. Card 2: a second, tiny phase — tens of thousands of instruction-and-answer pairs, written by people — and now it answers the question you asked. Card 3: people are shown two answers and say which is better; a reward model learns to imitate that judgement, so the preference can be applied a million times without them.
Click 4 opens what “reinforcement learning” actually means, because the room hears the phrase daily and has usually never seen it: the model writes an answer, a score comes back, the weights move toward higher scores, and round again. That is the whole idea — no labelled right answer, just a signal that this was better than that.
Click 5 is the 2026 sentence: where the score comes from is the whole difference. From people, you get a chat model tuned to be liked. From an automatic check — does the code run, is the proof right — you get a reasoning model, and nobody has to watch. Say that the numbers on the cards are orders of magnitude, not measurements: the vendors do not publish this any more, as the size chart already showed.


Ouyang, L., Wu, J., Jiang, X., Almeida, D., Wainwright, C., Mishkin, P., Zhang, C., Agarwal, S., Slama, K., Ray, A., et al. (2022). Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 35, 27730–27744.

title: CADC
section: What the tuning left in the model
text:
What the tuning left in the model

The model you prompt is a chat model: its label on “Not good at all” is a next-token prediction shaped by all three phases
The answer format, the hedging, the refusal to pick a side on a mixed review — trained in, by somebody else, for a general user
Preference tuning optimises for what a rater liked, which is not the same as what your codebook calls correct; a fluent, agreeable answer scores well either way
A base model, before any of this, is worse at following your instruction and less shaped by anyone’s idea of a good answer. Neither is neutral


You are prompting an instrument that was tuned to be helpful to somebody else. A coder following your codebook is something else.

title: CADC
section: Transfer, and two ways to use it
text:
Transfer, and two ways to use it



Transfer learning is the ability: what a model learned in pre-training carries over to tasks it was never trained on. Nobody trained Llama to code film reviews, and it codes them
Fine-tuning uses it by training further on our coded sample, a few hundred to a few thousand texts, until the weights fit our codebook. The BERT route; it needs a GPU and week 3’s split and test
Prompting is simply how we talk to the model. The codebook goes into the input and the weights stay as they are. The route of this lecture
Fine-tuning still wins on narrow tasks with enough coded data (Alizadeh et al., 2025); prompting wins on cost of entry



  
  PRE-TRAINED MODEL
  predict the next token, trillions of times
  
  transfer
  works for tasks it never saw
  
  
  
  FINE-TUNING
  + our coded texts
  the weights change
  a GPU, a split, a test
  
  PROMPTING
  + our codebook, in words
  the weights stay fixed
  only the input changes
  
  
  labels
  labels



Transfer is what the pre-trained model brings. Fine-tuning and prompting are two ways to use it, and this week uses the one without a training loop.


Alizadeh, M., Kubli, M., Samei, Z., Dehghani, S., Zahedivafa, M., Bermeo, J. D., Korobeynikova, M., & Gilardi, F. (2025). Open-source LLMs for text annotation: A practical guide for model setting and fine-tuning. Journal of Computational Social Science, 8(1), 17. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42001-024-00345-9

title: CADC
section: What a large language model is
text:
What a large language model is

A transformer decoder with billions of weights, pre-trained to predict the next token on a large share of all written text, then tuned to answer
“Large” is doing the work: the same architecture at a hundred million weights writes plausible sentences; at a hundred billion it translates, summarises, codes and follows a codebook it has never seen
It runs as a service (an API you send text to) or as weights you download and run yourself
What it is not: a database, a search engine, a reasoner with a model of the world, or a coder who read your instructions carefully. It is a next-token machine that has read a great deal


Everything an LLM does for you is generated. Including the label, including the confidence, including the explanation.

title: CADC
section: A language model, small enough to see
text:
A language model, small enough to see

  


After Bycroft, B. (2023). LLM visualization. https://bbycroft.net/llm · the numbers in the tiles are invented; the shapes are a real decoder’s.


Seven clicks; let the model turn while you talk. Every tile is one number, and nothing here is a metaphor: this is how many numbers a tiny GPT holds and where they sit. Click 1: the four tokens of “the film was not” are rows copied out of the embedding table, one row per token of the vocabulary, with the position added. Click 2: each vector makes a query, a key and a value; queries against keys give the 4 × 4 table of attention weights, and its upper half is empty because a decoder may not look ahead. “not” looks back at the three words before it. Click 3: the feed-forward network, four times as wide, one token at a time. Both results are added to the stream that rises through the model. Click 4: the stack, three blocks here, the same two operations each time. Click 5: only the last token’s vector is read, one score per token of the vocabulary, a softmax, and the tallest bar is the prediction.
Click 6 is the size. Llama 3.1 8B, the model of the cold open, is this machine with 32 blocks, 4,096 numbers per token instead of 12, and 128,256 tokens in its vocabulary: about eight billion weights against this toy’s few thousand. Bycroft’s visualization, which this drawing follows, runs a real small GPT in the browser and is worth an evening.

title: CADC
text:
The models, September 2026

  


Four clicks. The columns matter more than the names, which will be out of date by the time this is taught — check them the week before. Closed: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI; used through an API; the strongest models and the ones you cannot inspect, pin or run yourself. Open weights: Meta, DeepSeek, Alibaba, Mistral, Google’s Gemma; downloadable, so a version can be frozen forever. Third column: what this deck actually ran, through Ollama, on the laptop in front of the room — three to twelve billion weights, two to eight gigabytes. Last click, the three questions that decide which column a study can use: where does the text go, can the version be pinned, what does a text cost.

title: CADC
text:
Bigger every year

  


Six clicks, one chart, and the last click is the point. The old deck’s version had nine points and GPT-4 at 1.76 trillion as if it were a disclosed figure; this one separates what is counted from what is claimed. Click 1: the published counts, 94 million to 175 billion in three years. Click 2: the row above the chart — from GPT-4 on, nobody at the frontier publishes a count; these models are placed by date only. Click 3: the line continues, dashed, through what exists instead of counts: GPT-4 near 1.8 trillion as a mixture of experts (a 2023 leak, never confirmed), Grok 3 and 4 at 3 trillion and Grok 5 at 6 trillion in training (xAI’s own statements, as reported, November 2025), and the 2024 chat models nearer 200 billion (estimates stated in a Microsoft paper, Ben Abacha et al. 2024). Say plainly that none of this is a publication; the dashed line is drawn on evidence that would not pass a methods section. Click 4: open weights are counted exactly because you can download them; by 2025 they reach a trillion, mostly as mixtures of experts where only a fraction of the weights fires per token, so total weights overstate the compute. Click 5: the band this deck lives in, three to twenty-six billion, a hundred times below the 2020 frontier and ahead of GPT-3 on most benchmarks. Click 6: the same chart with the axis turned linear, over two seconds. Everything below half a trillion settles on the floor, GPT-3 included, and the claimed frontier climbs alone. Let it sit. Names and claims checked on 13 September 2026; re-check before class.


Kaplan, J., et al. (2020). Scaling laws for neural language models. arXiv:2001.08361 · Ben Abacha, A., et al. (2024). MEDEC: A benchmark for medical error detection and correction in clinical notes. arXiv:2412.19260 (the 2024 parameter estimates) · GPT-4 and Grok figures: leak (SemiAnalysis, 2023) and xAI statements (2025), unconfirmed.

title: CADC
section: Talking to a model from R
text:
Talking to a model from R


library(tidyllm)

llm_message("In two sentences: what is a codebook
             in content analysis?") |>
  chat(ollama(.model = "llama3.1:8b",
              .temperature = 0)) |>
  get_reply()

llm_message() builds the conversation; chat() sends it to a provider — here a local Ollama server, but openai(), claude() or gemini() slot in unchanged
.temperature = 0: take the most probable token every time
get_reply() pulls the answer out as a string



Output



In content analysis, a codebook is a detailed
guide that outlines the specific codes,
categories, and definitions used to analyze and
interpret the content of texts, images, or other
data. The codebook serves as a reference point for
researchers to ensure consistency and reliability
in their coding process, and it typically includes
information on code definitions, examples, and
rules for applying the codes to the data.



A model that can define a codebook can be handed one. That is the whole trick of Part IV.



The same four lines are the first thing Tuesday’s lab runs. Note the provider swap: the pipe stays identical when a study moves from a local model to a frontier model through an API, which is how the two frontier rows in Part V were made.

title: CADC
text:
Break

Ten minutes. After the break: the prompt as an instrument, and what moves its score.

title: CADC
text:
Deductive, inductive — and instructed










Dictionary · week 2
Classifier · week 3
Language model · week 4




The rules come from
you, as a word list
coded examples, learned
you, as a codebook in words


What the machine reads
listed words, one by one
the features of coded texts
the whole text, in context


Coded texts needed
none
thousands, split in two
none — or a handful, as examples


Scored against
the gold standard
the held-out part of it
the gold standard, all of it


Logic
deductive
inductive
deductive rules, inductive machine




The codebook is back in your hands, as in week 2. The reader is the inductive machine of week 3. Validation is unchanged since week 2.


The distinction the old deck opened with, extended by one column. The interesting cell is bottom right: the researcher supplies the rules (deductive), but the thing applying them was built inductively from text nobody chose for this purpose. That is why the prompt behaves like an instrument — its readings drift with wording, model and version — and why Part IV treats it as one.

title: CADC
section: The steps, with a language model
text:
The steps, with a language model

  


Week 3’s five cards with two changed, outlined in this week’s colour. Step 1 is identical — the hand-coded sample is still the only place meaning enters. Step 2 was “train on part of it”; now it is “write the prompt”, and the split is crossed out: nothing is trained, so nothing needs sealing. Step 3 scores the prompt on all the coded texts, since none were used for training — a real advantage: two hundred coded texts are two hundred test cases. Steps 4 and 5 are as before, with one addition each: the cost is now per text, and the prompt and model version travel with the labels.

title: CADC
text:
One classification


codebook <- "You are coding sentences from restaurant reviews for a
  content analysis. Codebook: positive = the sentence expresses a
  favourable evaluation of the restaurant, its food, staff or
  experience; negative = an unfavourable evaluation.
  Code the following sentence.\n\nSentence: {text}"

sentence <- yelp_test$text[1]

llm_message(str_replace(codebook, stringr::fixed("{text}"), sentence)) |>
  chat(ollama(.model = "llama3.1:8b", .temperature = 0)) |>
  get_reply()

The prompt has three parts: the role, the codebook with a definition per category, and the text
The same wording every time; only the text changes



Output



sentence: Stopped by during the late May bank holiday
off Rick Steve recommendation and loved it. 


Based on the codebook, I would code this
sentence as: **Positive** Reasoning: The
sentence expresses a favourable evaluation
of the restaurant, as indicated by the word
"loved it". The fact that the reviewer stopped
by based on a recommendation from Rick Steve
also suggests a positive predisposition
towards the restaurant.



human label: positive 



A label, and usually a sentence around it. A reply is text; a variable is not. That gap is the next slide.

title: CADC
text:
Structured output


schema <- tidyllm_schema(
  name       = "coding",
  label      = field_fct("the code", .levels = c("positive", "negative")),
  confidence = field_dbl("how sure you are, 0 to 1"),
  reason     = field_chr("one short sentence"))

llm_message(str_replace(codebook, stringr::fixed("{text}"), sentence)) |>
  chat(ollama(.model = "llama3.1:8b", .temperature = 0,
              .json_schema = schema)) |>
  get_reply_data()

A schema declares the fields and the allowed values; the server constrains the decoding so the reply cannot be anything else
get_reply_data() returns an R list: the label is a factor level, not a sentence to parse
The confidence and the reason are generated text too. Useful to read; not measurements
Note the order of the fields. The model fills them in the order you declare, so a reason before the label lets it write before it commits. In this deck’s own runs one model needed exactly that



Output



$label      positive 
$confidence 0.9 
$reason     The reviewer mentions that they
'loved it', which is a strong positive
sentiment. 



Structured output ends parse failures: twelve in this deck’s free-text runs, none under a schema. It does not end wrong answers: in the paper in Part V, the reply format alone moves small models by up to twelve points.



Lab A on Tuesday builds this schema. Two warnings to plant now. The “confidence” is a number the model generated, not a probability it computed — the cold open showed the actual distribution, which the API does not return. And constraining the output changes the model’s behaviour. In this deck’s own runs Llama 3.1 answered “positive” to 274 of 284 Dutch headlines when the reply was a bare label, and coded sensibly the moment it could write one sentence first; Lab B can reproduce it. Part V shows the same model skewed by the bare label under the paper’s prompt. Field order is not cosmetic.

title: CADC
text:
Two hundred sentences


schema <- tidyllm_schema(name = "coding",
  label = field_fct("the code", .levels = c("positive", "negative")))

code_one <- function(text) {
  llm_message(str_replace(codebook, stringr::fixed("{text}"), text)) |>
    chat(ollama(.model = "llama3.1:8b", .temperature = 0, .seed = 42,
                .json_schema = schema)) |>
    get_reply_data() |> pluck("label")
}

coded <- yelp_test |>
  mutate(pred = map_chr(text, code_one, .progress = TRUE),   # ~100 s
         pred = factor(pred, levels = levels(label)))

One function, mapped over the texts: the loop is the study
Two hundred sentences take a hundred seconds on this laptop with the 8-billion-weight model; the cached result is what the next slides score



Output

title: CADC
text:
Zero-shot, few-shot, chain of thought

  
  
  
  Zero-shot
  the codebook and the text
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  mixed
  
  
  Few-shot
  a handful of coded examples added
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  “a real treat, start to finish” → positive
  
  “two hours I will not get back” → negative
  
  “great acting, dull story” → mixed
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  mixed
  
  
  Chain of thought
  reasoning asked for, then the label
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  reason step by step, then give the label
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
  mixed
  
  
  codebook
  
  the text to code
  
  reasoning, asked for and given back


Only the middle of the prompt changes: few-shot adds to what goes in, chain of thought to what comes back. Which of them helps is measured on the next slides, on forty-eight texts.


Three prompt designs. Zero-shot: the codebook and the text, and the model’s general ability does the work. Few-shot: a handful of coded examples in the prompt, which anchor the categories the way a coder-training session does. Chain of thought: the model is asked to reason before it answers; slower by an order of magnitude, sometimes more accurate on hard categories, and it leaves a rationale to read. Which one helps depends on the task, the model and the codebook, so it is measured, not assumed.
Read it left to right and the whole comparison is one idea: the codebook and the text are identical in all three columns, so anything that differs in the answer comes from the part that was added.
Point at the blue bar in the middle column — those examples cost tokens on every single text you code, which is why few-shot gets expensive at scale. Then the purple in the right column: it appears twice, once in the prompt where you ask for reasoning and once in the reply where you get it. That second appearance is the whole cost story — the model generates all of it before the label arrives, which is where the order of magnitude goes.
The reply is the same word in all three panels on purpose. This slide is about the shape of a prompt, not about which one is right; the scoring comes next.

title: CADC
text:
The prompt as codebook




Label the review as positive, negative, or mixed.
Use 'mixed' whenever the review contains BOTH substantial praise AND substantial criticism, even if one outweighs the other.





# few-shot: the examples appended for this definition


The effects are dated, but the story still lands. → mixed 
Superb cast, wasted on a script that goes nowhere. → mixed 
Gorgeous from start to finish. → positive 




The Playground’s prompt lab: forty-eight film reviews, hand-coded on three fields, from which two codebooks are derived — a broad mixed (any praise and criticism together) and a narrow one (only when the verdict is genuinely unclear)
They disagree on 13 of the 48 texts: the borderline ones
Every definition was run zero-shot, few-shot and with chain of thought, on three local models, at temperature 0


A prompt is a codebook. Two defensible codebooks give two different gold standards — before any model is involved.


PLAYGROUNDThe prompt is the instrument

The data behind the next three slides is the Playground tool’s; students can reproduce every dot. The design is a small factorial: four definitions of “mixed”, three techniques, three models, one run at temperature 0 plus three at 0.8. It was all run locally, so nothing left the machine and every raw reply is archived.

title: CADC
section: Does few-shot help? Does reasoning? DATA · 48 FILM REVIEWS, HAND-CODED FOR THIS COURSE
text:
Does few-shot help? Does reasoning? DATA · 48 FILM REVIEWS, HAND-CODED FOR THIS COURSE













Three models, two codebooks, three techniques: eighteen scores on the same forty-eight texts
No technique wins everywhere. Few-shot helps one model on one codebook and hurts another; chain of thought costs ten times the time for gains you would not bet on
The differences between models are as large as the differences between techniques


“Few-shot helps” is a hypothesis about your task. Test it on your gold set; do not import it.


PLAYGROUNDThe prompt is the instrument

Read the figure as a factorial, not a league table: within a row, do the shapes separate? Across rows, do the models? The honest summary is that the effects are small, inconsistent and interact — which is exactly why Lab A asks for two prompts and two models rather than one of each. Chain-of-thought’s rationales are archived in the grid and are worth reading aloud: they are fluent, and sometimes wrong for fluent reasons.

title: CADC
section: The codebook moves the score DATA · THE SAME 48 FILM REVIEWS, TWO DERIVED CODEBOOKS
text:
The codebook moves the score DATA · THE SAME 48 FILM REVIEWS, TWO DERIVED CODEBOOKS








review
broad gold
narrow gold




Slow, but worth it.
mixed
positive


Well acted, but pointless.
mixed
negative


Gorgeous cinematography throughout.
positive
positive







One hand-coding, two gold standards. Broad calls a review mixed whenever it has praise and criticism; narrow only when it reaches no verdict. They differ on 13 of the 48 reviews, like the first two rows
Each prompt gave the model one of the two definitions. A panel holds one gold standard fixed and compares the two prompts on it












Against either gold standard, the prompt with the same definition scored higher in 5 of 6 comparisons, by up to 31 points. The prompt has to carry the definition the coders used.



Make the setup explicit before the dots. The forty-eight reviews were coded by hand once, on three facts: the verdict, whether the review has both praise and criticism, and whether the verdict is clear. A definition of mixed turns those facts into a label. Under the broad definition, “Slow, but worth it.” is mixed: there is praise and criticism. Under the narrow one it is positive, because the reviewer comes down on one side. One coding, two gold standards, which differ on 13 reviews.
Each prompt carried one of the two definitions. Read one panel at a time: the gold standard is fixed, and the two dots are the two prompts. Against the narrow gold standard the narrow prompt wins for every model; against the broad one for two of three. Qwen is the exception there: given the broad definition it calls 20 of the 48 reviews mixed, where the coders found 15.
Do not compare a model’s dots across the panels. The narrow gold standard has only two mixed reviews, so a model that rarely says mixed scores well on it whatever its prompt: Llama 3.1 with the broad prompt called only 4 of 48 reviews mixed, where the broad coding has 15. That is also the lesson for validation. A definition in the prompt that differs from the one in the coders’ instructions makes the accuracy measure agreement with a different construct.

title: CADC
section: Run to run DATA · THE SAME 48 REVIEWS, THREE PASSES AT TEMPERATURE 0.8
text:
Run to run DATA · THE SAME 48 REVIEWS, THREE PASSES AT TEMPERATURE 0.8













The same prompt, three times, at temperature 0.8: the model samples from its distribution instead of taking the top token
Up to a fifth of the texts change label between runs — the borderline ones, again
At temperature 0 with a fixed seed a local model is deterministic. An API model is not guaranteed to be, and a retired version is gone


A coder who changes a fifth of the labels on a second pass is not reliable. Neither is a prompt. Measure it the same way.



Reiss, M. V. (2023). Testing the reliability of ChatGPT for text annotation and classification: A cautionary remark. arXiv:2304.11085.


This is Reiss’s (2023) point in local numbers: instability is a property of the instrument. Two consequences for the lab: run at temperature 0 and fix the seed; and when a study reports one run of an API model, ask what a second run would have given. Week 2’s intercoder agreement has an exact analogue here — κ between two runs, no gold standard needed.

title: CADC
text:
What to report

The prompt, verbatim, including the codebook and any examples — it is the instrument
The model and its version, the provider, the date of the run, temperature and seed
A validation on a hand-coded gold set, with the metric that fits the class balance — and the humans’ own agreement on the same texts
Sensitivity: at least two prompt wordings and at least two models, with the scores side by side; and run-to-run agreement if the temperature was above zero
Parse failures, and what was done with them
Where the text went, and the raw replies archived


Six lines that turn a prompt into a method section. Lab A asks for every one of them.

text:
Four generations, one gold set DATA · 200 HELD-OUT YELP SENTENCES · MODELS IN FREE TEXT












Every row is scored on the same 200 held-out sentences of Kotzias et al.’s Yelp set. The dictionary’s silences count as errors; the two classifiers were trained on the other 800 sentences; the language models saw none of them.



The 2013 dictionary, the 2019 classifier, the 2023 embedding, the 2024–25 language models: each generation beats the last on the same sentences
Every local model here, down to the three-billion one on a student laptop, beats last week’s best classifier — with no training data at all
The two bottom rows are frontier models through an API: Haiku .98, Opus .995 — and .995 is where the twelve-billion model on your laptop already sits. Sentence 145, two slides on, is why nobody scores higher


This is the figure the course was built toward. The rest of Part V is why it is not the end.



Read it upward. The dictionary’s number counts its silences as errors, which is what it would cost you to use it. The two classifiers are week 3’s regressions, refitted at render on the same split and trained on eight hundred sentences; the language models on none. One marker per model, the free-text reply: on this easy task the three reply formats agree within three points. On the Dutch headlines in the paper’s figure, they do not. The two frontier rows, Claude Haiku 4.5 and Opus 4.6, ran through the Anthropic API with the same prompt as the local models.
