title: CADC
section: The one sentence every model got wrong DATA · 200 HELD-OUT YELP SENTENCES · SENTENCE 145
text:
The one sentence every model got wrong DATA · 200 HELD-OUT YELP SENTENCES · SENTENCE 145

“Nice blanket of moz over top but i feel like this was done to cover up the subpar food.”




The gold standard says


positive


One label, assigned once when Kotzias et al. built the sentence set in 2015; used by hundreds of papers since, and by this course since week 2. Nobody checked it — until fifteen coders disagreed with it at once.




All 15 cells say


negative


Five models, three reply formats, every single one. Claude Opus, asked to give its reason before its label:


“While the sentence acknowledges a positive element (nice blanket of mozzarella), the overall sentiment is negative, suggesting the cheese was used to disguise subpar food quality.”




Kotzias, D., Denil, M., de Freitas, N., & Smyth, P. (2015). From group to individual labels using deep features. KDD ’15, 597–606 — the “Sentiment Labelled Sentences” set (UCI). Sentence 145 of the course’s 200 held-out sentences; all fifteen model cells from results/llm2.


Stop on this one; it is the best lesson in the Yelp block and it fell out of the data by accident.
Opus scored .995 in all three reply formats on the two hundred sentences, which looked like an artefact until we checked: three different files, three different kinds of reply, and the one sentence all three get “wrong” is this one. Then the other four models: negative in every format they were run in. Fifteen cells, fifteen times negative. Read the sentence. The reviewer is saying the cheese hides bad food. The gold label is wrong; the models are right — and the largest one explains why, in one sentence, better than the gold standard’s author managed with a single click.
Three things follow. First, .995 was never a coincidence across formats: it is the ceiling of this gold standard. Two hundred sentences, one mislabelled, and the best models reach that ceiling in every format. Every “.99” in the Yelp figure is “perfect, minus the mislabelled one”.
Second — and this is the transferable rule — a disagreement between a good model and your gold standard is a question to ask of the gold standard, not only of the model. In your own validation, read every case where your best model and your coders disagree. Some of those are the model’s errors. Some are yours. The gold standard is a measurement too, and it was made by people who were tired at sentence 145.
Third, the arithmetic: a gold standard’s own error rate is a hard ceiling on any accuracy you can measure against it. If your coders were wrong five per cent of the time, no method can score above .95 against them and the ones that do are matching the errors. The paper this deck ends on reports its gold standard’s inter-coder reliability for exactly this reason — a single trained coder agrees with the expert gold at .82 and a majority of three at .88, so no method scored against that gold can be read as more precise than that.
Validation cuts both ways. That is the sentence to leave them with.

title: CADC
section: Last week’s table, four rows longer DATA · 300 HELD-OUT ARXIV ABSTRACTS · MODELS IN FREE TEXT
text:
Last week’s table, four rows longer DATA · 300 HELD-OUT ARXIV ABSTRACTS · MODELS IN FREE TEXT













The arXiv abstracts of week 3, three disciplines, a hundred held-out abstracts each — a harder task: long texts, and statistics overlaps with both neighbours
The three local models land within two points of each other, .74 to .76, and the frontier models at .76 and .78 — all of them still lean toward computer science for anything with an algorithm in it
The classifier trained on 4,200 coded abstracts beats every one of them at .83 — with coded data and a narrow construct, training still wins


Zero-shot is not free accuracy. With coded data and a narrow construct, last week’s classifier beats a frontier model.



The contrast with the Yelp figure is the lesson: sentiment in restaurant reviews is something every model has read a million examples of; distinguishing a statistics abstract from a computer-science one is not. Every model over-assigns “computer science” — roughly 150 of 300 abstracts against 100 in the gold standard — because anything with an algorithm in it reads as computer science to a model trained mostly on code and the web.
The frontier rows are the lesson of the slide. Haiku is steady at .76 to .77 whatever the reply format, Opus a little above it at .78 to .79, and the three local models are only a point or two behind — and all five are beaten by a logistic regression on sentence embeddings that week 3 trained on 4,200 coded abstracts. Where you have coded data and a narrow, specialised construct, training still wins — and it costs nothing per text afterwards. The classifiers are last week’s, refitted at render on the same seed, scored on the 300-abstract subset the language models saw.
A caution worth telling, because it happened while building this deck. An earlier version of this prompt said “Code the following abstract” — and with “computer science” as one of the categories, that one word moved the small models by up to forty points: Gemma answered 298 of 300 abstracts with a Python function, and even where no model wrote code, Llama 3.2 gained 24 points when the verb became “classify”. The frontier model did not move at all. Check every prompt for words that overlap with the label set.

Values below .70 in colour; for the language models they all sit in two columns, because every model makes the same error: statistics abstracts are called computer science. Recall on statistics is .33 to .59 for the models, .75 for the classifier that learned arXiv’s convention from 4,200 examples.


Read the columns, not the accuracy column. Physics is solved by everyone, .9 and up. Computer science has high recall and low precision for every model: it is the sink — anything with an algorithm in it falls in. Statistics is where the models lose, recall .33 to .59, because an abstract about an estimator or a learning method reads as computer science to a model that learned its categories from the web, where “statistics” is a narrower word than it is on arXiv.
The trained classifier is at .75 on statistics. Not because it understands statistics better — because it learned from 4,200 examples where arXiv authors draw that line. That is the difference between a construct and a convention, and a trained model learns conventions. Opus is the least affected model, .59 recall and .66 precision on the two problem columns, and that is the whole of its edge over Haiku.
Two practical points. Report per-class recall, always, for any task with more than two classes — one weak class hides inside a respectable accuracy. And when every model fails the same class in the same direction, suspect the label scheme before you suspect the models; the sentence on the Yelp slide two back was the same lesson with n = 1.

title: CADC
text:
What the literature says · 1












Gilardi et al. (2023), reported averages; the four datasets are 2,382 and 1,856 tweets, 1,606 news articles, and 500 tweets from 2023.



Gilardi, Alizadeh & Kubli (2023): relevance, stance, topic and frame coding of tweets and news. ChatGPT’s zero-shot accuracy beat crowd workers by about twenty-five points on average; its agreement with itself beat the trained annotators’; a third of a cent per text
Törnberg (2023): party affiliation from 500 politicians’ tweets. GPT-4 beat every individual expert and the crowd majority, with higher reliability — and the same bias toward “Democrat” as the humans
Both are about GPT versions that no longer exist


The early results were real and are not reproducible. Read them for the design: crowd, expert and model on one gold set.



Gilardi, F., Alizadeh, M., & Kubli, M. (2023). ChatGPT outperforms crowd workers for text-annotation tasks. PNAS, 120(30), e2305016120. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2305016120 · Törnberg, P. (2023). ChatGPT-4 outperforms experts and crowd workers in annotating political Twitter messages with zero-shot learning. arXiv:2304.06588.

title: CADC
text:
What the literature says · 2













Heseltine & Clemm von Hohenberg (2024): GPT-4 against expert coding of tweets and news in four countries. Binary tasks above ninety percent; three-class sentiment at eighty-one, below the two experts’ own agreement of eighty-seven
Their fix is the design to copy: run the model twice, and give only the disagreements — five to thirteen percent of the texts — to a human
Longer texts and other languages: slightly worse, not dramatically


The human baseline decides the verdict. A model at 81 is good when the humans are at 87, and nothing else tells you that.



Heseltine, M., & Clemm von Hohenberg, B. (2024). Large language models as a substitute for human experts in annotating political text. Research & Politics, 11(1). https://doi.org/10.1177/20531680241236239


The human baseline is the bridge to the next slide. Heseltine and Clemm von Hohenberg’s verdict depends on the two experts’ own agreement, and the paper on the next slide puts one trained coder and three coders into the figure for the same reason. A caution from Ollion et al. (2024) belongs here too: the early successes cluster on simple, well-known constructs; on the theory-laden categories social scientists actually code, results are poorer. Sentiment in Dutch economic headlines is a middle case.

title: CADC
section: The row the paper could not add DATA · 284 DUTCH HEADLINES · FOURTEEN MODELS · MASUR & VAN ATTEVELDT (IN PREP.)
text:
The row the paper could not add DATA · 284 DUTCH HEADLINES · FOURTEEN MODELS · MASUR & VAN ATTEVELDT (IN PREP.)





The 2021 comparison, redone with language models: the same 284 headlines, the same expert gold standard, the paper’s codebook in the prompt
Dashed lines are the 2021 benchmarks: the best classifier, a CNN (.63), crowd coding (.77), one trained coder (.82) and three coders (.88)
One row per model and one panel per reply format. Open dots without examples, filled dots with six



Masur, P. K., & van Atteveldt, W. (in prep.). Sentiment coding with large language models: Extending the validity comparison of van Atteveldt, van der Velden and Boukes (2021). Figure 1 · van Atteveldt, W., van der Velden, M. A. C. G., & Boukes, M. (2021). The validity of sentiment analysis. Communication Methods and Measures, 15(2), 121–140.


Weeks 2 and 3 ended on the 2021 table: dictionaries far below, supervised classifiers in between, humans on top. This is the figure from the follow-up paper with Wouter van Atteveldt, which adds the row that did not exist in 2021: fourteen instruction-tuned models, ten open-weight and four hosted, coding the same 284 expert-coded headlines with the paper’s codebook.
Read it in three moves. First the dashed lines: those are the 2021 methods and the humans, and the CNN at .63 was the best any machine did then. Then one panel: every row sits to the right of the CNN, and the upper rows reach the line of one trained coder. Then across the panels: the same model can move by ten points with the reply format, which is the instrument effect of Part IV on a real gold standard. Open against filled is zero-shot against six examples, and the arrow shows which way the examples pushed. The bars are bootstrap intervals.
A word on what is not in the figure. This deck’s own runs used a different prompt, and there Llama 3.1 in the bare-label format answered “positive” to 274 of 284 headlines; Lab B can reproduce that. With the paper’s prompt the same model did not collapse, but it called 72 per cent of the headlines neutral and dropped from .70 to .59. A failure like this belongs to the model, the prompt and the format together, which is why the label distribution is always reported.

title: CADC
section: What the paper finds DATA · 284 DUTCH HEADLINES · MASUR & VAN ATTEVELDT (IN PREP.)
text:
What the paper finds DATA · 284 DUTCH HEADLINES · MASUR & VAN ATTEVELDT (IN PREP.)

Every model, in its best format, beat every automated method of 2021 without a single coded example. The CNN (.63) was trained on more than 6,000 headlines
Four models matched one trained coder (.82) without examples. The best, Gemini 3.8 Flash, reached .86; none reached three coders (.88)
Price bought little: Claude Opus 5.5 cost 25 times as much as Gemini 3.8 Flash and was less accurate. The best open models came within .03
The reply format moved small models by up to .12 and the strongest by less than .01. Six examples helped weak models and cost some strong ones a little


In 2021 the advice was to code by hand or to train a classifier. On this gold standard a prompted model now sits between one trained coder and three.


Masur, P. K., & van Atteveldt, W. (in prep.). Sentiment coding with large language models: Extending the validity comparison of van Atteveldt, van der Velden and Boukes (2021).


Four findings, each with a number from the paper. Stay longest on the third and the fourth. The third is the practical one for a thesis: an open model on a desktop computer, with nothing leaving the building, is within three points of the best hosted model on this task. The fourth is the methodological one: the reply format and the examples are part of the instrument, and their effect differs between models. No model collapsed onto one label, but the format skewed some: Llama 3.1 8B called 72 per cent of the headlines neutral when it could only give a label. The two rules the paper ends on are the ones Lab B asks for: report the reply format as part of the instrument, and always report the distribution of predicted labels.

When the model’s score on our gold set is acceptable, its labels are silver: not hand-coded, but validated. We use them as the variable itself, or as training data for week 3’s classifier: cheaper at scale, pinned forever, and often as accurate (Pangakis, Wolken & Fasching, 2023)


Either way the hand-coded gold set is what makes the label a measurement. The model does not replace it; it makes it go further.


Pangakis, N., Wolken, S., & Fasching, N. (2023). Automated annotation with generative AI requires validation. arXiv:2306.00176.

title: CADC
text:
Not only text




Climate march, Dam square, Amsterdam, 12 September 2026. Photo: Ainali, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0; faces pixelated in the original upload.


img <- base64_enc(readBin("climate-march.jpg", "raw",
                          file.size("climate-march.jpg")))
prompt <- "Code this photo for a study of protests.
1. Protest: yes or no.
2. Crowd: none, a few people, a group or a crowd.
3. The text on the signs, word for word.
4. The topic of the protest, in three words."

request("http://localhost:11434/api/chat") |>
  req_body_json(list(model = "gemma4:12b", stream = FALSE,
    messages = list(list(role = "user", content = prompt,
                         images = list(img))))) |>
  req_perform() |> resp_body_json() |>
  pluck("message", "content")

The same kind of call, with an image attached: a vision-language model reads pixels into the same vector space as words
The prompt is a codebook again, with four variables for one photo



A real coding task from visual communication research: is this a protest, how large is the crowd, what do the signs say, what is it about. The photo is from the climate march in Amsterdam on 12 September 2026, published on Wikimedia Commons under CC BY-SA 4.0 with the faces already pixelated. Let the room read the signs first, before the next slide shows what the model read; they are the gold standard for the third variable.
The call goes to Ollama’s API directly rather than through tidyllm, because tidyllm 0.4.0 returned empty replies for vision models that answer in a “thinking” field first, and the raw call is a few lines anyway.

title: CADC
section: What the model read DATA · ONE PHOTO · GEMMA 4, 12 BILLION WEIGHTS, LOCAL
text:
What the model read DATA · ONE PHOTO · GEMMA 4, 12 BILLION WEIGHTS, LOCAL



Output · Gemma 4, 12 billion weights, local



1. Protest: yes
2. Crowd: a crowd
3. The text on the signs:
- "KINDEREN VOOR EEN GROENE TOEKOMST"
- "KLIMAAT NU, NIET NA100 JAAR"
- "KLIMAAT NU, NIET NA 100 JAAR"
- "SYSTEM CHANGE"
- "NO MORE"
- "REVOLT"
- "MADAME TISSURE"
- "REVOLT"
4. The topic of the protest: Climate change action 




The codes for the photo as a whole are right: a protest, a crowd, and the topic
The transcription is not. The clearest sign, Klimaat van rood naar groen doen!, is missing; toekomst completes a banner the frame cuts off; Madame Tissure is the waxworks museum’s shop sign, misread; and Revolt, No more and Klimaat nu, niet na 100 jaar are nowhere on the photo
Validation works as it did for text: hand-code a sample of photos, then score each variable on its own


The instrument reads images now, and it makes up text the way it makes up rationales. The method is the one we used for text.



Go through the reply line by line with the photo from the previous slide in mind. Protest, crowd and topic: right, and those are the variables a study of protest images usually codes. The signs: the model lists eight lines, and only two can be checked against the photo, System change and the green banner, whose last word it guessed. It misses the most legible sign of all, reads the shop sign of Madame Tussauds as a protest sign, and adds slogans that are not there. A fluent list of plausible protest slogans is exactly what a next-token machine produces when it cannot read.
So one prompt gives three trustworthy variables and one that would fail any check. Score them separately; a single accuracy over all four would hide it. The reply is what Gemma 4 (12B, local) said on the date stored in results/week4-live-calls.rds under “vision-protest”; delete that entry to ask again, and rewrite the second bullet if the reply changes.

title: CADC
text:
Before the first call

Personal data. Tweets, comments and interviews are personal data under the GDPR. Sending them to a vendor’s server is a transfer: a processing agreement, a purpose, and usually a data-protection assessment first. Local models avoid the question entirely
Terms. Vendors differ on whether your prompts are kept and whether they train on them. Read the terms of the API, not the chat product
Disclosure. The EU AI Act puts duties on providers; on researchers the duty is transparency: which model, which version, which prompt, which date, what it cost — the Instrument block of your AI disclosure
Ethics review. A method that reads and labels people’s words at scale is still human-subjects research


The first question is not “which model”. It is “may this text leave the building”. Answer it in writing.

title: CADC
section: What the model brings with it
text:
What the model brings with it

Bias. The model labels the way the text it learned from labels. Törnberg’s GPT-4 leaned “Democrat” as the humans did, and a codebook cannot fully correct a prior it cannot see
Contamination. A model that has read the benchmark reproduces its labels: Gilardi et al. lost fourteen points on one task with tweets from after the training cutoff
Confident nonsense. The label, the confidence and the rationale are all generated. A fluent reason for a wrong label is the normal case
Drift and death. A closed model is updated in place (Chen et al., 2024) and retired eventually, so any result on it is provisional (Ollion et al., 2024). Open weights stay the same file


None of this is an argument against the instrument. It is the list of things the validation has to be designed to catch.


Chen, L., Zaharia, M., & Zou, J. (2024). How is ChatGPT’s behavior changing over time? Harvard Data Science Review, 6(2). https://doi.org/10.1162/99608f92.5317da47 · Ollion, É., Shen, R., Macanovic, A., & Chatelain, A. (2024). The dangers of using proprietary LLMs for research. Nature Machine Intelligence, 6(1), 4–5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-023-00783-6


Chen, Zaharia and Zou asked GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 the same questions in March and June 2023 and got materially different answers under the same model names. The published literature on “ChatGPT as annotator” is mostly about versions that no longer exist: read it for the design, not the numbers. Open weights with a checksum are the reason this course runs on Ollama.

title: CADC
section: Same text, different name DATA · THE PLAYGROUND’S AUDIT STUDY · LLAMA 3.1 8B
text:
Same text, different name DATA · THE PLAYGROUND’S AUDIT STUDY · LLAMA 3.1 8B













Four applicants with the same CV, word for word; only name, gender, age, nationality and university differ. A fair ranker puts each first in one round out of four
Llama 3.1 ranked a woman first 32 times in 100 and a man 18 times; a 30-year-old 35 times, a 55-year-old 13; a North American degree 39 times, a South Asian one 17
Coding the same post for sentiment, the author’s gender moved the share coded negative by half a point, and no nationality or name by more than 1.4 points


The same model and the same names: a large bias where the text leaves the decision open, almost none where the text decides. Audit the model on the task we use it for.


PLAYGROUNDSame text, different name

The data are the Playground tool Same text, different name, here for one model, Llama 3.1 8B, the model of the cold open, at temperature 0.8. Hiring: four applicants with identical work histories; the name (and the origin it signals), the stated nationality, age, gender and university were drawn independently for each of them, 1,070 rounds. Coding: forty real posts, each coded under sixty randomly drawn authors.
Read the top panel against the dashed line. If the CV were all that counted, every group would be ranked first 25 times in 100, give or take three by chance. A woman is ranked first almost twice as often as a man, a 30-year-old more than twice as often as a 55-year-old, and a degree from North America or Western Europe more than twice as often as one from South Asia. If the top-ranked applicant were the one invited, men here would be selected at about half the rate of women; US employment guidelines treat anything below four fifths of the most-selected group’s rate as evidence of adverse impact (the “four-fifths rule”).
Then the bottom panel, the same model and the same kind of names on a coding task: the dots sit on the line. Nationality and name origin, not drawn here, move the share coded negative by about a point at most; for moderation (“should a moderator review this post?”) by up to three.
The comparison is the point. With identical CVs the name is the only thing that differs, so the model’s preferences decide the outcome. In coding the post decides, and the name nudges. Real CVs differ, but close calls are exactly where the name would decide. The other two models in the tool lean the same way on gender and university and differ on age; Qwen 3.8 refused most ranking rounds, which the tool shows. All of this holds for these models and these designs; for any other model or task, it has to be measured.

title: CADC
text:
What you can now do

Say what a transformer does with a sentence: tokens, vectors, attention, a stack of layers, one probability per next token
Explain why a classification by a language model is a next-token prediction, and what that implies for the “confidence” it reports
Write the loop: a codebook in a prompt, a schema, a map over texts, a confusion matrix against a gold set
Name what moves a prompt’s score — wording, examples, model, temperature, output format, version — and how each is measured
Place dictionary, classifier, embeddings and language model on one gold set, and say which you would defend and why


Four generations of method scored the same way. That was the plan of the course, and homework 4 does it on your own gold set.

title: Classifiers & neural nets
text:
WEEK 3 · CLASSIFIERS


Part I · Week 3 of 8 · the 2010s, then 2013+




This week a machine writes the word list. You hand it your labels, it learns the weights, and then it learns the training set a little too well.




ObtainRepresentClassifyValidatesame two steps as last week, a different machine doing them






THE LECTURE



Monday · 105 minutes



Stop declaring the weights and let labelled texts supply them. Train, test and overfitting; one tidymodels workflow from split to F1; a network learning in front of you and then taken apart; words as vectors, and what changing the representation does to a classifier that stays the same.
Open the slides  Download PDF 



The deck opens in its own tab so you can keep it beside this page. Day, time and room for every session are on the schedule.




THE LABS · BOTH MANDATORY




Tuesday · Lab A · 105 min



One tidymodels pipeline end to end on the lecture’s abstracts, and three algorithms on one test set. Then try to beat van Atteveldt et al. on their own headlines.
Open Lab A




Thursday · Lab B · 105 min



Neighbours, analogies and why good sits next to bad. Then embeddings instead of word counts, for the same classifier, and a classifier of your own for resolution tweets (Homework 3).
Open Lab B




Each lab opens with a ten-minute check-in you do on your own. It is not graded, but you need at least six of the eight to pass (how that works).





Playground · optional · any time



Three tools: the machine writing the word list, the machine learning the data too well, and the space the words end up living in.



The same word list as last week, except the data writes it. Follow the weights as they appear, trade precision against recall, and see train and test pull apart.
Open naive Bayes →



As you raise model complexity, training error falls while test error turns back up. A “leak the test set” toggle makes the reported number lie.
Open overfitting →



50,000 real word vectors. Search any word for its true neighbours, try king − man + woman, and check the two-dimensional map against the real distances.
Open embeddings →







THE HOMEWORK



3



Homework 3 of 4 · due Sunday · required



A classifier that finds one category of resolution tweets, trained once on word counts and once on word embeddings, and what accuracy hides. You start it in Lab B.
Open the homework in Lab B How homework works
